A useful independent benchmark for acceptance criteria: the arc42 quality model sets enterprise-ERP usability thresholds of **≥80% of ≥12 first-time users completing 5 predefined core tasks within 30 minutes using only in-application guidance, ≥75% per-task success, SUS ≥68** (quality.arc42.org). These are concrete numbers you can write into vendor acceptance criteria.

A methodological warning from a 2026 pre-post ERP redesign study (205 paired evaluations, higher-education context): task time fell 364.84 → 220.86 s and errors fell 74.6%, but correlations between **perceived usability and objective performance were only weak-to-moderate**. Satisfaction surveys are not proficiency evidence — instrument the transactions themselves.

### 5.3 Training-time reduction ranges, by evidence tier

- **Controlled/consulting sources:** 25–40% faster learning curves (JENRS synthesis); ~40% MTC reduction via event-driven in-ERP microlearning (Upscend); 40% task-time reduction via user-centered redesign (Aalto).
- **Vendor-aligned sources:** up to 50–60% training-time reduction claims (SAP Screen Personas, Fiori partner data); 77% new-hire time reduction (Epicor); 68% error reduction with Fiori+Personas+RPA (WJARR single-author paper, unclear peer review).
- **Planning assumption:** budget for **30–50% reductions in training time, task time, and error rates** on redesigned role-based views; treat 60–80% figures as upper bounds contingent on excellent secondary-path design and proficiency-based training. And scale the supervisor-cohort baseline by the Rice meta-analysis: older trainees need roughly **1.25 SD more elapsed training time**, so calendar plans built on young-user benchmarks will under-deliver.

ERP training budgets run **5–50% of implementation budgets** (scitepress.org 2012 training study) — for this cohort, plan toward the upper half, and prefer floor-integrated training: best-in-class organizations are 66% more likely to sustain ERP user groups and 55% train new employees after initial go-live, integrating training with daily work rather than pulling people off the floor (AllenComm).

---

## 6. Role-Based Views vs. Comprehensive Dashboards: The Synthesis

**The role-tier model is the documented best practice.** Manufacturing dashboard literature (ifactoryapp.com, connect981.com, thickdot.com) converges on three tiers over a single data foundation:

| Role | Time horizon | Primary decisions | Critical metrics | Aggregation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operator | Seconds–minutes | Stop/continue the line | OEE, scrap, downtime cause | Real-time, single line |
| **Supervisor** | **Minutes–hours** | **Resequence jobs, escalate, reassign labor** | **Schedule adherence, WIP aging, downtime, scrap, labor variance** | **Shift- and line-rolled** |
| Plant manager | Days–months | Capacity, cost, capital | Trended cost, throughput, OTD | Plant-rolled, weekly/monthly |

"Give an operator a director's dashboard and they'll ignore it within a week; give a director an operator's dashboard and they'll drown in cycle-time noise" (ifactoryapp.com). The implementation pitfall: three separate reporting pipelines drift apart within a year — build the data foundation once, aggregate three times.

**The quantitative case against comprehensive dashboards:**

- Dashboards averaging **15+ KPIs see 40% lower interaction rates** than those with 5–7 focused metrics (ThickDot operator-dashboard research; cybsoftware.com independently recommends "the 5–7 metrics that directly impact daily decisions").

# The Anthropology of Gift Economies: From the Kula Ring to the Blockchain

## A Literature Review

---

## Direct Answer and Central Argument

A century of gift-economy scholarship — from Malinowski's Trobriand ethnography (1922) through Mauss's *Essai sur le don* (1925), Sahlins's reciprocity typology (1972), and the feminist corrections of Weiner (1976, 1992) and Strathern (1988) — does not face a simple verdict from contemporary digital practice. The evidence across open-source software, social-media attention economies, and cryptocurrency governance supports a differentiated conclusion:

1. **Open-source software most directly extends Mauss** — but modifies him in a way he did not anticipate: the software gift is given not by suspending property but by *reconfiguring* it (copyleft, the GPL). What circulates is a meta-gift: the legal and technical capacity to produce further gifts (Kelty 2008, *Two Bits*, https://twobits.net/pub/Kelty-TwoBits.pdf).
2. **Social-media attention economies place the greatest strain on classical theory.** They look Maussian in form (Likes, mentions, shares as recognition-gifts) but function as extraction: Fourcade and Kluttz's "accumulation by gift" describes a regime in which the digital gift "masks the structural asymmetry between giver and gifted… permits the creation of the new commodity of personal data, obfuscates its true value, and naturalizes its private appropriation" (*Big Data & Society*, 2020, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092). This directly violates Sahlins's reading of the *hau*: "one man's gift should not be another man's capital."
3. **Cryptocurrency is the most theoretically generative case because it re-engineers the material conditions the classical binary presupposed.** Blockchain reintroduces rivalry and alienability into a domain of digital abundance, "at the expense of the non-rivalry that used to characterize information goods" (HICSS Tribal Governance paper, https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstreams/4f9b5036-92e9-4920-839c-90264d63a8a3/download). Attempts to algorithmically encode Mauss's three obligations in smart contracts and token governance repeatedly reproduce plutocracy — the 2016 DAO collapse ($50 million drained) and the Giveth ethnography's finding that an anti-neoliberal DAO "paradoxically reproduce[d] and extend[ed] many of the same conditions they seek to overcome" are the emblematic results.

Across all three domains, **Gregory's 1982 gift/commodity binary is the principal casualty**: no digital phenomenon sits cleanly on either side. And the feminist critique is vindicated with almost laboratory precision — the most-cited survey figures show **1.5% of F/LOSS participants were women versus 28% in comparable proprietary technical roles** (an ~18.7× disparity), and women's OSS labor concentrates in the invisible maintenance work that, exactly as Weiner showed for Trobriand women's *doba*, the prestige economy fails to register.

The strongest synthesis the literature supports: digital gift economies do not refute classical theory — they expose its constitutive tensions and specify the precise mechanisms by which gift logics are simultaneously activated and captured.

---

## Part I: The Classical Foundations

### 1. Malinowski and the Kula (1922): The Foundational Case

Bronisław Malinowski's *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922) established the kula as the paradigm case of non-market exchange and simultaneously founded the method — participant observation — that made it legible (full text: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/55822/55822-h/55822-h.htm). The system's parameters are precise:

- **Scale**: the kula spans **18 island communities** of the Massim archipelago, including the Trobriands, and involves **thousands of individuals** (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kula_ring).
- **Structure**: two classes of valuables circulate in opposite directions around a closed ring — **red shell-disc necklaces (*soulava*) clockwise**, **white shell armbands (*mwali*) counterclockwise** — exchanged between permanent dyadic partners (*karayta'u*) according to fixed rules, magic, and public ceremony. An opening gift (*vaga*) must be closed by a return gift (*yotile*); no one keeps a valuable for long.
- **The puzzle**: Malinowski's organizing question — why would men "risk life and limb to travel across huge expanses of dangerous ocean to give away what appear to be worthless trinkets?" — was answered politically: the valuables are "of high value, but of no real use," neither consumable nor media of exchange outside the ceremonial system; they are held "in order to acquire prestige and rank" (https://www.britannica.com/topic/kula-trade), and the system is "clearly linked to political authority."

Malinowski's most consequential analytic move was the distinction between **kula** (ceremonial, relationship-constituting exchange) and ***gimwali*** (utilitarian barter and haggling) — two coexisting spheres within one society. Frazer's preface framed the stakes: kula is "not based on a simple calculation of utility, of profit and loss," and the book was meant to lay to rest the phantom of "Primitive Economic Man." This empirical separation of a prestige sphere from a commodity sphere is the seed of the entire gift/commodity debate.

Three points about the kula's afterlife matter for the contemporary argument:

- **Scholarly footprint**: Macintyre's (1983) bibliography lists **625 publications** on the kula — it became, per Ekeh (1974) and Gregory (1982), the canonical example of the difference between "economic" and "social" exchange (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S037887330700072X).
- **Emergent order**: the ring "has neither been intentionally created by the individual actors nor designed by a central authority. It is the unintended by-product of so many doings" — which is precisely the self-image of open-source protocol governance two generations later.
- **Historical caveats**: Steinmüller argues the "peaceful" kula Malinowski observed was partly an artifact of colonial pacification, which redirected prestige goods from warfare into exchange; Persson's 1983 re-examination (*Oceania* 54(1): 32–47) documented substantial variability in the ring's extent. The classical case was never as stable as its textbook version.

### 2. Mauss (1925): The Gift as Total Social Fact

Mauss's *Essai sur le don* appeared in the 1925 *L'Année Sociologique* — the first issue after World War I, which had killed **twelve of Mauss's colleagues, including his uncle Émile Durkheim**. The essay was thus political from birth; Jane Guyer's expanded 2016 translation (HAU Books, https://haubooks.org/the-gift/) restores its framing as a mixed-economy manifesto whose closing hope was that peoples and classes might learn "how to confront one another without massacring each other." David Graeber stresses this against readings of Mauss as a gift-economy utopian.

The core claims:

- **Total prestation**: in "archaic societies," exchange occurs not between individuals but between collectivities, and what circulates includes "ceremonies, feasts, rites, military services, women, children, dances, celebrations, fairs" — the gift is a *fait social total*, at once religious, juridical, moral, political, and economic.
- **The triple obligation**: to **give**, to **receive**, and to **reciprocate**. Gifts are "in theory voluntary, in reality given and reciprocated obligatorily." To refuse is to reject the relationship; to fail to repay is to lose honor and standing.
- **The *hau***: drawing on the Māori informant Tamati Ranapiri (via Elsdon Best), Mauss argued that the thing given carries "the spirit of the gift" — "to present something to someone is to present something of oneself." The *taonga* seeks return to its origin; the counter-gift (*utu*) is the *hau* of the first gift. This thesis of the **inalienability of the gift** became the pivot of all subsequent theory.
- **Potlatch and agonistic giving**: Northwest Coast chiefs competed through conspicuous giving and even destruction of wealth; giving more than a rival could repay placed him in permanent subordination. Gift economies were never Edenic alternatives to markets — they were arenas of hierarchy and political struggle.

The **Malinowski–Mauss fault line** still structures the field: Malinowski individualized kula exchange (strategic prestige-seeking by rational actors); Mauss socialized it (the obligation is structural and spiritual, not psychological). Is gift exchange fundamentally self-interested — closer to the market than it appears — or fundamentally relational, an alternative to it?

**The *hau* controversy** produced the field's most instructive secondary debate (catalogued in Sahlins, *Stone Age Economics*, https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf):

- **Lévi-Strauss** (introduction to Mauss's *Sociologie et anthropologie*, 1950): Mauss was "mystified by the native"; the *hau* is merely how a people *represents* the unconscious structural necessity of reciprocity — a "mystic cement" gluing together what exchange as a unified principle already explains.
- **Raymond Firth**: Mauss conflated distinct senses of *hau*; the real sanctions are secular — the desire to continue useful relations and maintain prestige and power.
- **Sahlins's reconstruction**: *hau* means something like "**return on**" or "**product of**" — the yield of a good, as the *hau* of a forest is its productiveness. Ranapiri's three-party example demonstrates turnover: "the gift has had issue." The ethical principle is that **the fruits of a gift must flow back to the original giver** — a distinction between gift and capital that, as Part III shows, reads as a direct anticipation of platform appropriation.
- **Bill Maurer** (2016, *HAU* 6(2), https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.14318/hau6.2.017): the "force in the thing" in Mauss derives not from Polynesia at all but from Mauss's construction of the Roman legal institution of *nexum* (debt-bondage) — a reminder that the canonical "indigenous" concept was always partly a European legal-theoretical artifact.

### 3. Sahlins (1972): Reciprocity Indexed by Social Distance

Marshall Sahlins's "On the Sociology of Primitive Exchange" (1965; Chapter 5 of *Stone Age Economics*, 1972) fused Mauss, Polanyi, and Lévi-Strauss into the field's most durable typology. The master variable is not the object exchanged but the **social (kinship) distance** between transactors, yielding three modes arrayed on a continuum:

1. **Generalized reciprocity** — "what Mauss called 'communism'": diffuse, solidary transfers among close kin; no ledger, no stipulated or timed return (household sharing, forager meat distribution).
2. **Balanced reciprocity** — a middle zone "governed by fairness": direct exchange of equivalents within a specified time, "whether in the exchange of sisters or the tit-for-tat murders of the blood-feud" (kula partnerships, inter-village trade, bride-price).
3. **Negative reciprocity** — "attempting to get something for nothing": haggling, barter, theft — the arm's-length pole where social bonds are weakest.

Sahlins's portable formulations: "If friends make gifts, gifts make friends" — material flow underwrites social relations — and the scope caveat that the typology "applies only insofar as the economy and social relations have not been modified by the historic penetration of states" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology)). Sillitoe's extension by **sphere of production** — subsistence goods circulate under generalized reciprocity while externally sourced wealth objects are competitively exchanged for status — anticipates the deliberate sphere-separation engineering of cryptocurrency commons (Part III).

David Graeber's foreword to the Routledge Classics edition notes the scheme's adoption "by archaeologists, historians, classicists, literary theorists, political theorists, psychologists, art historians, sociologists, philosophers, and students of religion," while "the only discipline that has never made significant use of the theoretical tools provided in this collection is economics itself" (https://davidgraeber.org/articles/foreword-to-the-routledge-classics-edition-stone-age-economics-marshall-sahlins/). Graeber's own reformulation — **everyday communism / exchange / hierarchy** ("On the Moral Grounds of Economic Relations," *Journal of Classical Sociology* 2014, https://doi.org/10.1177/1468795X13494719) — grounds the tripartition in moral baseline rather than kinship distance, arguing everyday communism ("from each according to their abilities, to each according to their needs") is the default of all human sociality, not an exotic primitive residue.

### 4. Gregory (1982): The Binary Formalized

Christopher Gregory's *Gifts and Commodities* (1982) gave the distinction its canonical form: "In a class-based society the objects of exchange tend to assume the alienated form of a commodity… In a clan-based society the objects of exchange tend to assume the nonalienated form of a gift." Commodity exchange presupposes **reciprocal independence** (transactors as strangers; the transaction can be forgotten); gift exchange presupposes **reciprocal dependence**, measured by Sahlins's kinship distance; in gift economies "things and people assume the social form of persons," in commodity economies, of objects (http://haubooks.org/viewbook/gifts-and-commodities/10_ch03). Gregory's crucial empirical finding — that in colonial Papua New Guinea **gift and commodity economies expanded simultaneously**, with a "paradoxical efflorescence of gift exchange" under capitalism rather than its displacement — is the single most important bridge to the digital cases: capitalist commodity value is "everywhere created through tapping and transforming non-capitalist social relations."

---

## Part II: Feminist Critiques — Gendered Labor in Gift Exchange

The feminist literature demonstrated that the classical canon rested on an unexamined base of gendered, invisible labor — and its findings turn out to be the most empirically portable part of the entire tradition.

### 1. Rubin (1975): Women as Gifts, Not Givers

Gayle Rubin's "The Traffic in Women" turned Lévi-Strauss against himself: reading *The Elementary Structures of Kinship* (1949) as a gloss on Mauss, she showed that the incest taboo functions as "a rule obliging the mother, sister, or daughter to be given to others. It is the supreme rule of the gift" (https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/pdf/rubin_the_traffic_in_women.pdf). Marriage is "a most basic form of gift exchange, in which it is women who are the most precious of gifts." The classic theory of reciprocity **presupposes women as objects of exchange rather than subjects** — the founding observation of the "sex/gender system" concept.

### 2. Weiner (1976, 1992): The Forgotten Dimension and Keeping-While-Giving

Annette Weiner's restudy of the Trobriands is the most direct ethnographic correction to Malinowski. On her first day of fieldwork, three-quarters of a mile from Malinowski's own site, she witnessed a mortuary ceremony (*sagali*) in which women distributed **up to 30,000 banana-leaf bundles in a single day, each nominally worth about one Australian cent** — wealth of which Malinowski's account said almost nothing (*Women of Value, Men of Renown*, 1976). These bundles and fiber skirts (*doba*) were **women's wealth**: made, exchanged, and controlled by women, embodying sexuality, reproduction, and nurture — "a cosmic statement of regeneration." Male yam exchange and female bundle exchange were interlocked: a man gardens not for himself but for his sister and her husband, and husbands must help wives accumulate wealth for the *sagali*.

*Inalienable Possessions: The Paradox of Keeping-While-Giving* (1992, https://www.ucpress.edu/books/inalienable-possessions/paper) generalized the finding into theory: the theoretical fixation on reciprocity obscured the more fundamental politics of **keeping**. Inalienable possessions — objects, myths, sacred knowledge "imbued with cosmological significance" that must not be given, or if circulated must finally return — anchor rank and authority. Her programmatic claim: "the motivation for reciprocity is centered not in the gift per se, but in the authority vested in keeping inalienable possessions… the authentication of difference rather than the balance of equivalence [is] the fundamental feature of exchange." She also revised Mauss on the *hau*: "not all gifts must be returned. Only gifts that are 'immoveable property' can become inalienable gifts."

The framework was contested. Jonathan Friedman's review called its architecture "vague and often self-contradictory"; a sharper ANU critique ("Inalienable ethnography") argued the paradox "is more appropriately seen as deriving from Western presuppositions of individual boundedness, subjectivity, possession, ownership, and hierarchy." Margaret Jolly criticized Weiner for essentializing "an unchanging Trobriand order" and timeless female values.

### 3. Strathern (1988): The Dividual and the Critique of Comparison Itself

Marilyn Strathern's *The Gender of the Gift* (1988, https://www.ucpress.edu/book/9780520072022/the-gender-of-the-gift) radicalized the critique in both directions. Against Western anthropologists *and* feminist scholars alike, she argued that categories like "exploitation," "oppression," "labor," "society," and "the individual" are Western gendered constructs that mis-describe Melanesia. Melanesian persons are **dividuals** — partible, constituted by the detachable substances and relationships that circulate in exchange; gender is a mode of relational differentiation (among the Melpa, production of trade goods versus transaction), not a fixed attribute of bounded individuals.

David Lipset's rejoinder ("The 'Dividual Androgyne' and Me") charged that Strathern mistook "a virulently anti-female ideology… for benign accommodation between the sexes," and that the dividual "paradoxically affirms Lévi-Strauss' classic demonstration… that 'the gender of the gift' is invariably female." A further critique ("Controlling Fictions") framed the dividual model as "ideological relativism… fraught with dangerous political consequences." The **Weiner–Strathern disagreement** — extend reciprocity theory by adding keeping (Weiner) versus reject the imported categories altogether (Strathern) — remains unresolved and, as one review put it, "continues to haunt contemporary feminist anthropology."

### 4. Extensions: Joy, Bourdieu, Wainberg

Morny Joy's *Women and the Gift* argues the very architecture of the gift positions women as "the given… or as the all-giving in the mode of self-abnegation occasioned by infinite care" — feminine subjectivity as giver is excluded by design. Pierre Bourdieu cut across the debate by treating the gift as structured misrecognition: "The objective truth of the gift is exchange; its subjective truth is disinterestedness" — economic capital converted to symbolic capital through collective denial of the economic (https://shs.cairn.info/article/E_RDM_052_0074/pdf?lang=en). Romina Wainberg (2023, *Feminist Theory*) extended the critique to Amazonian perspectivism, arguing Viveiros de Castro's unmarked perspective is male and that both perspectivism and Western objectivism are "made possible by the erasure of women's capacity for transcendence."

---

## Part III: Contemporary Practices as Test Cases

### 1. Open-Source Software: Mauss Extended — or Superseded?

**The gift-culture thesis.** Eric Raymond imported the anthropological vocabulary directly: *The Cathedral and the Bazaar* (1997) contrasted proprietary "cathedral" development with the Linux "bazaar" (Linus's Law: "given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow"), and *Homesteading the Noosphere* (1998) declared open source "a 'gift culture' in which members compete for status by giving things away… gift cultures are adaptations not to scarcity but to abundance. In gift cultures, social status is determined not by what you control but by what you give away" (http://www.catb.org/~esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/homesteading/ar01s06.html). Because code is reproducible at near-zero marginal cost, the operative scarcities are attention, reputation, and standing — mapping directly onto Maussian prestige.

**Anthropological refinements.** Christopher Kelty's ethnography *Two Bits* (2008) supplies the deepest analysis: free software constitutes a **recursive public** — "a public that is vitally concerned with the material and practical maintenance and modification of the technical, legal, practical, and conceptual means of its own existence as a public." The decisive point: software is given **by reconfiguring property (copyleft), not by suspending it** — the gift's defining feature is its license, a dimension classical gift theory, forged among non-propertied exchange systems, never theorized. David Zeitlyn (2003, "Gift Economies in the Development of Open Source Software") adds that developer subgroups parallel lineages, governed by an "axiom of kinship amity" in which direct calculation is inappropriate and Bourdieu's symbolic capital tracks reputation; Bergquist and Ljungberg (2001) show "the giver gets power from giving away," with gift dynamics operating as peer-review quality control. Kastrinou-Theodoropoulou's ethnography makes the strongest claim: "Like a modern-day kula ring, the Linux code… one cannot keep it for one's self, it contains obligations and a promise of future reciprocity."

**The strongest challenge.** Greger Petersen and others argue FOSS is **not** a gift economy but **social sharing**: the Maussian three-party structure and the obligation to receive are missing when code is "left at a publicly accessible place for anyone to take," given to "the community," not to a particular partner. Dave Elder-Vass likewise notes many digital goods are available "without any obligation to reciprocate."

**Resolution**: the panel evidence supports a split verdict. Among core developers — where code review, pull requests, credit, and reputation operate — the exchange is recognizably **balanced reciprocity** in Sahlins's middle circle, and Raymond's prestige account holds. At the point of anonymous mass consumption, the Maussian structure dissolves into sharing. Meanwhile **corporate co-optation** reproduces Weiner's keeping-while-giving with precision: firms give away peripheral components while retaining the platform layer — "the wealth of open cultural production relies on combining multiple dimensions of gifting with fiscal and hidden forms of capital" (First Monday Blender study, https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/download/6944/5627).

**Gender: the feminist critique confirmed quantitatively.**

- **1.5% of F/LOSS participants were women versus 28% in technical roles in proprietary-software firms** (https://culturedigitally.org/2012/06/engendering-change-gender-advocacy-in-open-source/) — an ~18.7× disparity, roughly a 97% shortfall from parity.
- A 2022 systematic review of **51 articles (2000–2021)** found only ~5% of projects had women core developers; women authored **under 5% of pull requests** but had equal or higher acceptance rates (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3510460).
- A 2025 study of 20 popular GitHub projects found active female contributors under 10%, with men over-represented in the top decile (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10664-025-10653-x).
- Dawn Nafus's "'Patches don't have gender'" shows how "openness" ideologically "separat[es] persons from one another and reliev[es] them of obligations… created in the course of other forms of gift exchange," de-legitimizing the social ties needed for women's inclusion (https://doi.org/10.1177/1461444811422887). CSCW's invisible-labor literature and AoIR's 2026 findings confirm women's contributions concentrate in maintenance and stability work — rendered invisible "because they take place out of sight, or because they lack physical form."

This is Weiner's finding replicated in digital infrastructure: the prestige economy of visible gifts rests on gendered labor it does not register.

### 2. Social Media Attention Economies: The Gift as Extraction

**Recognition-gifts.** One strand reads the Like button and Twitter Mention Maussianly: "gift exchange has nothing to do with goods exchange, but with mutual recognition," producing a "Like economy" — "the interference between gift exchange and market economy which is daily at work online" (*Theory, Culture & Society*, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0263276415619474).

**Accumulation by gift.** The critical counterweight is Fourcade and Kluttz's "A Maussian Bargain" (2020): against "accumulation by dispossession," they note enrollment is experienced as benign — "signing up for a 'free' service, responding to a 'friend's' invitation, or being encouraged to 'share'." Digital gifts feature "signs of liberality, a fuzzy temporality, and an absence of commensuration," and the resulting relation "masks the structural asymmetry between giver and gifted… permits the creation of the new commodity of personal data, obfuscates its true value, and naturalizes its private appropriation." Nachtwey and Schaupp (2024, https://doi.org/10.1177/20539517241259639) formalize the mechanism as **three-step data commodification** — appropriation as use-value, secondary commodification decoupled from use-value, and cybernetization (selling behavioral influence) — and relocate exploitation from the individual to "the community of those who interact in a particular field."

**Platform-native gifting.** TikTok ethnography finds virtual gifts in "dual manifestation": they subjectify (constituting the influencer's recognized self) while the platform "monitors and calculates the gifts… acting like a real bureaucracy that classifies and ranks users" — monetization of the self within "an economic system centered on the attention of others, a perishable resource" (https://revistasociologieromaneasca.ro/sr/article/view/1809). Derrida- and Bataille-influenced work concludes gift exchange "persists not as a pre-capitalist residue but as a constitutive feature of platform capitalism," structured by "instability, contradiction and impossibility."

**Ethnographic correctives.** Golub et al. (2021) on Solomon Islanders' Facebook Buy-and-Sell groups show platform use adapted to "moral economic practices that emphasize the accumulation of wealth not in a capitalist, but in a relational sense" — co-presence of gift and market, as Mauss and Gregory would predict. Work on KakaoTalk, LINE, and WeChat (whose Hongbao enables "playful, communal monetary exchanges largely detached from traditional, obligation-driven gifting") proposes a "Channel-Oriented Gifting Cycle" that "extends classical gift-exchange theory" — the channel itself becomes part of the gift's meaning.

**Verdict**: attention economies are the strongest *challenge* to the classical model. The gift form is activated (recognition, fuzziness, obligation) while the substance is inverted — Sahlins's dictum that "one man's gift should not be another man's capital" is systematically violated, and Bourdieu's gift-as-misrecognition fits better than Mauss's gift-as-bond.

### 3. Cryptocurrency Governance: Engineering Scarcity, Encoding Obligation

**The technical pivot.** Before blockchain, digital goods were non-rival and abundant — the precondition for Raymond's gift culture. Blockchain makes it possible to "differentiate something from something else (like who owns a bitcoin) without relying on non-digital authorities," enabling a move "from openness and gift economy, well exemplified by FOSS, to a digitally native economy, **at the expense of the non-rivalry** that used to characterize information goods." Cryptocurrency thus *re-creates the scarcity and alienability conditions the gift/commodity distinction presupposed* — the deepest sense in which it "reinforces" classical models: it re-manufactures their material premises.

**Give-to-get and hybrid objects.** Airdrops distribute tokens "at zero cost"; "billions of dollars of tokens have been airdropped for reasons such as marketing and decentralisation" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00191-024-00874-6). Allen, Berg, and Lane distinguish three purposes — community building, regulatory protection, cryptoeconomic security — and note airdrops "have more similarities to equity than cash": the gift creates a claim on future governance and value, not merely a relational bond. Ethnographic work accordingly treats cryptocurrencies "as a hybrid — they hold the qualities of a gift (authority, name) and could be used to speculate with on the crypto stock-exchange (commodity)" — the "authority, name" attributes echoing Malinowski's named kula valuables.

**Commons governance.** "When Ostrom Meets Blockchain" (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3272329) identifies **six blockchain affordances** for commons governance: tokenization; formalization and decentralization of rules; autonomous automatization; decentralization of power over infrastructure; transparency; and codification of trust. The Ğ1/Duniter libre currency operationalizes Ostrom's principles with a **universal dividend** — a design best described in Weiner's terms as inalienable wealth held collectively but redistributed continuously. Rennie, Potts, and Tan's validator ethnography frames blockchain governance as an attempted transition "from a Limited Access Order to an Open Access Order." Merfield's LSE ethnography (two years' fieldwork) concludes Bitcoin and Ethereum communities "are not simply protest movements… but rather serious experiments in alternative forms of governance" (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/135613/1/Merfield_201649740.pdf).

**The failure modes.** The 2016 DAO collapse — **$50 million drained** through a code vulnerability — demonstrated that "immutable" smart contracts cannot accommodate the ambiguity and renegotiation social life requires. The Giveth ethnography (2025) found a DAO explicitly missioned to "dismantle hegemonic neoliberal structures" instead "paradoxically reproduce[d] and extend[ed] many of the same conditions": uncompensated labor sacrifice plus token-weighted **plutocracy**. A 2025 Frontiers review of DAOs against Ostrom's principles found token- and reputation-based mechanisms "susceptible to plutocracy, voter apathy, and collusion," with digital governance capable of replicating "neo-colonial dynamics in the Global South."

**Verdict**: cryptocurrency is the strongest evidence that **the moral dimension of gift exchange cannot be algorithmically formalized without losing what made it effective**. Encoding Mauss's three obligations in code does not eliminate power; it renders power opaque — a finding that confirms, rather than refutes, the classical insistence that gifts work through ambiguity, temporality, and embedded social relation.

---

## Part IV: Synthesis — Reinforce, Modify, or Replace?

**By domain**: FOSS *reinforces and modifies* Mauss (gift as social bond; but the bond is manufactured by license, and the circulating object is a meta-capacity). Attention economies *strain and invert* the model (gift rhetoric in the service of asymmetric extraction; "accumulation by gift" names a form that is neither Mauss's mutual obligation nor the market's terminal transaction). Cryptocurrency *re-engineers the binary's material premises* while demonstrating the non-transferability of gift morality into code.

**Across domains, the scoreboard by theorist**:

- **Gregory (1982) — principal casualty.** No digital phenomenon sits cleanly on either side of the gift/commodity line: code is given but legally constrained; the Like is simultaneously gift and surveillance instrument; tokens are simultaneously commodity and political voice. But Gregory's own finding — that gifts and commodities co-expand and convert into one another — turns out to be the most prescient single claim in the literature.
- **Sahlins — most portable.** The social-distance continuum maps onto digital contexts with surprising precision: generalized reciprocity within Discord servers and close-knit dev teams; balanced reciprocity in code review and pull requests; negative reciprocity in platform extraction. His scope caveat (the typology presumes economies unpenetrated by states) and Sillitoe's sphere analysis both find direct application in crypto sphere-engineering. What dissolves is the assumption that distance is kinship-geographic: a GitHub collaborator on another continent may be "closer" than a neighbor, with distance now algorithmically mediated.
- **Mauss — modified, not refuted.** The triple obligation persists wherever digital communities have durable membership; prestige-through-giving drives contribution from Linux to YouTube. The two genuine challenges are reproducibility (the gift's power no longer derives from material sacrifice or risk) and the pseudo-gift's third party (the platform) that is neither giver nor receiver in the cycle.
- **Weiner — quietly vindicated twice over.** Keeping-while-giving describes platform strategy (give services, keep data, algorithms, and attention metrics) and crypto design (collective inalienable wealth, continuous redistribution); and her core feminist finding — invisible gendered labor beneath visible male prestige exchange — is reproduced in FLOSS with measurable precision.
- **Strathern — unexpectedly prescient.** The dividual, composed of detachable circulating relations, reads as a description of the datafied platform subject; but Lipset's warning applies: celebrating the digital dividual risks mistaking an extractive ideology for benign relationality.
- **Bourdieu and Derrida — the rising interlocutors.** Where the digital gift functions as misrecognition (accumulation by gift), Bourdieu outperforms Mauss; where the "pure gift" is structurally unavailable, Derrida reframes gifting as the constitutive limit of platform capitalism rather than its residue.

**Three unresolved tensions** organize the research frontier: (1) whether gift and commodity are analytical types or historical residues; (2) whether feminist anthropology has resolved gendered labor — Weiner foregrounds women as producers of inalienable wealth, Strathern relocates gender to personhood itself, Lipset charges the dividual with concealing male ideology; (3) whether digital gifts reproduce or invert classical logics — the evidence supports *both, simultaneously, specified by mechanism* rather than a verdict for either.

**Notable blind spots in the reviewed literature**: minimal engagement with non-Anglophone anthropological traditions; underdeveloped postcolonial critique of the gift/commodity binary as itself a Western imposition; race and racialized labor in digital gift economies largely untreated relative to gender; legal-property analysis rarely extending beyond copyleft (data trusts, patent pools); and the environmental externalities of proof-of-work scarcity engineering treated only obliquely.

---

## Conclusion

Roughly a century after *Argonauts*, the kula remains anthropology's most-cited single ethnographic case — 625 publications and counting — but its analytical uses have multiplied beyond anything Malinowski anticipated. Mauss's *hau* provoked Sahlins's secular counter-reading ("one man's gift should not be another man's capital"); Lévi-Strauss universalized reciprocity while Firth secularized it; Gregory formalized the binary; Weiner exposed its gendered silences; Strathern challenged its ontology; Bourdieu drained it of naïve altruism. The contemporary digital applications are not merely new ethnographic sites for old theory: open source shows the gift can be *manufactured by property law*; attention economies show the gift can be *weaponized as extraction*; cryptocurrency shows the gift's moral substance *cannot be compiled*. The discipline that began by asking why men risked their lives to give away worthless trinkets now confronts systems in which billions of people give away attention, code, and data under the sign of the gift — and the classical canon, properly modified, remains the best available apparatus for seeing what is being kept.

---

# Cold-Weather Equipment Selection for a Mongolian Mining Operation at −40°C
## Caterpillar vs. Komatsu vs. Volvo CE — Excavators & Haul Trucks, with Russian/CIS Alternatives

---

## 1. Direct Answer and Recommended Strategy

**For a −40°C Mongolian mining fleet, the evidence supports a Caterpillar + Komatsu dual-brand strategy as the only low-risk foundation.** Both have full-service dealerships in Ulaanbaatar (Barloworld Mongolia for Cat, Transwest Mongolia for Komatsu), in-country parts warehouses and component rebuild centers, documented cold-weather packages, proven fleets operating in the South Gobi, and structured Mongolian-language training pipelines.

- **Haul trucks (primary):** Komatsu 930E-5 / HD1500-8 or Cat 793/785 with full Cold Weather Packages and "Fuel Optimized" (non-DEF) engine ratings. Komatsu has the strongest at-scale Mongolian track record (28× 930E-4SE at Oyu Tolgoi since August 2012); Cat has the deepest parts and rebuild infrastructure.
- **Excavators:** Cat 6040/6060 hydraulic shovels or Komatsu PC4000–PC7000 class with factory cold-weather packages (both documented operating at Mongolian mines).
- **Volvo CE: not recommended as a primary fleet.** No verifiable dedicated mining-equipment dealer, no published −40°C factory rating, a maximum rigid-hauler class of 95 t (R100E), and parts routed via third-party air freight from Mumbai (5–7 days). Volvo articulated haulers may earn a support-fleet role with on-site spares, but not production duty.
- **Russian/CIS alternative:** BelAZ is a legitimate, proven *supplement* — factory-rated −50°C across its line, 200+ units in Mongolia since the 1970s, and an official distributor (United BelAZ Machinery) with a ~16 billion MNT parts warehouse — but sanctions-driven engine-sourcing risk and weaker technology make it unsuitable as a sole source. UZTM-KARTEX electric rope shovels (rated to −60°C in northern variants) are a niche option where grid power exists.
- **Fuel procurement is as important as machine selection:** Mongolia imports ~95% of its diesel from Russia; you must contract Arctic-grade diesel per GOST R 55475-2013 (CFPP ≤ −44°C) and budget for ~50 kW/machine shore power for overnight pre-heating.

---

## 2. Summary Comparison Matrix

| Criterion | Caterpillar (Barloworld Mongolia) | Komatsu (Transwest Mongolia) | Volvo CE | BelAZ (CIS alternative) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Cold rating** | Standard −18°C; −32°C cold-start package; coolant/antifreeze to −50°C on mining trucks; arctic fluids available | KMG shovels rated to −50°C with pre-heating; factory hot-start options on trucks; proven at −40°C in Gobi and Scandinavia | No published −40°C rating; arctic oils recommended only | **Factory −50/+50°C** across product line |
| **UB dealer** | Barloworld Mongolia (Wagner Asia, est. 1996; acquired Feb 2020 for $216.8M); ~600 staff | Transwest Mongolia (est. 2009, exclusive rights; Sumitomo + SMS Equipment backing); ~203 staff | Only a small sales presence (Gansag/GSG LLC); Volvo *Trucks* is on-road only | United BelAZ Machinery (UBM), official distributor since 2012; ~160 staff |
| **Workshop / rebuild** | 975 m² UB shop, 9 lifts, cranes to 10T, Component Rebuild Center, S·O·S lab | Component rebuild shop (engines, transmissions, cylinders, electrics); 300+ rebuilds/yr; Khanbogd facility (2022) | None identified | 2,289 m² UB service base; generator/motor repair shops |
| **Parts in-country** | **~36,000 SKUs / ~2.76M units** across 4 branches; $130M/yr after-sales business | UB parts warehouse + undercarriage stock; remanufacturing relocated in-country | None; third-party air freight from Mumbai, 5–7 days | 16B MNT (~US$4.5M) warehouses in UB + Umnugovi |
| **Cold fuel strategy** | Fuel blender/heater; −50°C coolant; Fuel Optimized (no DEF) engines | Hot-start 220V options; heated body; non-emissionized engines (no DEF freeze risk) | DEF-dependent aftertreatment problematic; DEF freezes at −11°C | Simple engines; GOST arctic-fuel native design; SFC 196–201 g/kWh |
| **Training in Mongolia** | Wagner Training Institute (2001); ~150 technicians/6 intakes; 100% employment; Cat MTA | Transwest Technical Institute (2024); KGM co-delivered training; Mongolian-language instruction | None found | Factory training in Zhodino, Belarus |
| **Mongolian fleet proof** | Oyu Tolgoi (6060, 7495); Ulz Group 773E | **Oyu Tolgoi 28× 930E-4SE since 2012**; Erdenet 18× HD1500-8 | Minimal | 200+ units; Erdenet; 17× 75135 at Tavan Tolgoi (Gobi-spec) |
| **Sanctions/logistics risk** | None | None | None | **High** — Cummins/MTU engine sourcing constrained; secondary-sanction banking friction |
| **Relative cost** | High capex, low opex | High capex, low-mid opex | Medium-high capex, high support risk | Low capex (~$1M per 130-t truck), higher maintenance burden |

---

## 3. Reliable Operation at −40°C: Engineering Reality

### 3.1 The baseline: no machine in this comparison starts unaided at −40°C

Every OEM closes the −40°C gap the same way: external-power pre-heating of coolant, engine oil, hydraulic oil, and batteries, plus arctic-grade fluids and heated storage or idle-management infrastructure. What differs is how far each factory gets you out of the box.

### 3.2 Caterpillar

- Standard cold-start rating for large machines is **−18°C**; the optional cold-start package (e.g., battery-operated engine heater on the Cat 345/395) extends this to **−32°C** ([Cat 345 key features](https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20250618-aa054-f8b96), [Cat 395](https://www.cat.com/en_US/products/new/equipment/excavators/large-excavators/126440.html)). −40°C is 8°C below Cat's best published cold-start option — site infrastructure is mandatory regardless of brand.
- **Cold Weather Package** (documented on the 6040/6060 mining shovels): engine coolant heater, engine oil heater with thermostat, hydraulic oil heater with thermostat, hydraulic-oil cooler bypass valves, fuel blender (mixes #1/#2 diesel to hit target cloud point), auxiliary cab pre-heater; requires ~**50 kW of 400V three-phase external power**. Recommended below −10°C ([Cat 6040 spec](https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20210601-35dac-75766)).
- Mining trucks (785/789D/793/797F): antifreeze/coolant protection to **−50°C (−58°F)**, 240V coolant and oil heaters, fuel filter with water separator **and fuel heater**, engine-delay shutdown timer (prevents turbo coking), air-start option, exhaust body heating, heated mirrors, Mesabi frost-resistant radiator, deluxe cold-weather cab ([Cat 785 specalog](https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20240909-c65b1-7536b), [789D specalog](https://www.eltrakbulgaria.com/uploads/Products/NewSeries/MiningTrucks/789D.pdf), [Cat 793 spec](https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20221205-dfa81-b707a)). One caveat: the standard cab heater is rated to −30°C ambient — spec the auxiliary/deluxe cold-weather cab at −40°C.
- The 6020B shovel's modular field assembly was validated at −30°C with no schedule penalty ([Caterpillar CM20160201](https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20160201-48357-52819)).
- Cat 6060 shovels and 7495 rope shovels already operate at Oyu Tolgoi ([OT GET procurement EOI](https://www.ot.mn/en/procurement/eoi/supply-of-g-e-t-for-mining-equipment)).

### 3.3 Komatsu

- Komatsu Mining Germany explicitly rates hydraulic shovels for **−50°C** with pre-heating of engine, water, hydraulic oil, and lubrication. Below −25°C, normal operation halts and external pre-heating engages; hydraulic oil must reach −20°C (~1000 cSt) before the main engine starts, with crankshaft speed held at half-rated until viscosity falls to 100–10 cSt. Arctic builds use special steel grades for cast/forged structures and bolted joints, insulated cabling, and cold-rated high-pressure hoses ([OneMine: Adaptation of hydraulic shovels for arctic temperature of Yakutia region](https://onemine.org/documents/adaptation-of-hydraulic-shovels-for-arctic-temperature-of-yakutia-region)).
- Trucks (930E-5/930E-5SE, 980E-5, 860E-1K): 220V hot-start heaters for engine oil, coolant, and hydraulic oil; heated dump bodies; radiator shutters; cold-weather suspensions. The 980E-5 routes engine exhaust through the body to prevent payload freeze-sticking — engineered for Canadian oil sands, directly transferable to the Gobi ([Komatsu 930E-5](https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/930e-5), [980E-5](https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/980e-5), [Komatsu tech report 2017](https://www.komatsu.jp/en/-/media/home/aboutus/innovation/technology/techreport/2017/en/180330_06e.pdf)).
- PC4000-6 shovel: KIM HOTSTART coolant heating, heated engine-oil reserve tank, and an engine-independent HYDRONIC cab water heater with programmable start times — a genuine shift-start advantage at −40°C ([PC4000-6 manual](https://www.manualslib.com/manual/3641219/Komatsu-Pc4000-6.html?page=151)). Komatsu also builds factory "Extreme Cold Terrain Spec" excavators (e.g., PC400-7) rather than dealer retrofits.
- **Reliability caveat:** a study of Komatsu D-375A/A5 dozers in northern Russia found component failure rates rise 2×–6× at low temperature, with −25°C the embrittlement threshold for rubber/polymer parts ([study](https://exa.ai/library/publication/9vvm1yl0lv4)). Arctic packages are not optional at −40°C; they are the difference between rated life and chronic downtime.
- **Field proof:** 28× Komatsu 930E-4SE have operated at Oyu Tolgoi since August 2012 ([OT open-pit mine](https://en.eot.mn/open-pit-mine)); Erdenet accumulated ~16,000 hours on HD1500-8s over two years, reporting +7.9% haulage volume and −5.8% cost per m³ ([Erdenet Today](https://erdenettoday.mn/art/7169)). Komatsu's Mine 4D platform runs 24/7 at Kevitsa, Finland at −40°C ([International Mining](https://im-mining.com/2026/05/12/komatsus-mine-4d-technology-offering-real-time-visibility-at-kevitsa-operation/)).

### 3.4 Volvo CE

- No published factory −40°C rating was found for any Volvo CE excavator or hauler. Cold-weather guidance covers arctic-grade oils, nightly fuel-tank filling, water-separator draining, and DPF regeneration before cold shutdown — useful practice, not an arctic certification ([Volvo CE winter guide](https://www.volvoce.com/en-ca/discover/guides-and-advice/2021/diesel-engine-dos-and-donts-to-prep-for-winter-season/)).
- Structurally, Volvo's Tier 4/Stage V aftertreatment (EGR, DOC, DPF, SCR) adds cold failure modes, and DEF freezes at −11°C. The largest rigid hauler, the R100E, is 95 t — below the 130–290 t classes that dominate Mongolian production mining. Volvo articulated haulers are genuinely excellent in rough, cold terrain and could serve a support-fleet role, but the product line does not cover primary production haulage.

### 3.5 BelAZ (CIS alternative) — the deepest factory cold rating

BelAZ publishes a **−50°C to +50°C operating envelope** across its mining range, with liquid pre-start heaters and pneumatic starting:

| Model | Payload | Engine | Specific fuel consumption |
|---|---|---|---|
| BelAZ-75710 | 450 t | 2× MTU DD 16V4000 | 198 g/kWh |
| BelAZ-75605 | 360 t | 3,300 hp | 196 g/kWh |
| BelAZ-75306 | 220 t | Cummins QSK 60 | — |
| BelAZ-7513A/75131 | 130–136 t | MTU 12V4000 / Cummins KTA50-C (1,600 hp) | 201 g/kWh |
| BelAZ-7558B | 90 t | Cummins KTA 38-C with pre-heating | — |

([BelAZ-75710](https://belaz.by/upload/iblock/651/BELAZ_75710.pdf), [75306](https://belaz.by/upload/iblock/d44/BELAZ_75306.pdf), [7513A](https://belaz.by/upload/iblock/3a9/BELAZ_7513A.pdf), [7558](https://belaz.by/upload/iblock/5ce/BELAZ_7558_English.pdf), [75605](https://belaz.by/upload/iblock/a29/_75605.pdf)). SFC of 196–201 g/kWh is competitive with Western diesel-electric drives (190–200 g/kWh class) at nominal power. The 17 BelAZ-75135s delivered to Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi were explicitly configured "for the extreme climatic conditions of the Gobi Desert" ([Belarus Minprom](https://minprom.gov.by/belazy-serii-7513-budut-rabotat-v-pustyne-gobi/)).

For completeness: Liebherr's R 9150 Arctic Package is validated at ALROSA's Udachny mine at **−55°C to +40°C** ([brochure](https://budmain.org.ua/upload/filescatalog/items/0/06aff05bd8ef30d68369e7a787c0.pdf)), and UZTM-KARTEX's EKG-20KM-KhL rope shovel is rated to **−60°C** with steel impact-tested at −50°C — the most extreme rating found, but in a rope-shovel-only product line.

---

## 4. Local Service Centers in Ulaanbaatar

### 4.1 Caterpillar — Barloworld Mongolia (deepest footprint)

Wagner Asia Equipment (est. 1996; 100% US-invested) was Caterpillar's best-performing Eurasia/CIS dealer for seven consecutive years before Barloworld acquired it in February 2020 for US$216.8M ([IM-Mining](https://im-mining.com/2020/02/04/barloworld-makes-plans-establish-eurasia-equipment-unit/), [Mongolian Business Database](http://www.mongolianbusinessdatabase.com/base/companydetials?id=3449)). Today:

- HQ in Bayangol District, UB; branches at **Zaamar, Darkhan, Tsogttsetsii, Khanbogd (Oyu Tolgoi corridor), and Zamiin Uud**; ~600 employees ([Barloworld Mongolia](https://www.barloworld.mn/en/service/main)).
- Main shop: 975 m², two overhead cranes (3.2T and 10T), 9 service lifts sized for 773/D9/980/390 classes, 350 m² wash bay, Cat contamination-control 4-Star certified, ISO 9001:2015; 100+ shop mechanics, 50+ field mechanics with 20+ vehicles, 24/7 hotline and Mongolia-wide dispatch ([field service](https://www.barloworld.mn/en/service/field)).
- **Component Rebuild Center** in UB: torque converters, transmissions, differentials, wheel groups, gearboxes, cylinders — warranty-backed to Cat spec ([CRC](https://www.barloworld.mn/en/service/component)). S·O·S fluid-analysis lab in-country.

### 4.2 Komatsu — Transwest Mongolia (fastest-localizing)

Exclusive Komatsu dealer since 2009, backed by Sumitomo Corporation and SMS Equipment Canada ([Transwest about](https://www.transwest.mn/en-ca/about-us/)). HQ at No. 30 Erchim Khuch St 1, Bayangol District (+976-7575-9905).

- ~203 employees, 120+ service specialists; **300+ component rebuilds, 50+ machine assemblies, and 200+ on-call services annually** ([Service Catalogue](https://www.transwest.mn/getmedia/55fdc3ac-a9dc-473f-8e07-4dd02340b8e0/Service-Catalogue.pdf)).
- Engine/transmission overhaul, hydraulic cylinder remanufacture, welding/fabrication with line boring, 500-ton vertical press; track presses for pin-and-bushing turns; 24-hour on-call welding trucks.
- **All refurbishment/remanufacturing relocated from China/Japan into Mongolia** — a structural turnaround-time advantage ([Mongolian Mining Journal](https://www.mongolianminingjournal.com/a/73666)).
- Second service facility commissioned in **Khanbogd soum, Umnugovi (2022)** — at Oyu Tolgoi's doorstep.

### 4.3 Volvo CE — effectively absent for mining

Volvo CE's dealer locator lists Mongolia, but no named CE workshop or staffed facility could be verified ([dealer locator](https://www.volvoce.com/global/en/global-dealer-locator/)). What exists: Volvo *Trucks* Mongolia (on-road only, [volvotrucks.mn](https://www.volvotrucks.mn/en-mn/)) and a small sales presence (Gansag/GSG LLC) promoting the R100E. Mining-class parts route through third-party traders air-freighting from **Mumbai in 5–7 days** (sea: 14–28 days) ([Parts Trading Co.](https://partstrading.com/suppliers/volvo-parts-mongolia/)). For a −40°C breakdown on a production machine, that pipeline is disqualifying.

### 4.4 BelAZ — United BelAZ Machinery (better than commonly assumed)

Contrary to some assessments, BelAZ *does* have an official Mongolian distributor: **United BelAZ Machinery LLC (since 2012)**, with ~160 staff (130 technical), a 2,289 m² UB service base, parts-and-tire warehouses in UB and Umnugovi valued at **16 billion MNT (~US$4.5M)**, 24/7 mine-site support points, and permanently assigned Belarusian factory specialists ([ikon.mn](https://ikon.mn/n/272t), [Minprom](https://minprom.gov.by/belazy-serii-7513-budut-rabotat-v-pustyne-gobi/)). UBM was created specifically to fix grey-import parts/service failures.

---

## 5. Parts Inventory for Rapid Repair

- **Caterpillar:** ~**36,000 SKUs / ~2.76 million units** stocked across four Mongolian branches under ISO 9001 and Cat contamination-control standards ([Barloworld Mongolia](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/barloworldmongolia_partsavailability-reliability-operationalexcellence-activity-7455421923053740032-dal1)); the after-sales business exceeds **US$130M/yr** spanning parts warehouse, CRC, warranty, and logistics. Backed by Barloworld's 1.4M-part network.
- **Komatsu:** UB parts warehouse with undercarriage stock, Track Management System for proactive inspection, genuine and Reman parts via My Komatsu; in-country remanufacturing eliminates the China/Japan loop for major components ([undercarriage](https://www.transwest.mn/en-ca/parts-and-products/undercarriage/)).
- **Volvo CE:** no OEM stock in-country; 5–7-day air freight minimum.
- **BelAZ:** 16B MNT centralized warehouse, short logistics chain from Zhodino via Russia — but that chain runs through a sanctions-affected banking/logistics environment.

**Systemic logistics context:** imports route mainly through China; Tianjin port congestion has stranded ~6,000 containers with delays up to three months, and logistics add an estimated **15–30%** to equipment cost in Mongolia ([GBR Mongolia Mining 2024](https://projects.gbreports.com/mongolia-mining-2024/equipment-and-technology-maturing-in-a-realm-of-unpredictability)). This magnifies the value of whichever OEM holds the largest in-country inventory — today, Cat and Komatsu. Negotiate consignment stock for high-failure cold-weather SKUs: hydraulic hoses, fuel/water separator elements, coolant hoses, undercarriage components, and batteries.

---

## 6. Fuel Efficiency and Diesel Strategy at −40°C

### 6.1 Fuel supply is the binding constraint

At −40°C, standard winter diesel gels. Mongolia applies the Customs Union fuel regulation TR CU 013/2011, and the operative cold-fuel standard is **GOST R 55475-2013**, with grades rated by limiting filtration temperature: −32, −38, −44, −48, −52°C ([standard text](https://meganorms.com/gost-r-55475-2013.html)). **You must contract Arctic grade (CFPP ≤ −44°C) or blend with kerosene/cold-flow additives.** Cat's fuel-blender option and Komatsu's low-viscosity fuel charts exist precisely for this.

Supply risk is real: Mongolia imports ~**95% of its petroleum from Russia**; recent export-control disruptions left national diesel reserves around 85,600 t ≈ **21 days of supply**, prompting a guaranteed winter-delivery agreement from October and diversification via China/South Korea ([IntelliNews](https://www.intellinews.com/hit-indirectly-by-sanctions-mongolia-struggles-to-find-workarounds-351043/), [IBTimes Mongolia](https://mn.ibtimes.com/mongolia-expands-fuel-supply-beyond-russia-china-south-korea-1812481)). Dual-sourcing your fuel contract matters more than dual-sourcing your trucks.

### 6.2 Quantified cold-weather fuel penalties

- Winter-blend diesel carries ~**5–10% lower energy content** ([EPRI TR-104843](https://restservice.epri.com/publicdownload/TR-104843/0/Product), [ATBS](https://www.atbs.com/post/diesel-winterization)).
- Cold-soaked viscosity, extended warm-up, and idling: light-duty fleets lose ~15% MPG at −7°C and up to 24% on short trips; heavy diesels lose ~5–10% on long runs, with **effective fleet penalties of −15% to −30% if unmanaged, versus −5% to −12% with pre-heating and idle management** ([Element Fleet](https://www.elementfleet.com/insights-and-resources/insights/blogs/fleet-fuel-management-how-cold-temperatures-affect-fuel-economy), [Freightliner](https://www.freightliner.com/blog-and-newsletters/how-adverse-weather-affects-fuel-economy/)).
- Aerodynamic drag rises ~2% per 10°F drop (~1% MPG per 2% drag).

### 6.3 OEM-specific mitigation

- **Idle management pays fastest:** ThermaStart autonomous idle management on Komatsu 830Es ran through Canadian tundra at −30°C without idling, starting engines only when block temperature, battery voltage, or air pressure demanded ([Rosco Mining](https://www.roscomining.com/post/thermastart-komatsu-830e-cold-weather)); a seven-truck Cat 793F fleet saved a documented **US$5M over five years** with the same approach.
- **Avoid DEF at −40°C:** DEF freezes at −11°C, and Komatsu's own documentation shows thaw times up to **70 minutes** before DEF flows ([Construction Equipment](https://www.constructionequipment.com/earthmoving/rigid-frame-trucks-off-highway/product/10752402/komatsu-komatsu-930e-5-haul-truck)). Both Cat ("Fuel Optimized" rating on the 785) and Komatsu (non-emissionized 930E-5SE engine) offer **non-SCR engine options for markets outside North America/Europe** — specify these for Mongolia; they remove an entire cold failure mode.
- Nominal efficiency claims (Komatsu 930E-5: up to 5% better than predecessor via on-demand cooling; Cat Smart/Eco modes; Volvo A60 "up to 15%"; EC350E 9%) are temperate-climate numbers — treat them as such in TCO modeling. BelAZ SFC of 196–201 g/kWh at nominal power is competitive, though partial-load cold performance is unpublished.

---

## 7. Operator and Technician Training for Mongolian Workers

- **Caterpillar / Barloworld:** The **Wagner Training Institute** (est. ~2001) was described as setting "the standard for vocational education in the entire country" ([Wagner Equipment](https://wagnerequipment.com/wagner-training-institute/wti-staff/)), with instructors certified through the Caterpillar Instructor Accreditation Program. The apprentice program with the Mongolian-Korean Technical College has trained **~150 technicians across six intakes with 100% graduate employment** ([news.mn](https://news.mn/en/12137/)); customer mechanics attend paid 10-month theory+practice courses ([Energy Resources](https://en.energyresources.mn/post/179240)). Globally, Cat offers the Mining Technology Academy, Level I/II/Competent operator certification, and OEM-control simulators ([Cat Training](https://www.cat.com/en_US/support/cat-training.html)). Barloworld retains accredited in-country instructors and sends staff to Cat's Tinaja Hills center.
- **Komatsu / Transwest:** The **Transwest Mongolia Technical Institute** (opened 2024, with Komatsu Ltd., Sumitomo, SMS Equipment, and Komatsu Germany/America) integrates an Australian curriculum, Komatsu systems, and locally designed modules ([Bus-Ex profile](https://www.bus-ex.com/article/transwest-mongolia-llc-forging-local-excellence-through-innovation-skills-green-technology)). Recent deliveries include advanced 930E-4SE hydraulic training for Oyu Tolgoi's maintenance department in Mongolian and English, and a 10-day PC7000-11D program co-delivered with Komatsu Germany Mining at Nariin Sukhait (June–July 2025). An MOU with the German-Mongolian Institute for Resources and Technology (GMIT) feeds internships. Assembly of Erdenet's HD1500-8s was done jointly with mine technicians — embedded on-the-job training.
- **Volvo CE:** no in-country mining training program identified.
- **BelAZ:** UBM sends Mongolian specialists to the Zhodino factory for operations and service training ([news.mn](https://news.mn/en/135983/)) — substantive but BelAZ-specific.
- **National ecosystem to plug into:** Oyu Tolgoi's US$85M training investment including Immersive Technologies PRO3 simulators (2011, with Custom Mine Site) ([Immersive Technologies](https://www.immersivetechnologies.com/news/news2011/news_2011_21.htm)); the Rio Tinto/University of Queensland **South Gobi Underground Mass Mining Institute** (March 2025, first cohort of 28) ([Australian Mining](https://www.australianmining.com.au/rio-tinto-debuts-world-class-training-program-at-oyu-tolgoi/)); and the German-government-partnered **Mining Machinery Operation Technician** program at the Ömnögovi Polytechnic, >80% local students ([MCPG](https://mcpg.mn/en/9281/)).

**Verdict:** Komatsu currently has the most localized, structured pipeline (dedicated institute, Mongolian-language instruction, mine-site co-delivery); Cat has the deepest historical bench. Either supports a Mongolian-majority workforce; Volvo and BelAZ do not, at equivalent depth.

---

## 8. Russian/CIS Alternatives in the Regional Trade Context

**BelAZ** holds ~30% of the global ultra-class (>100 t) haul-truck market and has supplied Mongolia since the Soviet era; Erdenet's fleet has long been "mainly BelAZ" (30/45/55/130 t) ([Belta](https://eng.belta.by/economics/view/belaz-to-ship-3m-worth-of-haul-trucks-to-mongolia-103863-2017/)). Strengths: factory −50°C rating; roughly **$1M per 130-t truck** — a fraction of Western ultra-class pricing; short logistics from Belarus; a real in-country service organization (UBM); fuel systems native to GOST arctic diesel. Weaknesses: shorter component life and higher maintenance frequency than Cat/Komatsu; no autonomous-haulage or fleet-telematics equivalent to MineStar Command/FrontRunner; inferior cab ergonomics (an operator-retention issue in a tight labor market); no excavator line (BelAZ's first Mongolian bulldozer shipped only in 2020); and a **material sanctions exposure** — BelAZ trucks depend on Cummins and MTU engines whose supply is now constrained, potentially forcing substitution with lower-performing Russian-sourced engines on new units.

**UZTM-KARTEX** (St. Petersburg/Yekaterinburg) is the CIS excavator answer where rope shovels fit: the EKG-12K (12 m³) is already at Erdenet (four units by 2020, with +30% productivity and −20% electricity cost expected versus predecessors) ([EANews](https://www.eanews.ru/ekaterinburg/20200629115534/uztm-karteks-postavit-ekskavatory-v-mongoliyu)), and the EKG-20KM-KhL northern variant is rated to **−60°C**. Electric drive eliminates diesel cold-start risk entirely — but requires grid power at the face, and the service network in Mongolia is thin. There is no credible CIS alternative to Western hydraulic mining shovels yet (BelAZ's BX20012 hydraulic excavator is a new, unproven entrant).

**Trade-structure context:** Russia supplies ~28% of Mongolia's imports and ~95% of its fuel; an EAEU–Mongolia interim trade agreement (December 2024) and expanding business-forum ties (February 2026) ease CIS procurement ([Russian Council](https://russiancouncil.ru/en/analytics-and-comments/analytics/russia-and-mongolia-forging-stronger-trade-relations/), [The Diplomat](https://thediplomat.com/2026/02/with-speaker-uchrals-trip-mongolia-and-russia-look-to-expand-economic-links/)). However, Western sanctions create secondary-sanction anxiety among Mongolian banks and buyers transacting with Russian counterparties, and payment/logistics friction is documented ([IntelliNews](https://www.intellinews.com/hit-indirectly-by-sanctions-mongolia-struggles-to-find-workarounds-351043/)). Meanwhile **China already supplies 65–70% of Mongolia's construction-machinery imports by value** (Sany, XCMG gaining at small/medium scale), with Japanese OEMs holding the large-mining segment ([IBI Crossborder](https://www.ibicrossborder.com/upload/ai_report/en/html/20260718003522-f2bb78fbbc.html)). Note also: mines with international financing or Western ownership (e.g., Rio Tinto's Oyu Tolgoi) may face lender- or compliance-driven restrictions on sanctioned-jurisdiction equipment — verify before shortlisting BelAZ for such sites.

---

## 9. Final Recommendations

1. **Primary production haulage:** Komatsu 930E-5 (290 t) for large open pits — the proven Oyu Tolgoi platform — or Cat 793F/785 with Barloworld support. Specify: full Cold Weather Package, **Fuel Optimized / non-emissionized engine** (no DEF), heated body, air start where available, cold-weather suspensions, −50°C coolant.
2. **Loading:** Cat 6060/6040 or Komatsu PC4000–PC7000 with factory cold packages (coolant/oil/hydraulic heaters, HYDRONIC-type independent cab heating, fuel blender). Standardize on the same dealer as your trucks where possible.
3. **Exclude Volvo CE from the primary fleet** unless Volvo CE appoints a full-service Mongolian dealer with bonded parts stock; consider Volvo articulated haulers only for support duty with on-site critical spares and a regional support agreement.
4. **BelAZ as a supplement, not a sole source:** 75131/75135 (130 t) or 75306 (220 t) can lower capex on auxiliary or mid-tier haulage, backed by UBM's UB/Umnugovi warehouses — but retain a Western support partner for high-value powertrain/hydraulic rebuilds, confirm engine provenance (Cummins/MTU vs. substituted Russian units) in the purchase contract, and clear sanctions compliance with your financiers first.
5. **Fuel and fluids procurement (all brands):** contract **Arctic-grade diesel to GOST R 55475-2013 with CFPP ≤ −44°C** with winter-delivery guarantees; stock anti-gel additives; use −50°C coolant, arctic hydraulic oil, and synthetic low-viscosity engine oils; install **~50 kW per machine of 400V three-phase shore power** at parking areas for overnight pre-heating — the single largest lever on cold-start reliability and cold fuel waste; deploy automated idle management (ThermaStart-class) fleet-wide.
6. **Workforce:** anchor technician development with Transwest's Technical Institute and Barloworld's apprentice program; add simulator-based operator training (Immersive Technologies PRO3 precedent at OT); partner with the South Gobi Underground Mass Mining Institute and Ömnögovi Polytechnic for pipeline hiring. Given tight South Gobi labor supply, evaluate autonomy readiness (Cat MineStar Command / Komatsu FrontRunner) in the 5-year plan — both are commercially proven and reduce exposure to operator scarcity and cold-shift risk.
7. **Parts SLA:** negotiate consignment stock with Barloworld and Transwest for cold-weather high-failure SKUs (hoses, separator elements, coolant components, undercarriage, batteries, DEF-system parts if any Tier 4 units remain); given documented 15–30% logistics cost adders and Tianjin congestion, in-country stock — not factory lead time — should drive the dealer-weighting in your scoring model.

**Caveats:** figures on dealer staffing, inventories, and BelAZ's Mongolian footprint derive from dealer publications and trade press (2020–2026) and should be re-verified in RFP due diligence; no public source provides a like-for-like 5–10-year TCO model at −40°C — build your own using the cold fuel-penalty ranges (−5% to −12% managed, −15% to −30% unmanaged) and the downtime economics above; and confirm Volvo CE's current status directly with Volvo CE Region Asia if policy requires a three-way bid.

# The State of Deepfake Detection Research Since 2022

## Executive Summary

Since 2022, deepfake detection research has undergone three simultaneous transformations. **Architecturally**, the field migrated from CNN backbones (XceptionNet, EfficientNet) to Vision Transformers, hybrid designs, and—most consequentially—parameter-efficient adaptation of foundation models such as CLIP. **Empirically**, the central finding of the period is the collapse of benchmark performance in deployment: models scoring 0.95–1.00 AUC on academic datasets fall to 0.43–0.63 AUC on real-world content, an aggregate decline of roughly 45–50% across modalities, documented most rigorously by the Deepfake-Eval-2024 in-the-wild benchmark (Chandra et al.; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4). **Institutionally**, detection has become compliance infrastructure: the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), the U.S. TAKE IT DOWN Act (Pub. L. 119-12, signed 19 May 2025), and China's Deep Synthesis Provisions (effective 10 January 2023) now impose marking, disclosure, and removal obligations that detection and provenance technologies are expected to operationalize.

The scale of the threat has grown in parallel: an estimated 500,000 deepfakes were shared on social media in 2023, and deepfakes detected in fraud cases rose roughly fourfold between 2023 and 2024 (Chandra et al., 2025). The sections below address each requested dimension with specific benchmark results and citations.

## 1. Video Detection Methods

### 1.1 From CNNs to Transformers

The pre-2022 foundation remains the reference point: FaceForensics++ (FF++; Rössler et al., ICCV 2019) established the standard evaluation protocol, with XceptionNet achieving ~97.7% AUC on high-quality intra-dataset evaluation. Through 2022–2024, architectures shifted decisively toward Vision Transformers (ViTs) and hybrid designs. A 2024 systematic review of studies on FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF found that **transformer-based architectures exhibit approximately 11.33% cross-dataset performance decline, versus more than 15% for CNN-based approaches, though at 3–5× higher computational cost** (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68).

The survey "A Timely Survey on Vision Transformer for Deepfake Detection" (https://arxiv.org/html/2405.08463) catalogued 14 ViT-based detectors. Representative published results:

- **UIA-ViT (2022)**: AUC 99.33 on FF++ (HQ); cross-dataset AUCs of 94.68 (DFD), 82.41 (Celeb-DF-v2), 75.80 (DFDC).
- **M2TR (2022)**: AUC 99.51 (FF++ HQ), 99.92 (FF++ RAW), 95.5 (Celeb-DF).
- **ISTVT (2023)**: 99.0% accuracy FF++ (HQ), 96.15% FF++ (LQ), 99.8% Celeb-DF, 92.1% DFDC.
- **FA-ViT** (Forgery-aware Adaptive ViT; https://arxiv.org/html/2309.11092): freezes pretrained ViT parameters and trains adaptive modules; reports **93.83% AUC on Celeb-DF and 78.32% AUC on DFDC in cross-dataset evaluation**.
- **DeepFake-Adapter** (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.00863): the first parameter-efficient tuning approach for deepfake detection, inserting global and local adapters into a frozen ViT.
- **FakeFormer** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.21964): a Learning-based Local Attention mechanism identifying artifact-vulnerable patches, with generalization gains across FF++, Celeb-DF, WildDeepfake, DFD, DFDCP, and DFDC.

Other notable directions include frequency-domain methods (F3-Net: 97.52% accuracy on FF++ HQ but only 57.87% AUC cross-dataset to DFDC), temporal methods (LipForensics: 97.1% mean accuracy on the FF++ leave-one-out benchmark; FTCN), patch-level methods (LaDeDa: ~99% mAP on standard benchmarks; its distilled Tiny-LaDeDa variant is 375× more compute-efficient for edge deployment, but reaches only 93.7% mAP on the WildRF social-media dataset; https://arxiv.org/html/2406.09398), and self-supervised video frameworks (UniForensics: 98.8% average AUC on FF++ leave-one-out and 95.3% on Celeb-DFv2 via Dynamic Video Self-Blending; https://www.alphaxiv.org/overview/2407.19079).

### 1.2 Diffusion-Era Image Forensics

The shift from GANs to diffusion generators broke earlier detectors. Ricker et al. (2024; https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2024/124220/124220.pdf) showed GAN detectors fail on diffusion-generated images—largely because diffusion outputs lack the grid-like frequency artifacts of GANs—though retraining on diffusion data yields near-perfect detection that transfers back to GANs. Subsequent universal detectors include:

- **ZED** (Zero-shot Entropy-based Detector; https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15875): +3% average accuracy over prior SOTA without any AI-generated training data.
- **APN** (Artifact Purification Network): 5.6–16.4% higher accuracy on GenImage and 1.7–50.1% on DiffusionForensics for cross-generator detection.
- **Community Forensics** (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04125v1): 2.7 million images from 4,803 generators; demonstrates that **training-data diversity drives generalization more than architecture**—a finding echoed across the literature.
- **LoL (Learning on Less)**: with only 1% of training data, a 13.6% average accuracy improvement across 8 diffusion models.

## 2. Audio Detection Methods

### 2.1 Core Architectures and Self-Supervised Front-Ends

RawNet2 (raw waveform + SincNet filters) and **AASIST** (heterogeneous stacking graph attention layers with a max graph operation; Jung et al.; https://mm.kaist.ac.kr/pubs/pdfs/jung22c.pdf) remain the dominant end-to-end architectures. AASIST reported a 20% relative improvement over prior SOTA, and even AASIST-L (85K parameters) outperformed all competing systems on ASVspoof 2019 LA (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01200v1).

The decisive post-2022 shift is to **self-supervised learning (SSL) front-ends**—wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, WavLM, Whisper—paired with lightweight back-ends:

- **wav2vec 2.0 + augmentation** (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2202.12233): pretrained only on bona fide speech; lowest EERs reported for ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF at the time, an almost **90% relative improvement** over baseline.
- **Frozen SSL + logistic regression** (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.05384v2): fewer than 2,000 learned parameters reduced cross-dataset EER from **30.9% (RawNet2) to 8.8%** across eight datasets—a 71.5% relative reduction—with better calibration.
- **ARawNet2** (Interspeech 2023; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/li23h_interspeech.pdf): attention-based channel masking; EER of **4.61% on ASVspoof 2019 LA**, 8.36% on ASVspoof 2021 LA, 19.03% on ASVspoof 2021 DF.
- **Whisper + AASIST** (https://faculty.cs.gwu.edu/xiaodongqu/papers/HCII_2024_572_Whisper_Qian.pdf): SOTA progression on ASVspoof 2021 DF from 15.64% EER to **2.85% EER**; critically, the same methods score far worse in the wild (24.73–34.81% EER on In-the-Wild data).
- **TO-RawNet**: orthogonal regularization on Sinc-conv filters plus TCNs; 66.09% relative EER reduction on ASVspoof 2019 LA vs. RawNet.

### 2.2 Challenge-Defined Performance

- **ADD 2022** (first Audio Deepfake Detection Challenge; https://arxiv.org/html/2202.08433v3): Track 1 (low-quality fake audio) was genuinely hard—**best EER 21.7%, mean across 48 submissions 31.7%**; Track 2 (partially fake) best EER 4.8%. ADD 2023 moved to manipulation-region localization and algorithm recognition (top system WEER 12.45%).
- **ASVspoof 5 (2024)** (https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08739v1): crowdsourced data, neural codecs, and—for the first time—adversarial attacks; EER was replaced by **minDCF** as the primary metric because operational deployment requires pre-set thresholds and unequal miss/false-alarm costs. Results include: ParallelChain Lab ensemble minDCF **0.2660** (Track 1 closed; https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/tran24_asvspoof.pdf); USTC-KXDIGIT **0.3948 minDCF / 14.33% EER closed, 0.0750 minDCF / 2.59% EER open** (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/chen24_asvspoof.pdf); SHADOW's codec-augmented FwSE-ResNet34 minDCF 0.44 (47% improvement over baseline); AASIST3 with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks reporting minDCF 0.5357 closed / 0.1414 open with 22.67%/4.89% EER (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/borodin24_asvspoof.pdf). The organizers' summary: many solutions perform well, but "performance degrades under adversarial attacks and the application of neural encoding/compression schemes."
- **CD-ADD** (EMNLP 2024; https://aclanthology.org/2024.emnlp-main.286.pdf): 300+ hours from five zero-shot TTS models; with attack-augmented training, Wav2Vec2-large reached **4.1% EER** and Whisper-medium 6.5%, with one minute of target data sufficing for few-shot adaptation; the authors warn neural codec compression "greatly affect[s] detection accuracy."
- **VoiceWukong** (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.06348v1): tested 12 detectors against voices from 34 commercial/open-source tools; **AASIST2 achieved the best EER at 13.50%** while all others exceeded 20%; a multimodal LLM (Qwen2-Audio) showed no detection ability at all.

Interpretable audio detection has also emerged: **SLIM** (NeurIPS 2024) learns style-linguistics dependencies from real speech to produce interpretable mismatch scores, and **TADA** applies adversarial training-time augmentation to RawNet2/AASIST.
