# Voice-Only vs. Hybrid Touch-with-Audio Checkout for Blind and Low-Vision Grocery Shoppers: A Research Synthesis

## 1. Direct Answer

Across every dependent variable you asked about — task completion, numerical input errors, user confidence, and cognitive load during large-cart verification — the evidence converges on one conclusion: **neither sequential voice-only workflows nor conventional screen-reader-only touch navigation is optimal for grocery checkout. A hybrid architecture — touch gestures with continuous, per-action audio feedback, augmented by optional voice input and chunked spoken summaries — is the best-supported pattern**, and the advantage grows with cart size.

The headline findings:

- **Hybrid multimodal input (touch + speech + motion gestures) is ~3.5× faster and produces ~87% fewer interaction errors than unimodal TalkBack-style navigation**, with 71% of blind participants preferring it and 66.7% reporting greater confidence (n=12; "Designing and usability evaluation of multimodal input modalities for visually impaired persons on mobile platforms," Springer 2025, https://www.springerprofessional.de/designing-and-usability-evaluation-of-multimodal-input-modalitie/50977076).
- **Voice-only confirmation is the weakest link for payment authorization**: blind users reviewing dictated content by ear detect only **~40% of ASR errors** — no better than sighted listeners — so a misheard "12" versus "2" will most often survive audio review (ACM TIIS 2020, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3382039).
- **Quantity adjustment should be a discrete +/- stepper with per-step audible echo**, not free numeric entry, not a slider, and not a "set quantity to N" voice command as the primary mechanism. Counter-based numeric input shows significantly lower task time (p < .001), mental demand (p = .045), effort (p = .039), and frustration (p = .011) than keypad-style entry (A Comparative Evaluation of Accessible Input Modalities, 2026, https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc).
- **WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4 (Error Prevention — Legal, Financial, Data) legally and functionally requires a pre-authorization review step** for financial transactions, and the European Blind Union's 2026 payment-terminal survey documents that blind customers currently "lack an independent check at the moment of authorisation" — a trust failure no visual polish can repair (https://www.euroblind.org/sites/default/files/documents/EBU%20survey%20on%20accessibility%20of%20payment%20terminals_June2026.pdf).
- **For 15+ item cart verification, sequential voice read-back exceeds auditory working memory by a factor of 2–3×**. Auditory-verbal span is roughly 5–7 items, and spoken line items at 5–8 seconds each imply 75–120 seconds of continuous listening with ~2-second phonological-loop decay. The evidence-aligned mitigations are **information filtering plus chunking**: grouped line-item summaries (name + quantity + subtotal as one utterance), "three at a time, never twenty" spoken review with running totals, and a persistent, screen-reader-navigable list with per-item jump-to-edit.

An honest scope note before the detail: **no published study directly randomizes BLV participants between voice-only and hybrid checkout for a 15+ item grocery cart**. The synthesis below triangulates from (a) assistive-technology input studies with BLV participants, (b) general modality-comparison experiments with workload instrumentation, (c) mobile commerce accessibility audits and case studies, and (d) WCAG 2.2 guidance and implementation evidence. Population and task limitations are flagged where they matter. The 15-item threshold in particular is *inferred* from working-memory span evidence and field reports, not directly manipulated as an independent variable — that is a genuine research gap.

---

## 2. Task Completion Rates

### 2.1 The baseline gap is large and abandonment-driven

The historical benchmark comes from the Nielsen Norman Group's accessibility testing program (104 participants; quantitative arm: 20 screen-reader users, 20 screen-magnifier users, 20 sighted controls on tasks including an e-commerce purchase). Success rates averaged **12.5% for screen-reader users versus 78.2% for sighted controls — a 6.3× completion gap** — with time-on-task of 16:46 versus 7:14 and 2.0 versus 0.6 errors per task (https://media.nngroup.com/media/reports/free/Usability_Guidelines_for_Accessible_Web_Design.pdf). This is 2001 desktop data; treat the magnitude as directional rather than current.

Commerce-specific data show abandonment is the dominant failure mode. Nucleus Research's interview study with 73 blind adults found **more than 70% of sites inaccessible to them, roughly two abandoned transactions per month per user, and about two-thirds of initiated transactions ending in abandonment** (https://cdn2.hubspot.net/hubfs/153358/Nucleus-The%20Internet%20is%20unavailable.pdf). Industry audits corroborate the mechanism: **89% of the top 100 US e-commerce sites have accessibility issues in checkout flows**, against a cross-industry average cart abandonment of 70.19% (https://accessibe.com/blog/cart-abandonment-impact-for-ecommerce).

The Contentsquare Foundation's 2025 audit — 250 pages across 50 European and global e-commerce sites, manually evaluated against 15 WCAG 2.2 criteria — found **94% of top European e-commerce sites have inaccessible checkout flows**, and **84% of audited pages failed to label buttons, fields, and elements** (WCAG 4.1.2 Name/Role/Value), rendering checkout "functionally invisible" to screen readers. Compliance scores by page type: **Product Listing 3.5/10, Cart 4.3/10, Delivery 4.4/10, Payment 5.1/10** (https://join.contentsquare-foundation.org/hubfs/RM/2025/Ecomm%203%20pager%20English.pdf). AudioEye's retail index independently found 17 expert-identified barriers across login, product, and checkout pages of top retailers, including **"Add to Cart" buttons that do not audibly announce state** (https://www.audioeye.com/digital-accessibility-index/2023/industry-reports/retail/). Critically, a usability-testing study estimates WCAG 2.1 conformance prevents only **41–71% of real-world accessibility problems**, with blind users overrepresented among the unresolved residue (https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1784326/FULLTEXT01.pdf) — conformance is necessary but not sufficient for completion.

### 2.2 Modality effects on completion

| Comparison | Finding | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Hybrid multimodal vs. TalkBack gestures (n=12 BLV) | **3.5× faster; 87% fewer interaction errors** | Springer 2025 (above) |
| Grocery navigation app field study | Preference ranking: **combined screen+audio > audio-only > screen-only**; proactive audio "less distracting and more efficient than periodically checking a screen" | EasyGO, Liao, Jin & Cheon, DIS 2024, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656156.3663719 |
| Multi-touch audio vs. button-based screen reader (n=10 blind) | Slide Rule **significantly faster**, preferred by 7/10, but more errors initially — a learnability cost | Kane et al., https://www.cs.rochester.edu/hci/pubs/pdfs/slide-rule.pdf |
| Voice-only computer-using agent (Wizard-of-Oz, n=12 VI) | End-to-end voice shopping is **feasible but fragile**; users adopted compensatory "double-checking" strategies throughout | CHI 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791681 |
| LLM-dialogue assistant vs. TalkBack | Reduced mental effort and task time; dialogue interface preferred | Insight, arXiv 2605.09803, https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09803v1 |
| Audio vs. vibration feedback for target location | Audio **41.3% faster, 35.2% fewer taps**; 6/10 still preferred vibration for real-world discretion | HCII 2018, https://www.yorku.ca/mack/hcii2018a.html |

The Instacart accessibility case study gives the starkest grocery-specific completion contrast: sighted participants completed all tasks in **under 5 minutes**; visually impaired participants took **13–32 minutes**, and **none rated any task "easy"** (https://www.shelbyrhodesux.com/portfolio/instacartcs). A 12-app Dutch supermarket evaluation via VoiceOver found **not one app offered an optimal screen-reader experience** — unlabeled buttons were ubiquitous, **prices were read in reverse** (€1.80 announced as "80 and 1" in Coop, Hoogvliet, EkoPlaza), product information was fragmented across multiple reading stops so users lost track of which price belonged to which product, and several apps gave **no audible feedback when items were added to cart** (https://accessibilitydesk.com/news/research-apps-of-supermarkets-for-the-blind-and-visually-impaired-people/).

A 40-day home deployment comparing voice-only (Echo Dot) versus voice+touch (Echo Show) with older adults found the touchscreen version cut setup time ~50% and latency ~20%, with **touch used for ~27% of interactions — users selectively deploy touch to confirm** even when voice is available (https://a11ybob.com/writing/reviews/69b2059145da129a951bec3b). That selective-deployment behavior is the hybrid thesis in miniature.

## 3. Input Error Frequencies — Especially Numerical Entry

Numerical entry is the most error-prone sub-task in non-visual checkout, and the failure modes differ sharply by modality. This is the strongest-evidenced area of the literature.

### 3.1 Screen-reader keypad targeting is slow and error-prone

Baseline VoiceOver-style entry of four-digit PINs took **7.5 seconds (~0.53 characters/second) with a 6.43% uncorrected error rate (SD 7.16)**, versus 3.52% (SD 5.87) for a chorded alternative — the screen-reader error rate was **1.83× higher** (F₁,₁₈₈₂ = 91.87, p < .0001) (University of Washington dissertation covering DigiTaps/Perkinput, https://digital.lib.washington.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/b7fba4e3-b8eb-436e-9f81-54c8787e89ae/content).

### 3.2 Per-entry audio echo buys accuracy at a speed cost — and it is worth it

DigiTaps (longitudinal, 16 participants including 6 blind) measured eyes-free number entry **without audio feedback at 0.87 characters/second with a 5.63% uncorrected error rate (SD 14.8)**; adding audio feedback after every input made entry slower but **significantly more accurate** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2501988.2502056). Haptic-only feedback was faster but less accurate than audio. Design implication: per-entry spoken echo is the accuracy-preserving default for any numeric field.

### 3.3 Structured gestures reduce *erroneous outcomes*, not just slips

GestureCalc (8 screen-reader users, longitudinal) produced **40.5% faster entry and 52.2% fewer erroneous calculations** than a standard screen-reader calculator; participants made more raw mistakes but corrected more of them. The authors note that **error recovery in long numeric expressions is costly because users must restart from the beginning**, which motivated a "shake to hear the entered expression" readback feature (https://faculty.washington.edu/wobbrock/pubs/assets-19.01.pdf). Expression-entry error was ≤3% in pilot and code-recall errors fell to zero by session 2 — learnability is real but requires repetition.

### 3.4 Voice entry: fast, fewer slips, but fatally weak error *detection*

In sighted-population benchmarks (limitation noted), speech dictation was **2.93–3.0× faster than touchscreen typing (153 vs. 52 WPM English)** with a corrected error rate of 5.30% versus 11.22% — but speech **left more errors in the final output (1.30% vs. 0.79% uncorrected, i.e., 64.6% higher)** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3161187). The decisive BLV-specific finding: when reviewing dictated text **by audio alone, blind participants identified only 40% of ASR errors**, statistically no better than sighted listeners (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3382039). Related work shows blind users spent **80.3% of their total interaction time editing** voice-dictated text (ASSETS 2013, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2513383.2513440) and needed an **average of 4.5 minutes to correct errors in a single sentence** (GestureVoice, ASSETS 2025, n=8, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3663547.3746388; GestureVoice's gesture+voice hybrid cut editing time by 53.8%).

Command grammar matters: a voice-billing field study measured **47% recognition accuracy for free conversational commands versus 55% for short constrained set-commands** (https://www.dsource.in/sites/default/files/case-study/voice-assisted-billing-interface-vabi/introduction/file/Voice-Assisted-Billing-Interface-VABI.pdf). Constrained grammars ("add two," "remove last") outperform open conversation.

**The structural conclusion:** majority-of-errors-undetected is the disqualifying property of voice-only numerical confirmation. Voice is acceptable for *initiating* an action ("add three apples") provided the result is echoed back and editable via touch; it is not acceptable as the sole verification channel for a value that costs money to get wrong.

### 3.5 Stepper/counter input beats both keypad and voice for quantities

The within-subject accessible-input study (N=8 visually impaired + N=11 blindfolded sighted) found **counter-based modalities consistently more efficient and lower in cognitive load**, with navigation-dependent (keypad) input imposing measurable overhead: task time p < .001, mental demand p = .045, effort p = .039, frustration p = .011 (https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc). A screen-reader layout study (30 students at a school for the visually impaired) adds that **equally-divided fixed buttons outperformed variable-area buttons (40.2s vs. 51.5s, p = .006)**, and list layouts produced roughly 2.5× more errors than grid layouts in some conditions (10 vs. 25 errors) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/3ll46nh442y). Discrete, fixed-position +/- buttons with audible counts give a reversible single-step recovery path that sliders and free entry cannot.

### 3.6 Security-sensitive numeric entry is a special case

Auditory feedback is often prohibited for PINs; an NCR study of four touchscreen PIN concepts with visually impaired users found a **tactile-anchored concept best** — a fixed tactile reference point for orientation (https://publications.ergonomics.org.uk/uploads/Evaluating-touchscreen-PIN-entry-with-visually-impaired-users.pdf). BLV self-checkout research documents the surrounding anxiety: users fear being charged incorrectly without knowing it, and dislike audible payment details and visible PIN entry (ACM TACCESS 2026, https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3816243). Biometric authorization under WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 (below) sidesteps most of this.

## 4. User Confidence Scores

Confidence tracks completion almost perfectly. In the NNGroup data, the subjective composite (satisfaction/confidence/frustration, 1–7 scale) was **2.5 for screen-reader users versus 4.6 for sighted controls, and the subjective score correlated with task success at r = 0.95** — any intervention that raises completion raises confidence mechanically (NNG report, above).

Modality-specific confidence findings:

- **Hybrid multimodal: 66.7% of participants reported it "easier and more confident"** than the unimodal accessibility-gesture baseline; 71% preferred it overall (Springer 2025, above).
- **PSSUQ (7-point) by modality:** voice 4.70, touch 5.21, **multimodal 5.47**; voice scored significantly lower on effectiveness, efficiency, comfort, and "liked using" (all p ≤ .039) (Human Factors 2018 supplement, https://sage.cnpereading.com/storage/sage/journal/article/HFS/2018/HFS_2018_60_8/unzip/ds-hfs-10.1177_0018720818788995/Supplement_B_-_Results_for_Subjective_Measures_productionready(afterproofs).pdf). Caveat: n=18 sighted participants in a non-shopping task — directional evidence only.
- **EasyGO grocery field study:** confidence/effectiveness ranking **combined > audio-only > screen-only** (DIS 2024, above).
- **BLV self-efficacy at checkout:** among 86 BLV survey respondents plus 10 contextual inquiries on retail self-checkout, **79% found in-store technology difficult or somewhat difficult, 65% rated it inaccessible, and 67% said it did not improve their experience**; current systems "negatively affected independence, self-efficacy, and equality" (ACM TACCESS 2026, above).
- An autonomous-ridesharing analogue (n with severe visual impairment) found audio-enhanced multimodal HMI let VI users reach trust and satisfaction levels **statistically comparable to non-VI users**, while removing audio feedback significantly degraded navigational confidence, vehicle identification, and overall UX (p < 0.05) (HFES 2025, https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/10711813251357895).
- A scoping review of 21 BLV e-commerce studies frames the design target as **"decision confidence"** — judging product suitability and transaction risk well enough to buy without ad hoc sighted assistance — and finds it "rarely supported by technical interventions" today (CHI EA 2026, https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3772363.3799042). Voice-only CUA users in the CHI 2026 study spontaneously demanded concise summaries and double-checking — the behavioral signature of low decision confidence.

## 5. WCAG 2.2: Binding Requirements and Implementation Case Studies

### 5.1 The criteria that matter most for this interface

| Criterion | Level | Direct application to grocery checkout |
|---|---|---|
| **SC 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)** | AA | For any financial transaction, at least one of: **Reversible** (submissions can be reversed), **Checked** (input errors checked with correction opportunity), or **Confirmed** (review/confirm/correct mechanism before finalizing). Sufficient techniques include G98 (review-and-correct before submit), G155 (checkbox in addition to submit), G164 (stated window to amend/cancel the order). The W3C's own example is an order-confirmation screen showing items, quantities, address, and payment method before final submit. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-prevention-legal-financial-data.html |
| **SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry** | A | Never require the same information twice in one process — auto-populate or offer selection ("billing same as shipping"). The W3C's stated intent is to **reduce cognitive effort**, because "requiring people to recall information previously entered can cause them to give up or re-enter the same information incorrectly." Browser autocomplete alone is *not* sufficient. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/redundant-entry.html |
| **SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum)** | AA | No cognitive-function tests (puzzles, memorized passwords without paste/manager support) at login or payment; biometrics and password managers must work. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ |
| **SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements** | AA | Quantity sliders must have single-tap +/- alternatives; "slide to pay" fails this for users who cannot perform sustained drags (and BLV research flags "slide to pay" specifically). |
| **SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)** | AA | +/- steppers and Pay/Confirm ≥ 24×24 CSS px minimum; 44×44 is the practical mobile target. |
| **SC 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)** | AA | Sticky cart bars and modals must not cover the focused element — a common screen-reader failure on checkout screens. |

WCAG2ICT extends these criteria to non-web software, i.e., native mobile apps (https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2ict-22/), and the W3C's WCAG2Mobile note applies them to mobile app contexts (https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2mobile-22/).

### 5.2 What implementation case studies show

- **The strongest ROI quantification:** a WCAG 2.1/2.2-AA-driven mobile checkout redesign reported **conversion among users with accessibility needs more than doubling, checkout errors down 40% across ALL users (not only disabled users), and annual revenue roughly 10× the project cost** (SCOUTb2, https://scoutb2.io/blog/mobile-checkout-redesign-doubled-conversions/). The cross-population error reduction mirrors the 87% interaction-error reduction in the multimodal study — accessibility engineering in checkout is a quality intervention, not a compliance tax.
- **An Indonesian mobile e-wallet redesign** (10 visually impaired participants) addressed screen-reader misinterpretation, gesture-only functions like "slide to pay," and over-long transaction flows, achieving a post-redesign **System Usability Scale of 93 and Single Ease Question of 6.7** (https://www.atlantis-press.com/article/125996193.pdf).
- **The Dutch 12-app supermarket evaluation** (above) is the most instructive failure catalog: unlabeled buttons everywhere, reversed price announcements, fragmented product cards, silent add-to-cart, voice search incompatible with screen readers, and broken back-gesture navigation. The best performers (Jumbo, Albert Heijn, Coop) were merely "reasonably functional." Grouping product card content — name, price, weight, and add-button announced as **one stop rather than four** — is a low-cost, high-impact fix validated directly by this audit.
- A Saudi delivery-app WCAG 2.2 evaluation found the same cluster of defects in registration, payment forms, and menus (https://www.eimj.org/uplode/images/photo/Accessibility_of_Saudi_Delivery_Applications_for_Visually_Impaired_Users..pdf).

## 6. Optimal Confirmation Strategies

The evidence converges on a **four-layer confirmation model**. No single modal dialog is sufficient.

**Layer 1 — Atomic per-action confirmation.** Every cart mutation (add, remove, quantity change) must emit an assertive live-region announcement ("Added 2 Honeycrisp apples — cart now 15 items, $62.40"). The BLV self-checkout study attributes much of the 79% difficulty rating to actions producing no audible feedback; without per-action confirmation, users cannot trust that cart state matches intent (ACM TACCESS 2026, above). The Shopify accessibility guidance states the same requirement: cart updates must remain "perceivable, reversible, and correctly associated," with status messages announced after every quantity change, removal, and update, and focus preserved after the action (https://shopifyaccessibilityguide.com/accessible-quantity-and-cart-controls/).

**Layer 2 — Aggregate summary on entering checkout.** Do not rely on the user scrolling through 15+ items to construct the total. The review screen should auto-announce count, total, and anomalies: "Cart contains 17 items, total $84.32, including 1 substitution and 1 item with a price change." The EBU's 2026 payment-terminal survey — covering reports from Belgium, Germany, Hungary, Iceland, Lithuania, Norway, and Switzerland — is unambiguous: where no pre-payment verification exists, "the process is based entirely on trust in the service provider, which is neither acceptable nor convenient," and mobile wallets that announce the amount only after the transaction are rejected by users (EBU 2026, above).

**Layer 3 — Explicit double confirmation at authorization, carrying minimal payload.** The VoiceCart design pattern is the cleanest implementation: its `place_order` action "refuses to run without `confirmed=true`," and the confirmation utterance carries "the two facts that cost money to get wrong, and nothing else" — the **total amount and the item count** (https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/saifbrand/voicecart). "Confirm payment of $84.32 to Whole Foods for 17 items? Say confirm or cancel, or press the confirm button." This is the auditory analogue of the sighted glance-then-press, and it directly implements WCAG 3.3.4's "Confirmed" prong.

**Layer 4 — Persistent, re-navigable receipt.** Post-payment, the receipt must be a permanent, screen-reader-friendly artifact. The EBU survey notes wallet users "receive a notification of the amount paid after the fact, with no itemised receipt against which to compare the charge," leaving chargeback paperwork as the only remedy. A confirmation that evaporates is not a confirmation.

Two supporting evidence threads: the Korean voice-notification UX guidelines for payment processes (2023) propose exactly three notification categories — **transaction-progress, failure/error, and detailed transaction summaries** — and found structured stage-by-stage announcements reduced the "significant psychological discomfort" visually impaired users reported during payment (https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/landing/article.kci?arti_id=ART003052668). And the voice-CUA shopping study found users independently converged on the same demands: concise summaries, limited option counts, double-checking, and proactive guidance (CHI 2026, above).

## 7. Error Recovery Mechanisms

Three structural realities shape recovery design for this population:

**(a) Visual error affordances are invisible.** Microsoft SCOPE's form-error research found screen-reader users may never notice an alert unless focus is programmatically moved to it; a red border is unobservable, and the user "would then need to intuit that there is an error and search the form for the written message" (https://home.cs.colorado.edu/~DrG/Microsoft-SCOPE-2021/form-error.html). Recovery must be **programmatic, not chromatic**: `aria-invalid="true"` on the field, the repair instruction bound via `aria-describedby`, and a submit-level summary routed through an **assertive live region** (`role="alert"`) so it interrupts and is heard. A useful error answers three questions in order — what happened, why, and how to fix it — in the user's vocabulary, never strands the user without a next action, and preserves all valid data (AccessKit/Percepta, https://accesskit.mabit.ca/en/percepta/error-recovery; implementation patterns at https://ecomdesignpro.com/ecommerce-form-errors/). Test the degraded states explicitly — out-of-stock, price-change, declined payment, session timeout — because that is "where otherwise usable interfaces break down."

**(b) Voice errors compound and must be intercepted at the field level.** Given 40% audio-only ASR error detection, 80%+ of dictation time consumed by editing, and 4.5 minutes to repair a sentence, the recovery design for any voice-accepted input is: (i) **echo each value back immediately** ("Did you say 3?"), (ii) require hard confirmation before any cart-mutating action commits, and (iii) provide **one-step undo** ("undo last add") so a single bad utterance costs a single step. GestureCalc's finding that long-expression errors force a full restart — and its shake-to-readback mitigation — generalizes: always offer a way to *hear the current accumulated state* without re-entering it (https://faculty.washington.edu/wobbrock/pubs/assets-19.01.pdf).

**(c) Reversibility beats prevention for quantity and cart edits.** FetchAid (n=12 BLV, parcel-locker task) demonstrated that an **explicit error-recovery mechanism with real-time feedback "substantially improved task accomplishment and efficiency, and reduced frustration and overall effort regardless of vision conditions and previous experience"** (CHI 2024, https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642213). Steppers give reversible single-step recovery; sliders and free entry do not. WCAG 3.3.4's "Reversible" prong (e.g., G164's amend/cancel window) extends this to the order level: a post-submission edit window is a legitimate conformance path and a genuinely better experience for this population.

## 8. Cognitive Load: Voice-Only vs. Hybrid for 15+ Item Cart Verification

This is where the evidence is most consistent — and most damning for sequential voice-only design.

### 8.1 The theoretical mechanism

Blind screen-reader users carry a **tripartite cognitive load**: they simultaneously manage the browser/app, the content, and the screen-reader software itself (Theofanos & Redish 2003, https://doi.org/10.17705/1thci.00015). Baddeley's working-memory model predicts the specific bottleneck: when all information is oralized, it flows through the **phonological loop, whose traces decay in roughly 2 seconds without rehearsal** (Giraud, Thérouanne & Steiner 2018, https://hal.science/hal-01731012v1/preview/Giraud,%20Th%C3%A9rouanne%20&%20Steiner%20(2018)%20IJHCS%20-%20Web%20accessibility%20[postprint].pdf). The foundational list-reading study established that synthetic speech "places far higher demands on short-term memory" than vision, and that as lists grow the user must hold several items simultaneously — trivial visually, punishing aurally (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/266180.266334).

Applied to your scenario: at **5–8 seconds per line item** (name, quantity, unit price, line total), sequential read-back of a 15-item cart requires **75–120 seconds of continuous listening** against a working-memory span of roughly 5–7 items. **A 15-item cart is 2–3× the natural auditory span.** The user must retain each item's identity, quantity, and price plus a running total while later items overwrite earlier traces. The interface — not the user — must externalize that memory.

### 8.2 Measured modality differences in workload

- **NASA-RTLX modality comparison** (n=18, sighted, non-shopping task — directional only): global workload **voice 49.73 vs. touch 37.16 vs. multimodal 37.75** (voice +33.8% over touch; p < .001 vs. touch, p = .001 vs. multimodal). Subscales: mental demand 65.35 vs. ~51; temporal demand 69.31 vs. 44.10 (+57.2%); frustration 46.67 vs. 22.78 (**2.05×**); self-rated performance 64.65 vs. 82.50 (−21.6%); situation awareness (3D-SART) dropped ~20.4% under voice. Only physical demand favored voice. Preference ranked voice last (Human Factors 2018 supplement, above). Critically for your question, **the modality × task-load interaction was stronger at high load** — voice's confidence and workload penalties grow exactly when verification burden grows. High-load trials raised global workload from 37.42 to 45.68 (+22.1%) across all modalities, so cart size is a real load multiplier under every modality; voice simply starts higher and degrades faster.
- **Multimodal vs. unimodal tabletop study** (n=20, dual-task paradigm): synergistic speech+touch produced "significantly less cognitive load" and was perceived as significantly more usable and intuitive than touch alone (CHI 2022, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3491102.3502062).
- **Severe-low-vision autonomous-vehicle HMI** (n=25): multimodal interaction "improved environmental perception, reduced cognitive load, and enhanced user experience," with **tactile + spatial audio the best combination** (Universal Access in the Information Society 2025, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/s10209-025-01240-4).
- **Counter-example worth respecting:** an in-vehicle infotainment study (n=14; EEG + eye-tracking + GSR) found hybrid mode produced **48% higher distraction than voice alone** (IJRIAS 2024, https://rsisinternational.org/journals/ijrias/articles/navigating-cognitive-workload-multimodal-evaluation-of-infotainment-accessibility-in-indian-drivers/). The reconciliation is task domain: safety-critical concurrent tasks penalize modality-switching costs that sedentary tasks reward. Your checkout is sedentary and single-task — the tabletop and SLVP results are the applicable ones.
- **Audio is a scarce channel for BLV users specifically:** for white-cane users, auditory guidance produced **22× higher cognitive load than haptic feedback** in short-range navigation, while blindfolded sighted controls showed no such gap — a warning against both audio flooding and blindfolded-sighted-only testing methodologies (https://www.lanfanshu.com/paper/61e5083616ad6f084cf62e43).

### 8.3 Verification behavior under load

The CHI 2026 voice-CUA study observed users managing "the cognitive load that arises from the ephemeral nature of voice interactions" by demanding "concise summaries, a limited number of options, double-checking, and proactive guidance" (above). A co-design study independently concluded a commerce VUI must provide "explicit confirmations and retrospective information" because "failed speech recognition and overwhelming information had a negative impact" (https://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1482523/FULLTEXT01.pdf). The voice-billing field study found manual long bills (7–8+ items) were "verified twice to prevent any calculation errors" — verification cost compounds with item count even for human cashiers. And with 40% audio-only error detection (§3.4), a 15-item spoken read-back is simultaneously **high-load and low-yield**: the user expends maximal effort and still misses most discrepancies.

### 8.4 The two evidence-backed mitigations: filtering and chunking

The panels surface two complementary strategies — use both:

1. **Information filtering.** Giraud, Thérouanne & Steiner (2018) ran three experiments with **76 blind participants** on filtered versus unfiltered websites, measuring cognitive load via dual-task paradigm and NASA-RTLX. Filtering produced **substantial benefits in cognitive load, performance, and satisfaction** (IJHCS 2018, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2017.10.011). For cart review: announce name + quantity + line subtotal as a **single grouped utterance per item**; suppress descriptions, nutrition, promotions. The Dutch supermarket audit shows the failure mode when this is ignored — fragmented cards cause users to lose which price belongs to which product, an error that compounds across 15 items.
2. **Chunking with externalized state.** VoiceCart's rule — "Three at a time, never twenty. A sighted shopper skims a long list; a listener cannot skip. So results come three at a time with the count of what is left" — is a direct application of the 1995 list-reading findings. Concretely: "Items 1–3 of 15: 2 Honeycrisp apples $4.50; 1 gallon milk $3.89; 3 bananas $1.17. Running total $62.40 of $84.32. Say 'next,' 'repeat,' or 'edit item 2.'" Pair this with a **persistent, searchable, screen-reader-navigable list with per-item jump-to-edit** so verification is item-level, not whole-cart-level. An EEG study of online shopping (2024) adds that accumulated cognitive load is sensitive to task uncertainty and negatively drives satisfaction, while interface convenience reduces accumulated load — efficient multimodal verification pays off in satisfaction directly (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/386458116).

One instrumentation caveat: a 2025 IJHCS systematic review (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2025.103515) and a 2026 ACM TOCHI meta-analysis of 522 CHI papers (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3837858) document convergent-validity and sensitivity weaknesses in NASA-TLX for HCI. Triangulate subjective workload with behavioral measures (dual-task, EEG, correction counts) in your own evaluations.

## 9. Recommended Architecture

Synthesizing everything above into a buildable spec, in priority order:

1. **Input layer: hybrid by default.** Touch exploration with per-element audio feedback as the backbone; voice as an optional accelerator for search and initial add-to-cart; motion gestures optional. Never voice-only for the checkout path; never silent touch.
2. **Product selection:** semantic grouping — each product card announced as one stop (name, price, weight, availability, add control). Verify price verbalization locale by locale (the "€1.80 → 80 and 1" bug). Announce "Added…" with updated count and running total after every add.
3. **Quantity adjustment:** fixed-position +/- steppers (≥44×44 px targets), per-step audible echo ("3 apples, $6.75"), long-press or double-tap for direct numeric entry as a secondary path. No sliders as the sole control (WCAG 2.5.7). Voice "set quantity to 3" acceptable only with immediate echo and touch-editable result.
4. **Cart review:** persistent navigable list + chunked spoken review (3 items per utterance, with position and running total) + aggregate auto-summary on entry (count, total, anomalies: substitutions, price changes, out-of-stock). Filter everything except name/quantity/subtotal.
5. **Payment authorization:** biometric or password-manager auth (SC 3.3.8); then a double confirmation carrying only total + item count; no re-typed data anywhere in the flow (SC 3.3.7); explicit review-confirm-correct step per SC 3.3.4 (G98 + G155, optionally G164 post-order edit window).
6. **Errors:** programmatic only — `aria-invalid`, `aria-describedby` repair text, assertive live regions, focus management to the first error; undo-last-action always available; degraded states (declined card, price change, stock loss) tested as first-class flows.
7. **Receipt:** permanent, itemized, re-navigable, screen-reader-friendly.

---

## 10. Caveats and Research Gaps

- **Small samples throughout.** Most quantitative studies run 8–30 participants; the headline 3.5×/87%/66.7% figures come from a single n=12 study and need replication before serving as benchmarks.
- **No study directly manipulates cart length** in a BLV checkout flow. The 15-item cognitive-load analysis is an inference from working-memory span, list-reading research, and field reports — a genuine gap your own evaluation program could fill.
- **Population skew toward blind users**; low-vision users with residual vision may prefer different hybrid balances and are underrepresented.
- **Baseline figures are dated or directional** (NNGroup 2001 desktop data; sighted-population PSSUQ/NASA-RTLX modality data).
- **Privacy and security of voice** for payment data spoken aloud in public is under-examined, as are cross-platform differences (VoiceOver vs. TalkBack), older BLV users, comorbid motor impairments (which can make touch gestures unreliable), and non-Germanic-language numeric verbalization.
- **LLM-based assistants** (Insight, voice CUAs) are promising for offloading summary and comparison load but carry hallucination, latency, and privacy risks that the cited authors themselves flag — treat as an assistive layer over a deterministic cart, never as the cart's source of truth.

**Bottom line:** build the hybrid, make every state change audible, make quantities discrete and echoed, make confirmation layered and minimal-payload, make errors programmatic, and for large carts externalize memory through filtered, chunked, navigable review. The evidence says this is faster (3.5×), cleaner (up to 87% fewer interaction errors; 40% fewer errors for *all* users in the SCOUTb2 redesign), more confidence-inspiring (66.7% gains; confidence tracks success at r = 0.95), and — via WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4/3.3.7/3.3.8 — increasingly a conformance requirement rather than an option.

# Independent Directors Under the NASDAQ Listing Standards

## 1. The Definition — NASDAQ Listing Rule 5605(a)(2)

An **"Independent Director"** under the NASDAQ rules is:

> "a person other than an Executive Officer or employee of the Company or any other individual having a relationship which, in the opinion of the Company's board of directors, would interfere with the exercise of independent judgment in carrying out the responsibilities of a director."

(Source: [NASDAQ Listing Center — Rule 5600 Series](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series); [SEC-filed rule text, Ex. 5 to SR-NASDAQ-2012-109](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2013/34-68640-ex5.pdf).)

The definition has **two layers**:

1. **A general judgment standard** — the board must affirmatively conclude the director has no relationship that would interfere with independent judgment. This is a substantive standard that can disqualify a director even if no bright-line test is tripped.
2. **Six categorical "bright-line" bars** (Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(F)) — relationships that *conclusively* preclude an independence finding, regardless of the board's view. For registered investment companies, a seventh alternative test (G) applies in lieu of (A)–(F).

Three embedded definitions matter:

- **"Executive Officer"** — the officers covered by Exchange Act Rule 16a-1(f) (president, principal financial/accounting officers, vice presidents in charge of principal business functions, and other policy-making officers) (Rule 5605(a)(1)).
- **"Family Member"** — a person's spouse, parents, children, siblings, mothers- and fathers-in-law, sons- and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law, and anyone (other than domestic employees) who shares the person's home. The in-law categories were added and domestic employees excluded by a 2019–2020 amendment (SR-NASDAQ-2019-049), realigning NASDAQ's definition with the NYSE's; non-resident stepchildren are not covered ([SEC approval order](http://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/assets/rulebook/nasdaq/filings/SR-NASDAQ-2019-049_Approval.pdf); [85 FR 9320 (Feb. 20, 2020)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/02/20/2020-03320/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-notice-of-filing-of-amendment-no-3-and)).
- **"Company"** — under the interpretive material (IM-5605), references to the Company include any **parent or subsidiary** consolidated in the company's financial statements, but not an entity reflected solely as an investment.

---

## 2. Eligibility Criteria — Who Qualifies

NASDAQ's test is essentially **negative**: there are no affirmative qualifications such as minimum share ownership, tenure, education, or credentials. A director qualifies as independent only if **all four** of the following are true:

1. **Not an insider** — the person is not an Executive Officer or employee of the Company (including its parents and subsidiaries).
2. **No judgment-impairing relationship** — the board, exercising its own judgment, concludes no relationship exists that would interfere with independent judgment. IM-5605 requires the board to make an **affirmative determination** to this effect for each director, not merely presume it.
3. **Passes every bright-line test** — the person does not fall within any disqualification in Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(F) (or, for investment companies, is not an "interested person" under (G)) — detailed in Section 3.
4. **Disclosed determination** — domestic issuers must disclose independence determinations under Item 407(a) of Regulation S-K; Foreign Private Issuers disclose which directors the board found independent in their next annual report (Form 20-F or 40-F) (Rule 5605(b)(1)).

**Key analytical point:** the bright-line tests are a *floor, not a ceiling*. A director can pass all six tests and still be found non-independent under the general standard. Conversely, **stock ownership alone is never disqualifying** — IM-5605 expressly provides that ownership of Company stock, even a significant or controlling block, does not by itself preclude an independence finding (a deliberate contrast with the "affiliated person" concept used elsewhere in securities regulation).

**Heightened eligibility for committee service:** the general definition is necessary but not sufficient for key committees:

- **Audit committee** members must additionally satisfy **SEC Rule 10A-3(b)(1)** ([17 CFR § 240.10A-3](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/240.10A-3)) — no consulting, advisory, or other compensatory fees from the Company other than board/committee fees, and not an "affiliated person" — must not have participated in preparing the Company's financial statements within the past three years, and must be financially literate (able to read and understand a balance sheet, income statement, and cash-flow statement), with at least one member "financially sophisticated" (Rule 5605(c)(2)(A)).
- **Compensation committee** members must be Independent Directors, and the board must additionally consider **the source of the director's compensation** (including consulting/advisory fees, per SEC Rule 10C-1) and **any affiliate relationships** that would impair judgment (Rule 5605(d)(2)(A)).

---

## 3. Disqualification Criteria — Who Cannot Serve

Rule 5605(a)(2)(A)–(G) categorically bars a finding of independence for the following persons. All dollar thresholds have been unchanged since at least 2012.

### (A) Current or recent employment — 3-year look-back
A director who **is, or at any time during the past three years was, employed by the Company**. The three-year clock runs from the date employment *ceases* — a former employee cannot be independent until three years after termination. (Nasdaq staff interpretive practice, reflected in company proxy disclosures, treats interim employment of less than one year that has since terminated as non-disqualifying.)

### (B) Compensation in excess of $120,000
A director who accepted — or who has a **Family Member** who accepted — **any compensation from the Company exceeding $120,000 during any period of twelve consecutive months** within the three years preceding the independence determination. **Exclusions:**
- (i) compensation for **board or board committee service**;
- (ii) compensation paid to a **Family Member who is a non-executive employee** of the Company; and
- (iii) benefits under a **tax-qualified retirement plan**, or **non-discretionary compensation**.

Per Nasdaq interpretive guidance, options granted for services are valued at grant using a commonly accepted pricing model (e.g., Black-Scholes) and count as compensation upon grant even if unvested. Audit committee members face a stricter fee bar under Rule 5605(c)(2)/Rule 10A-3, which permits *no* compensatory fees beyond board service.

### (C) Family ties to an Executive Officer — 3-year look-back
A director who is a **Family Member of an individual who is, or at any time during the past three years was, employed by the Company as an Executive Officer**.

### (D) Significant business relationships — 5% / $200,000 test
A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, a **partner in, controlling Shareholder of, or Executive Officer of any organization** to which the Company made, or from which it received, **payments for property or services** in the **current or any of the past three fiscal years** that exceed the **greater of 5% of the recipient's consolidated gross revenues for that year or $200,000**. **Exclusions:** (i) payments arising solely from **investments in the Company's securities**, and (ii) payments under **non-discretionary charitable contribution matching programs**. IM-5605 confirms the test reaches charitable organizations: a director who serves as an executive officer of a charity receiving Company payments above the threshold is not independent.

### (E) Compensation-committee interlock — 3-year look-back
A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, **employed as an Executive Officer of another entity** where, at any time during the past three years, **any of the Company's Executive Officers served on that other entity's compensation committee**.

### (F) Auditor affiliation — 3-year look-back
A director who is, or has a Family Member who is, a **current partner of the Company's outside auditor**, or who **was a partner or employee of the outside auditor and worked on the Company's audit** at any time during the past three years.

### (G) Investment companies — alternative test
For investment companies, **in lieu of (A)–(F)**, a director who is an **"interested person"** of the Company under **Section 2(a)(19) of the Investment Company Act of 1940** — other than solely by virtue of board or committee service — is not independent. This harmonizes NASDAQ's standard with the 1940 Act regime.

### The "exceptional and limited circumstances" safety valve
For the audit and compensation committees only, **one non-independent director** may serve for up to **two years** if the board determines, under exceptional and limited circumstances, that service is in the best interests of the Company and its shareholders, and discloses the determination. That director must not be a current Executive Officer, employee, or Family Member of an Executive Officer, and **may not chair the audit committee**; for the compensation committee, the exception is available only if the committee has at least three members (Rules 5605(c)(2)(B), (d)(2)(B)).

**Summary of the bright-line bars:**

| Bar | Relationship | Threshold | Look-back |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | Employment by Company | Any | Past 3 years (from cessation) |
| (B) | Compensation to director/Family Member | > **$120,000** in any 12 consecutive months | Past 3 years |
| (C) | Family Member is Company Executive Officer | Any | Past 3 years |
| (D) | Partner/control person/EO of transacting organization | > **greater of 5% of recipient's gross revenues or $200,000** | Current + past 3 fiscal years |
| (E) | Comp-committee interlock | Any | Past 3 years |
| (F) | Tie to outside auditor | Current partner, or worked on the audit | Past 3 years |
| (G) | Investment companies: "interested person" (ICA §2(a)(19)) | In lieu of (A)–(F) | Per 1940 Act |

---

## 4. Which Companies Must Have Independent Directors

### 4.1 The baseline mandate — every listed operating company with voting equity

Under **Rule 5605(b)(1)**, **a majority of the board of directors** of every NASDAQ-listed company must be Independent Directors as defined in Rule 5605(a)(2). Quantitatively, for a board of N directors, at least **⌊N/2⌋ + 1** must be independent — e.g., a 7-member board needs at least 4 independent directors; an 8-member board needs at least 5. Rule 5605(b)(2) additionally requires **regularly scheduled executive sessions** attended only by Independent Directors (Nasdaq guidance contemplates at least two per year). The Federal Register summarizes the regime as requiring "a majority of the board… be Independent Directors, and that the company's audit, compensation and nominating committees be comprised solely of Independent Directors" ([84 FR 49663 (Sept. 19, 2019)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/09/19/2019-20220/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-order-instituting-proceedings-to-determine)).

In practice this means the full requirement set applies to **domestic U.S. operating companies listing common stock or voting preferred stock** on any NASDAQ tier (Global Select, Global, or Capital Market):

| Requirement | Rule | Composition |
|---|---|---|
| Majority-independent board | 5605(b)(1) | > 50% of total board |
| Executive sessions | 5605(b)(2) | Independent Directors only, regularly scheduled |
| Audit committee | 5605(c)(2) | ≥ **3 members**, all independent under 5605(a)(2) **and** SEC Rule 10A-3(b)(1); financial literacy; one financially sophisticated member |
| Compensation committee | 5605(d)(2) | ≥ **2 members**, all Independent Directors, plus fee-source/affiliation review (SEC Rule 10C-1) |
| Director nominations | 5605(e)(1) | Nominees selected or recommended by an **all-independent nominating committee** or by a **majority of the Independent Directors** |
| Code of conduct | 5610 | Applies to all directors, officers, employees |

### 4.2 Exempt companies (Rule 5615)

| Category | Scope of relief | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **Controlled Companies** (> **50% of voting power** for director elections held by an individual, group, or another company) | Exempt from majority-independent board (5605(b)), compensation committee (5605(d)), and independent nominations (5605(e)) — **but not** executive sessions (5605(b)(2)) or the audit committee rules | Reliance must be disclosed ([Rule 5615, Ex. 5 to SR-NASDAQ-2024-019](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf)) |
| **Foreign Private Issuers** (Rule 5615(a)(3)) | May follow **home-country practice** in lieu of most Rule 5600 Series requirements | Must still: comply with the Notification of Noncompliance rule (5625) and Voting Rights rule (5640); maintain an audit committee satisfying Rule 5605(c)(3) whose members meet the Rule 10A-3(b)(1) independence standard; and disclose each requirement not followed and the home-country practice substituted |
| **Issuers of only non-voting preferred, debt, or derivative securities** (e.g., debt-only issuers, certain ETFs/ETNs, trust-issued receipts) (Rule 5615(a)(6)) | Exempt from Rules 5605(b), (d), (e), 5610, and 5620(a) | Audit committee requirements apply only to the extent of SEC Rule 10A-3; if the issuer later lists common or voting preferred stock, it becomes fully subject to the Rule 5600 Series ([Ex. 5, SR-NASDAQ-2025 filing](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2025/34-102513-ex5.pdf)) |
| **Asset-backed and other passive issuers** (IM-5615-1) — e.g., trusts/unincorporated associations without boards that passively hold securities | Exempt from Rules 5605(b), (c), (d), (e) and 5610 | — |
| **Registered management investment companies** | Independence is measured under the alternative §2(a)(19) "interested person" test (Rule 5605(a)(2)(G)) in lieu of (A)–(F); these funds are governed principally by the 1940 Act's own board-independence regime and are exempt from most Rule 5600 Series governance requirements, while remaining subject to audit-committee requirements (Rule 5605(c)(3)/Rule 10A-3) | — |

**A caution on scope:** some secondary summaries list limited partnerships as broadly exempt from the majority-board requirement; the better-corroborated position is that limited partnerships listed on NASDAQ are today generally subject to the Rule 5600 Series, and no current categorical limited-partnership exemption from the independent-director requirements should be assumed without checking the current Rule 5615 text.

### 4.3 Phase-in relief for newly listing and transitioning companies (Rule 5615(b))

Companies are not required to comply on day one in defined situations:

- **IPO companies:** majority-independent board within **12 months of the listing date**; audit committee must have **one qualified member at listing, a majority independent within 90 days, and be fully independent within one year**; compensation and nominations functions phase in on the same schedule (one independent member by the earlier of the IPO closing or five business days after listing, majority within 90 days, full compliance within one year).
- **Companies emerging from bankruptcy, transferring from another exchange or from Section 12(g) registration, or listing via carve-out/spin-off:** substantially similar 12-month schedules.
- **Companies ceasing to be Controlled Companies:** phase in on the IPO-style schedule measured from the date control ceases.
- **Companies ceasing to be Foreign Private Issuers or Smaller Reporting Companies:** a **6-month** phase-in to full compliance.

(Sources: [Ex. 5 to SR-NASDAQ-2024-019](https://www.sec.gov/files/rules/sro/nasdaq/2024/34-100208-ex5.pdf); [SEC approval order, 89 FR 70672 (Aug. 30, 2024)](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/08/30/2024-19496/self-regulatory-organizations-the-nasdaq-stock-market-llc-order-granting-approval-of-a-proposed-rule).)

### 4.4 Cure periods for losing compliance

If a company falls below a majority-independent board because of **one vacancy** or because **one director ceases to be independent for reasons outside the director's reasonable control**, it has until the **earlier of its next annual shareholders meeting or one year from the triggering event** to cure — but no less than **180 days** if the annual meeting falls within 180 days of the event — and must **notify NASDAQ immediately** upon learning of the noncompliance (Rule 5605(b)(1)(A)). Parallel cure periods apply to audit committee composition (Rule 5605(c)(4)) and compensation committee composition (Rule 5605(d)(4)); a company generally cannot stack a cure period on top of a phase-in period it was already using.

---

## 5. Related Development: The Vacated Board-Diversity Rules

For completeness on board-composition requirements: NASDAQ's former "comply-or-explain" board-diversity rule (Rule 5605(f)) and diversity-data matrix disclosure (Rule 5606) were **vacated by the Fifth Circuit sitting en banc on December 11, 2024** in *Alliance for Fair Board Recruitment v. SEC* ([opinion](https://www.ca5.uscourts.gov/opinions/pub/21/21-60626-CV0.pdf)), which held the SEC exceeded its Exchange Act authority in approving them. NASDAQ removed the rules effective **February 4, 2025**, and companies have no obligations under them (see [Covington client alert](https://www.cov.com/news-and-insights/insights/2024/12/fifth-circuit-vacates-nasdaqs-board-diversity-rules); [Davis Polk update](https://www.davispolk.com/insights/client-update/fifth-circuit-vacates-nasdaq-board-diversity-mandate)). The core independence framework described above is unaffected.

---

## 6. Consolidated Summary

| Element | Rule | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | 5605(a)(2) | Not an officer/employee; no relationship interfering with independent judgment, as affirmatively determined by the board; bright-line bars (A)–(F), or (G) "interested person" test for investment companies |
| Family Member | 5605(a)(2) | Spouse, parents, children, siblings, parents-in-law, sons/daughters-in-law, brothers/sisters-in-law, household members (excluding domestic employees) |
| Compensation cap | 5605(a)(2)(B) | $120,000 per any 12 consecutive months in prior 3 years (board fees, non-executive Family Member pay, qualified-plan/non-discretionary comp excluded) |
| Business-relationship cap | 5605(a)(2)(D) | Greater of 5% of recipient's consolidated gross revenues or $200,000, current + prior 3 fiscal years |
| Board composition | 5605(b)(1) | **Majority independent** (⌊N/2⌋ + 1); cure period: earlier of next annual meeting or 1 year (180-day floor) |
| Audit committee | 5605(c)(2); SEC Rule 10A-3 | ≥3 members, all independent under both tests; no financial-statement preparation in past 3 years; financial literacy + one financially sophisticated member |
| Compensation committee | 5605(d)(2); SEC Rule 10C-1 | ≥2 members, all independent; fee-source and affiliation review |
| Nominations | 5605(e) | All-independent committee or majority of Independent Directors |
| Principal exemptions | 5615; IM-5615-1/-3 | Controlled Companies (>50% voting power; keep executive sessions + audit committee); FPIs (home-country practice, keep 10A-3 audit committee, Rules 5625/5640); issuers of only non-voting preferred/debt/derivative securities; asset-backed/passive issuers; registered investment companies (alternative test; 1940 Act regime) |
| Phase-ins | 5615(b) | IPOs, bankruptcy emergences, transfers, spin-offs: up to 12 months; former SRCs/FPIs: 6 months |
| Diversity rules | (former) 5605(f), 5606 | Vacated Dec. 11, 2024 (5th Cir.); removed Feb. 4, 2025 — no longer in effect |

## 7. Caveats and Practical Notes

- The rule text cited reflects amendments through the **August 2024** phase-in amendments (SR-NASDAQ-2024-019) and the **February 2025** removal of the diversity rules; practitioners should confirm against the live [NASDAQ Listing Center rulebook](https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/rulebook/nasdaq/rules/nasdaq-5600-series), which NASDAQ amends periodically.
- The interim-employment (<1 year) carve-out and option-valuation mechanics derive from **Nasdaq staff interpretive practice and FAQs** as summarized in proxy disclosures, not from the face of Rule 5605(a)(2) itself.
- This analysis is confined to the NASDAQ listing standards. Independence determinations also interact with, but are distinct from, state-law fiduciary standards (e.g., Delaware's demand-futility and entire-fairness independence analyses), related-party transaction disclosure under Item 404 of Regulation S-K, D&O questionnaire practice, and the parallel (similar but not identical) NYSE Listed Company Manual §303A regime — each of which warrants separate analysis before a board makes or discloses a determination.
