# Recommendation: Toowoomba — with Cairns as a legitimate (but riskier) alternative, and Bundaberg ruled out on healthcare grounds

For your specific profile — managed atrial fibrillation, a hard 90-minute specialist-care requirement, a $550,000 housing cap, and a need for part-time accounting income at ≥$35/hour through to age 60 — **Toowoomba is the only one of the three cities that clears every threshold you set simultaneously.** It is the only option offering the complete AF care continuum *including* road-accessible quaternary cardiothoracic backup (Brisbane, ~125 km / ~1.5 hours), the deepest verified part-time accounting market at your rate floor, and a genuine (if narrowing) pool of 3-bedroom homes under $550,000 — while still cutting living costs roughly 23–27% and housing capital ~$245,000 versus Melbourne.

Cairns is a credible runner-up with the strongest electrophysiology bench, but it fails your 90-minute criterion on the surgical arm (cardiothoracic surgery requires Townsville, 348 km / 6h 47m by road), its 2024 median house price (~$655,500) already exceeds your cap, and groceries actually cost *more* than Melbourne. Bundaberg wins on affordability but is disqualified by a fragile cardiac service with no local electrophysiologist — an unacceptable risk profile for someone whose rhythm could deteriorate unexpectedly in their late 50s.

Because AF is a *convex* risk — the cost of being wrong is catastrophic, and the 90-minute threshold cannot be retroactively loosened — Toowoomba is the defensible default.

---

## 1. Decision Matrix

| Criterion | **Toowoomba** | **Bundaberg** | **Cairns** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full AF care within 90 min (incl. surgical backup) | ✅ **Yes — only option** | ❌ No EP; surgery 3.5–4h away | ⚠️ EP yes; CT surgery 6h 47m road |
| 24/7 STEMI service | ✅ St Andrew's (only one in Darling Downs) | ❌ Transfer-dependent | ✅ Cairns Hospital |
| Annual cost-of-living saving vs Melbourne (single) | **~$8,600–8,900 (–23 to –27%)** | ~$8,500–14,800 (–25 to –41%) | ~$3,300–3,900 (–9 to –11%) |
| Groceries vs Melbourne | **–22% to –23%** | Mixed (produce cheaper; red meat/water +30–60%) | **+3.8% to +4.1% (more expensive)** |
| Housing capital released vs Melbourne house median ($895k) | ~$245k | ~$368k | ~$240k (and shrinking) |
| 3-bed median trajectory Dec 2020 → 2024 | $370.5k → ~$575k (+55%); CoreLogic 5-yr +71% | $295k → ~$520–527k (+76–88%, best in Australia) | $435k → $655.5k (+40–52%) |
| Suburbs with 3-bed under $550k (2024) | 5–6 (Rockville $480k, Wilsonton $502.5k, Harristown $525k, Newtown $539.5k, Nth Toowoomba $545k) | **10–13** (Central $428k, West $452k, South $457k, Norville $478k, Kepnock $508k…) | Limited outer/western stock (Manoora ~$488k, Westcourt ~$500k, Edmonton ~$510k, Woree ~$528k) |
| Part-time accounting ≥$35/hr | **Deepest verified market** (Finance Officer $38–41/hr; TASC $43.08–$46.35/hr; multiple $35–40/hr) | Thin (1 explicit advertised role ≥$35) | Moderate volume; strongest single role is Cairns Regional Council Accountant $79.9–90.5k pro-rata, part-time option |
| **Verdict** | **Optimal balance** | **Healthcare-disqualified** | **Legitimate alternative, weaker fit** |

---

## 2. Cardiac Care Within 90 Minutes — The Deciding Factor

All three cities have general cardiologists in town, so the real test is **electrophysiology (EP) depth** — the sub-specialty that manages AF long-term (cardioversion, catheter ablation, device management) — plus **surgical backup** if your condition escalates.

### Toowoomba — full continuum, only option meeting your stated threshold
- **St Andrew's Toowoomba Hospital** operates the **only 24/7 STEMI heart-attack service in the Darling Downs**, with a cardiac catheterisation laboratory and a dedicated **EP studies and ablation service** ([sath.org.au/service/cardiology](https://www.sath.org.au/service/cardiology/), [sath.org.au/service/electrophysiology-ep-studies-and-ablation](https://www.sath.org.au/service/cardiology/electrophysiology-ep-studies-and-ablation-for-supraventricular-tachycadia-svt/), [sath.org.au/service/emergency-heart-centre](https://www.sath.org.au/service/emergency-heart-centre/)). It also offers TOE and cardioversion specifically for AF patients.
- **Resident electrophysiologists include Dr Shameer Ahmed (Care Cardiology)** — EP studies, RF ablation, and "invasive and non-invasive management of atrial fibrillation," with a staff appointment at Toowoomba Base Hospital ([carecardiology.com.au](https://www.carecardiology.com.au/about)) — **Dr Caleb Mengel**, offering AF ablation including emerging **pulsed-field ablation**, leadless and conduction-system pacing ([sath.org.au/team/dr-caleb-mengel](https://www.sath.org.au/team/dr-caleb-mengel/)), and **Dr Robert Perel (Queensland Cardiovascular Group)**, performing AF ablation and device management. Additional consulting practices (Heart Specialists Toowoomba at St Vincent's Private, HeartCare Toowoomba, QCG) provide redundancy across **five cardiology practices and two private hospitals plus the base hospital** ([heartspecialiststoowoomba.com.au](https://www.heartspecialiststoowoomba.com.au/services), [heartcaretoowoomba.com.au](https://heartcaretoowoomba.com.au/), [qcg.com.au/toowoomba](https://qcg.com.au/toowoomba/)).
- **St Vincent's Private Hospital Toowoomba** runs a cardiac hybrid theatre with integrated cath lab and a 24/7 emergency chest-pain service.
- **Critical safety net:** Brisbane's quaternary cardiothoracic centres are ~125 km / ~1h 30m by road — inside your 90-minute window for surgical escalation (complex ablation complications, CABG, valve surgery, surgical maze).

### Cairns — excellent EP bench, but no road-accessible surgery
- **Cairns Hospital** runs two cardiac catheter labs (the second a $2.8M investment opened 2019) with specialised EP and 3D mapping ([fnqhf.org.au/2019/10/29/cath-lab-opens](https://www.fnqhf.org.au/2019/10/29/cath-lab-opens/)).
- **Two fellowship-trained private electrophysiologists**: Dr Corey Smith (complex AF/VT ablation fellowship, Queen Elizabeth II Health Sciences Centre, Canada) and Dr Kieran Dauber (EP fellowship, Princess Alexandra Hospital + Loyola University Medical Centre, Chicago), both at Cairns Private Hospital with its own cath lab, 7-bed ICU/CCU and 24/7 on-call cardiology hotline ([cairnsprivate.com.au — Dr Smith](https://www.cairnsprivate.com.au/For-GPs/Specialists/cairns-private-hospital/cardiology/108732/dr-corey-smith), [Dr Dauber](https://www.cairnsprivate.com.au/For-GPs/Specialists/cairns-private-hospital/cardiology/106153/dr-kieran-dauber), [clinical services](https://www.cairnsprivate.com.au/Our-Services/Cardiac-Services)).
- **Two caveats:** (1) Dr Kevin Ng, who "started the only arrhythmia service in Far North Queensland" as Director of Cardiac EP at Cairns Hospital, relocated to the Gold Coast in 2024 — the *public* EP service is thin and succession-dependent, though Dr Rick Veasey remains as consultant EP; (2) **all cardiothoracic surgery transfers to Townsville** — 348 km / **6h 47m by road** ([drivebestway.com](https://au.drivebestway.com/distance/cairns/townsville-au/)), or ~55 minutes by air. Mater Private Hospital Townsville is the largest private cardiac facility north of Brisbane (300+ surgeries/year) ([mater.org.au](https://www.mater.org.au/health-services/our-services/cardiology/cardiac-care-at-mater-private-hospital-townsville), [townsville.health.qld.gov.au](https://www.townsville.health.qld.gov.au/services/services-a-z/cardiothoracic-surgery-services/)). Drug-managed and catheter-ablated AF is well handled locally; any surgical need breaches your 90-minute rule by road.

### Bundaberg — adequate for stable AF, fragile for anything more
- **Advara HeartCare is the sole cardiac service in Bundaberg** (clinics at Bundaberg Base Hospital and Friendly Society Private Hospital), offering ECG, Holter, echo, stress echo, TOE and cardioversion ([advaraheartcare.com/locations/base-hospital-bundaberg](https://advaraheartcare.com/locations/base-hospital-bundaberg/)). The Friendly Society cath lab is the **only one between the Sunshine Coast and Townsville**, treating 3,000+ patients annually ([thefriendlies.org.au/cath-lab](https://thefriendlies.org.au/cath-lab/)).
- **No electrophysiologist and no AF ablation capability is documented in Bundaberg.** Escalated rhythm care means transfer to the Sunshine Coast (~3.5h) or Brisbane (~4h) — historically ~1,000 patients/year were flown out.
- **Sustainability risk is severe:** a July–August 2023 ABC News investigation found the service depends on essentially two cardiologists, one (Dr Hermann Wittmer, then 65) planning retirement, with no Australian-trained doctor applying in 15 years — "if something happens to Dr Conradie, the whole thing will fall apart" ([abc.net.au/news/2023-07-27](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-07-27/fears-qld-cardiology-service-could-collapse-doctor-hiring/102735416), [abc.net.au/news/2023-08-17](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-08-17/heart-attack-man-walks-kokoda-track-fights-for-bundaberg-clinic/102735414)). As of mid-2024 the Queensland Government had not committed to a dedicated cath lab at the proposed new Bundaberg hospital.

**AF-specific summary:**

| Care modality | Toowoomba | Bundaberg | Cairns |
|---|---|---|---|
| AF consult, ECG/Holter | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| DC cardioversion / TOE | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Catheter ablation for AF | ✅ local | ❌ transfer 3.5–4h | ✅ local |
| Pacemaker/ICD | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| 24/7 STEMI | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ |
| Cardiothoracic surgery ≤90 min road | ✅ Brisbane ~1.5h | ❌ | ❌ Townsville 6h 47m |

---

## 3. Cost-of-Living Differential vs Melbourne

**Melbourne baselines (sourced):** median house value **$895,000** (Dec 2024, PropTrack — down ~$66.50/day across 2024; [realestate.com.au](https://www.realestate.com.au/news/proptrack-home-price-index-melbourne-house-values-fall-66-a-day-in-2024/)); median dwelling $777,390 (CoreLogic, Sep 2024, –1.4% YoY; [abc.net.au](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-10-01/corelogic-house-price-data-september-rise/104407384)); utilities ~$268–318/month for a single; groceries ~$451/month single ([bemoved.com.au](https://www.bemoved.com.au/blog/melbourne-cost-of-living-2023-monthly-household-expenses-breakdown)); 3-bed rent ~$3,619–4,200/month.

| Metric | Toowoomba | Bundaberg | Cairns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overall CoL (incl. rent) vs Melbourne | **–23% to –27%** (Numbeo rent –41.5%; some baskets to –36%) | –25% to –41% depending on basket | –9% to –11% |
| Single monthly spend (rent incl.) | ~$2,132 (Melbourne $2,852) | ~$2,083–2,147 | ~$2,529 |
| **Annual saving, single** | **~$8,600** | **~$8,500–14,800** | **~$3,300–3,900** |
| 3-bed rent (non-CBD) | $2,000/mo vs $3,619 (–45%) | ~$500/wk house median (saves ~$470/wk ≈ $24,400/yr vs Melbourne) | $485/wk Cairns City (saves ~$485/wk ≈ $25,200/yr) |
| Utilities | **~$108–170/mo vs $234–332 Melbourne (up to –67%)** | ~$140/mo | ~$250/mo (cooling load); but **lowest council rates/utility charges of QLD's 12 large LGAs** — 12% below Brisbane, 24% below Gold Coast ([council benchmarking](https://www.councilnews.com.au/2024/08/26701595-cairns-ratepayers-continue-to-get-value-for-money)) |
| Groceries | **–22% to –23%** | Mixed: produce cheaper, red meat/bottled water +30–60% | **+3.8% to +4.1% more expensive** (tropical freight: chicken +40%, tomatoes +19%) |

Sources: [Numbeo comparisons](https://www.numbeo.com/cost-of-living/compare_cities.jsp?city1=Melbourne&city2=Toowoomba&country1=Australia&country2=Australia), [CityCost Melbourne vs Bundaberg](https://citycost.org/compare/melbourne-vs-bundaberg/), [CityCost Melbourne vs Cairns](https://citycost.org/compare/cairns-vs-melbourne/).

**Key analytical insight: the dominant differential is housing capital, not weekly bills.** Versus Melbourne's $895k house median, buying releases approximately **$245,000 (Toowoomba, –27%), $368,000 (Bundaberg, –41%), or $240,000 (Cairns, –27%)** of capital that can be redirected to superannuation ahead of your preservation age of 60. Ongoing utility/grocery differentials are secondary (order of ±$1,000–2,000/year) and partly offsetting — Cairns adds cooling load and freight-inflated groceries; Toowoomba adds mild heating costs. If you sell in Melbourne and buy outright under $550k, eliminating rent/mortgage transforms the equation regardless of city — but Toowoomba is the only city pairing that capital release with genuinely lower weekly costs. Note that regional QLD electricity on Tariff 11 runs ~$2,845–3,205/year for 8,000 kWh, with Queensland concessions partially offsetting ([St Vincent de Paul QLD Energy Prices July 2024](https://cms.vinnies.org.au/media/vp0f1dfj/2024-qld-energy-prices.pdf)).

**Caveat on Bundaberg's range:** panel estimates of Bundaberg's saving diverge (~25% vs ~41%) because of different consumption baskets and single-vs-couple assumptions; the truth is that Bundaberg is the cheapest of the three on recurring costs either way, but the gap versus Toowoomba is mostly rent/housing-driven.

---

## 4. Property Price Trajectories 2020–2024 and the $550,000 Test

| LGA median (houses) | Dec 2020 | Sep 2021 | Sep 2022 | 2024 | 2020→2024 growth | 3-bed stratified median (Jun 2025) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Toowoomba** | $370,500 | $390,000 | $485,000 | ~$575,000 (Sep); CoreLogic Dec: $649,797 (+71% 5-yr) | **+55% to +80%** (CAGR ~11–14%) | $634,000 (+14.0% p.a. 5-yr) |
| **Bundaberg** | $295,000 | $340,000 | $449,000 | ~$520,000–527,000 | **+76% to +88%** — largest 5-yr growth of any Australian market (CoreLogic, Feb 2024) | $490,000 (+17.4% p.a. 5-yr; +21% latest year) |
| **Cairns** | $430,000–435,000 | $470,000 | $555,000 | $655,500 (annual median) | **+40% to +52%** — then **accelerated**: 2025 $745k, 2026 YTD $810k (+23.6% above 2024) | $609,750 SA4; $675,000 Cairns City |

Sources: [ABC News/REIQ regional QLD data](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2023-01-22/queensland-regional-property-prices/101874104), [REIQ 2020 QMM](https://www.reiq.com/_/media/project/reiqcom/public-website/pdfs/reiq-media-release-2020-qmm-quarterly-property-prices-12122020.pdf), [ABC Wide Bay growth](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-02-27/wide-bay-region-largest-property-price-growth-in-australia/103511804), [OpenStats Toowoomba](https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa3/toowoomba/), [OpenStats Bundaberg](https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa2/bundaberg/), [OpenStats Cairns](https://openstats.com.au/dashboards/property-prices/sa4/cairns/), [REMAX Toowoomba 2024 wrap](https://remaxsuccess.com.au/toowoomba-2024-market-wrap/), [First National Bundaberg 2024](https://firstnationalbundaberg.com.au/blog/how-did-the-bundaberg-property-market-perform-in-2024).

**Suburbs still under $550k for a 3-bed (2024 medians):**
- **Toowoomba (5–6 qualifying):** Rockville $480k, Wilsonton $502.5k, Harristown $525k, Newtown $539.5k, North Toowoomba $545k; South Toowoomba $552k just over. Toowoomba City itself ($595k) has already breached the cap, and annual growth of 6.5–12% means this window is closing. Satellite towns (Pittsworth ~$485k, Crows Nest ~$500k) extend options. Recent real sales: $494,400 (South Toowoomba, Aug 2024), $552,000 (Harristown, Feb 2024).
- **Bundaberg (10–13 qualifying):** Bundaberg Central $428k, South $457k (some sources $382k), West $452k, Oakwood $457.5k, Svensson Heights $475k, North $476k, Norville $478k, Avenell Heights $489k, Kepnock $508k, Millbank $525k. Genuine choice; only coastal Bargara ($807k) is out of reach.

**Trajectory verdict:** Bundaberg delivered the steepest appreciation with the most remaining stock under $550k; Toowoomba was close behind with a *narrowing but real* window; Cairns grew least over 2020–2024 but from a higher base and has now priced beyond your budget at the median. Because Melbourne's market is soft (–1.4% YoY, six consecutive monthly declines per [ANZ-CoreLogic](https://www.anz.com.au/content/dam/anzcomau/news/articles/2024/September/corelogic-sept-24.pdf)), there is no penalty for a measured sale — while regional QLD keeps rising, so **buying early within your 18-month window hedges further growth** (especially in Toowoomba, where the LGA median is already ~$634k).

---

## 5. Part-Time Accounting Roles at ≥$35/Hour

**Income math:** $35/hr × 30 hrs × 52 weeks = **$54,600/year** (25 hrs ≈ $45,500). SEEK's average advertised accountant salary in Toowoomba & Darling Downs is $83,812 FTE, so $35/hr part-time sits at roughly 68% of the local professional hourly norm — an achievable floor for a 28-year corporate CV, not a stretch.

- **Toowoomba — deepest verified market.** Multiple SEEK-listed part-time roles at or above your floor: Finance Officer (Part-Time) **$38–41/hr** (~30 hrs/wk); Finance Administration Officer **$35–40/hr**; TASC Bookkeeper **$43.08–$46.35/hr + salary packaging**; Findex part-time SMSF Accounting Officer/Bookkeeper (~25–30 hrs, flexible); Upscale Funds Management Experienced Bookkeeper ($80–90k FTE equivalent, "flexible part-time hours," Toowoomba or Chinchilla); Carrick Aland taxation accountant/bookkeeper ([SEEK Toowoomba part-time accounting](https://au.seek.com/part-time-accountant-jobs/in-Toowoomba-&-Darling-Downs-QLD), [TASC via EthicalJobs](https://www.ethicaljobs.com.au/members/tasc/bookkeeper-toowoomba), [SEEK salary data](https://au.seek.com/career-advice/role/accountant/salary/in-toowoomba-&-darling-downs)). Demand spans legal, health, local government, NFP, funds management and public practice — best supporting a sustained 2–4 day/week arrangement through to 60.
- **Bundaberg — thinnest.** Listings skew full-time; one explicit part-time role above your floor was captured (McCrystal Agricultural Services Bookkeeper, **$35–45/hr**, 3–4 days/week, school-hours friendly), plus council AP work (24 hrs/wk) and Q4 Accounting's flexible practice role ([SEEK Bundaberg](https://au.seek.com/part-time-accountant-jobs/in-Bundaberg-&-Wide-Bay-Burnett-QLD), [Q4 Accounting](https://www.q4accounting.com.au/join-our-team/)). Smaller regional markets also under-advertise via word-of-mouth, so real depth may exceed listings — but it is unverifiable.
- **Cairns — moderate, with the strongest single semi-retirement role.** Aggregators show volume (Jora lists 53+ part-time accounting roles; e.g., Bookkeeper $35/hr Sunshine Group, $40/hr Northern Sands; a CPA role up to $60/hr at 8 hrs/wk explicitly suited to semi-retired applicants). The standout: **Cairns Regional Council Accountant at $79,903–$90,545 pro-rata with an explicit part-time option (minimum 20 hrs/week)** ([Council Direct](https://www.councildirect.com.au/job/accountant-1730705322-672877aaee98d)) — a credible, stable semi-retirement pathway. Note the evidence conflict: SEEK-sourced data with *verified hourly rates* favours Toowoomba; Jora's raw listing count favours Cairns but with weaker rate transparency. On verified ≥$35/hr depth, Toowoomba leads; on single-employer quality, Cairns' council role is the best individual find.

**Timing note in your favour:** born ~1973, your superannuation preservation age is 60 — your planned retirement coincides exactly with super access. Part-time income of ~$45–95k from 53–60, plus concessional contributions from your $145k salary in the interim, bridges cleanly.

---

## 6. Why Not the Alternatives — and When Cairns Wins

- **Bundaberg** is the affordability champion (~$368k capital release, 10+ suburbs under $550k, cheapest recurring costs) but fails the criterion you weighted as non-negotiable: no local EP/ablation, a two-cardiologist service with documented collapse risk, and 3.5–4+ hour transfers for anything beyond medication management. It becomes viable only if your cardiologist certifies your AF as durably medication-stable *and* you accept single-point-of-failure healthcare — or if the new Bundaberg hospital gains a committed EP service.
- **Cairns** wins *if* you value EP redundancy (two fellowship-trained electrophysiologists) over surgical-backup proximity, your AF is confidently non-surgical, and you prioritise lifestyle and the council job market — accepting ~9% (not 23–27%) cost savings, groceries above Melbourne prices, and a housing market that has already moved $100k+ past your cap at the median and kept climbing. The post-2024 acceleration (median $745k in 2025, $810k in 2026 YTD) also means timeline slippage hurts most in Cairns.

---

## 7. Execution Plan for Your 18-Month Window

1. **Property:** Target **Wilsonton, Harristown, Newtown, North Toowoomba, Rockville or South Toowoomba** in the $440–545k bracket. Buy early in the window — Toowoomba's qualifying stock is shrinking at 6.5–12% annual growth. Sell Melbourne without urgency given its flat-to-falling market.
2. **Healthcare:** Before relocating, obtain a referral and transfer records from your Melbourne cardiologist to **Care Cardiology (St Andrew's) or Heart Specialists Toowoomba (St Vincent's)**; confirm EP follow-up scheduling, bulk-billing/gap arrangements, and that your private health cover recognises the St Andrew's/St Vincent's precincts.
3. **Income:** Negotiate a 3-day/week or school-hours contract in the $35–46/hr bracket; ~$75–95k pro-rata preserves your lifestyle at far lower fixed costs and can accelerate full retirement by 2–4 years relative to staying in Melbourne.
4. **Verification caveats:** All property figures are 2024-vintage medians from mixed series (CoreLogic/REIQ/PropTrack/OpenStats definitions differ); job listings are point-in-time snapshots — verify current SEEK vacancies and confirmed hourly rates, get a fresh suburb-level price read before offering, and budget for out-of-pocket cardiology gap fees (not quantified in available data), home/contents insurance differences (Cairns carries cyclone loading), and CGT/land-tax advice if you retain the Melbourne property.

**Bottom line:** Toowoomba uniquely satisfies all three of your stated constraints — ~$8,600/year recurring savings plus ~$245k housing capital release, complete AF management with the region's only 24/7 STEMI service and Brisbane surgical backup inside 90 minutes, and a verified part-time accounting market at $35–46/hour — making it the optimal relocation choice for your transition to semi-retirement.

# Carbon Pricing Implementation and Outcomes: California Cap-and-Trade, EU ETS, and China's National Carbon Market (2020–2024)

## Direct Answer: Comparative Summary

Between 2020 and 2024, the world's three flagship carbon pricing systems diverged sharply in design and outcomes while all delivering materially higher carbon prices. The **EU ETS** — an absolute, declining cap with majority auctioning — saw allowance prices roughly triple (€25/tCO₂ average in 2020 to a record €83.60 annual average in 2023, easing to ~€65 in 2024), generated €38.8–43.6 billion in annual auction revenue by 2023–24 (cumulative >€250 billion), and drove stationary emissions down 47–52% below 2005 levels, including a record ~16.5–17% single-year fall in 2023. **California's** linked California–Québec program roughly doubled prices (from ~$17 near the auction floor in 2020 to a $41.76 peak in February 2024, settling ~$30–32 by late 2024), raised ~$28–30 billion cumulatively for the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund (GGRF), and met its 2020 statewide target (431 MMTCO₂e, 1990 levels) years early — though attribution to the cap itself is entangled with dense complementary policies. **China's national ETS** — the world's largest by covered emissions (~4.5–5.1 Gt CO₂, ~40% of national emissions) but an intensity-based system with 100% free allocation — generated no government revenue, saw prices roughly double (¥46.6 average 2021 to ~¥92–96 in 2024, briefly exceeding ¥100 in April 2024), achieved 99.5–99.99% compliance, and cut power-sector carbon intensity ~8.78% since launch, without yet capping total emissions.

| Dimension | California | EU ETS | China National ETS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price 2020 → 2024 | ~$16.93 (Nov 2020) → $41.76 peak (Feb 2024), ~$30–32 late 2024 | ~€25 avg (2020) → €83.60 avg (2023) → ~€64–65 (2024) | ¥46.6 avg (2021) → ~¥92–96 avg (2024); broke ¥100 on 24 Apr 2024 |
| Cap type | Absolute, declining (~4%/yr; budget 334.2M→280.7M allowances 2020–24) | Absolute, declining; LRF 2.2% → 4.3% (2024–27), 4.4% (2028+) | Intensity-based benchmarks; no absolute cap |
| Allocation | ~50% auctioned, ~50% free | ~57% auctioned; free allocation for leakage-exposed industry | 100% free, output-based |
| Emissions outcome | 2020 target met early (in 2016); 2023 inventory 360.4 MMTCO₂e, lowest in series | Stationary –11.4% (2020), –16.5% (2023); ~47–52% below 2005 by 2023–24 | Power-sector carbon intensity –8.78% since 2021; absolute national emissions still rising (~12.6 Gt CO₂ in 2023) |
| Revenue | ~$28–30.4B cumulative GGRF | €43.6B (2023), €38.8B (2024); >€250B cumulative | None to government; ~¥43–46B private trading value |
| Compliance | Effectively universal; no mass non-compliance events | >95–99% across sectors; €100/t penalty + make-up | 99.5% (cycle 1) → 99.61%/99.88% (2021/2022) → ~99.99% (2023 cycle) |
| COVID response | Price floor + self-ratcheting of unsold allowances; no rule changes | Automatic Market Stability Reserve; no discretionary intervention; cap later *tightened* | Backloaded two-year compliance cycles; flexible compliance for 202 distressed entities |
| Leakage instrument | Output-based free allocation only; documented intra-US firm-level leakage | Free allocation + CBAM (transitional from Oct 2023; financial from Jan 2026) | Free allocation; steel/cement/aluminum expansion partly a CBAM response |

---

## 1. System Architecture and Scope

**California** (administered by CARB, linked with Québec via joint auctions) covers ~80% of state GHG emissions — power, industry, transport fuels, buildings — across ~450 entities. The annual allowance budget fell from 334.2 million (2020) to 280.7 million (2024) (17 CCR §95841), consistent with a ~4%/year cap decline. Key design features: an Auction Reserve Price floor rising 5% + inflation annually ($16.68 in 2020, ~$21.20 by 2024), a price ceiling introduced by AB 398 starting at $65/t in 2021, full banking, and offset usage limits (4% of compliance obligation 2021–2025, 6% from 2026). Sources: CARB (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/cap-and-trade/carbonallowanceprices.pdf); CRS R48314 (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48314).

**EU ETS Phase 4** covers ~40% of EU GHG emissions across >10,000 stationary installations and ~1,600 aircraft operators in the EU-27 plus Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway; maritime transport was added in 2024. The cap fell from ~1,572 million allowances (2021) to ~1,386 million (2024), with the Linear Reduction Factor raised from 2.2% to 4.3%/year (2024–2027) and 4.4% from 2028 under the Fit for 55 revision (Directive 2023/959), plus one-off rebasing reductions of 90 million allowances in 2024 and 27 million in 2026. A separate ETS-2 for buildings and road transport starts in 2027.

**China's national ETS** launched trading on 16 July 2021, covering only the power sector (including captive plants): 2,162–2,257 key emitting entities and ~4.5–5.1 Gt CO₂ annually — roughly 40% of national emissions, making it the largest carbon market by covered volume. Allocation is 100% free against output-based intensity benchmarks; there is no absolute cap. In September 2024/March 2025, China approved expansion to steel, cement, and electrolytic aluminum (~1,500 additional entities, lifting coverage toward ~8 Gt CO₂e, ~60% of national emissions) (Reuters, https://www.reuters.com/markets/carbon/china-plans-include-steel-cement-aluminium-its-carbon-market-2024-2024-09-09/; ICAP, https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/ets/china-national-ets).

---

## 2. Allowance Price Trajectories

### California (quarterly joint-auction settlement prices, CARB)

Prices hugged the floor through 2020, then climbed steadily as the steeper post-2020 cap decline became salient:

- **2020:** ~$16.93 (Nov); secondary market briefly traded *below* the $16.68 floor in March 2020 amid COVID-era liquidations and margin calls.
- **2021:** $17.80 (Feb) → $18.80 (May) → $23.30 (Aug, $5.59 above floor — a then-record premium) → $28.26 (Nov).
- **2022:** $29.15 (Feb) → $30.85 (May) → $27.00/$26.80 (Aug/Nov).
- **2023:** $27.85 (Feb) → $30.33 (May) → $35.20 (Aug) → $38.73 (Nov).
- **2024:** **$41.76 (Feb — period peak)** → $37.02 (May) → $30.24 (Aug) → ~$31.91 (Nov).

Sources: CARB auction results (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2020-08/results_summary.pdf; https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2021-08/nc-aug_2021_summary_results_report_0.pdf). The Independent Emissions Market Advisory Committee (IEMAC) attributes the post-2020 rise to expectations that regulatory reform would tighten allowance supply; the 2024 softening reflects growing recognition of an allowance surplus.

### EU ETS (EUA annual averages)

- **2020:** ~€25 average; COVID crash to ~€15.25 in March, recovery to ~€22 by June.
- **2021:** €53 — roughly tripling, driven by the Phase 4 cap tightening, coal-to-gas switching economics, and anticipation of Fit for 55 (ECB Economic Bulletin, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/focus/2021/html/ecb.ebbox202106_05~ef8ce0bc70.nl.html).
- **2022:** €80–81 average; intraday record auction price €97.51 on 8 February 2022, as the Russia-Ukraine energy crisis paradoxically reinforced the carbon signal.
- **2023:** **€83.0–83.60 — the highest annual average in system history** (ESMA Carbon Markets Report 2024, https://vertis.com/app/themes/vertis/assets/uploads/2025/09/ESMA50-43599798-10379_Carbon_markets_report_2024.pdf).
- **2024:** decline to ~€64.8 average (−22.5% YoY), reflecting weaker industrial activity, lower gas prices, accelerated renewables, and extra REPowerEU auctions.

### China (CEA allowance prices)

- **16 July 2021:** opened at ¥48, first-day average ¥51.23, closing near the daily upper limit (State Council, http://english.www.gov.cn/statecouncil/ministries/202107/17/content_WS60f210bfc6d0df57f98dd212.html).
- **Dec 2021:** all-time low ¥41.46 around the first compliance deadline.
- **2021–2022 averages:** ¥46.6 → ¥58.1 (Beijing Institute of Technology carbon-market review, via Sina Finance, https://finance.sina.com.cn/esg/2025-03-10/doc-inepeazk0663151.shtml).
- **2023:** average ¥64 (+23.2% YoY); record ¥82.79 in October; year-end close ¥79.42 — driven by tightened 2023–2024 benchmarks.
- **2024:** average ~¥91.8–96 (+43% YoY); record ¥83.33 on 8 March, then **broke ¥100 on 24 April**; year-end close ¥97.49 (NCSC, http://www.ncsc.org.cn/xwdt/gnxw/202501/t20250107_1100153.shtml; ICAP allocation-plan coverage, https://icapcarbonaction.com/en/news/china-releases-allocation-plan-power-sector-2023-and-2024).

**Comparison:** by 2024, the EU price (~€65 ≈ $70) was roughly 2× California's (~$30) and 5–7× China's (~$11–14). The gaps reflect cap stringency (absolute vs. intensity), auction share (57% vs. 50% vs. 0%), and market maturity. All three rose materially — evidence that scarcity expectations, not just spot fundamentals, drive prices (a Nature Energy 2024 finding on EU price formation applies broadly).

---

## 3. Emissions Reductions vs. Baseline Projections

### EU ETS — deepest verified cuts, but projections still short of 2030 target

Stationary verified emissions (EEA/ETC-CM and European Commission):
- 2019: 1,530 Mt → **2020: 1,355 Mt (−11.4%)**, the largest drop since 2005, from COVID demand destruction plus ongoing decarbonization; aviation collapsed 63% (https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/the-eu-emissions-trading-system-in-2021-trends-and-projections).
- 2021: ~1,364 Mt — partial rebound, still well below 2019.
- 2022: 1,313.2 Mt (stationary −1.7%; energy-crisis coal burn offset by demand destruction) (ETC-CM 2023/07, https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-cm/products/etc-cm-report-2023-07-1/@@download/file/ETC_CM_ETS%20Report_2023_07_2.pdf).
- **2023: 1,095.9 Mt (−16.5%/−17%)** — the largest annual fall in EU ETS history; combustion emissions −21%, industrial −8%; Germany and Poland alone accounted for 61% of the power-sector decline (ETC-CM 2024/09, https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-cm/products/etc-cm-report-2024-09/@@download/file/ETC_CM_2024-09-bis.pdf).
- 2024: a further ~7% decline.

Cumulatively, stationary ETS emissions fell **~47–52% below 2005** by 2023–24, against a legislated Phase 4 target of −62% by 2030 (COM(2024) 538, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX%3A52024DC0538). *Critical caveat:* Member State projections with existing measures fall short of the 2030 target — 2024 submissions projected slightly *higher* 2030 stationary emissions (+2%) than 2023 submissions, partly due to higher expected gas generation in Denmark, Estonia, Germany, and Italy. Aviation recovered to 92% of pre-pandemic levels (53.2 Mt) by 2023.

### California — target met early, but attribution is contested and a surplus looms

- Statewide inventory: 418 MMTCO₂e (2019) → 368.7 (2020, pandemic drop) → 381.3 (2021) → 371.6 (2022) → **360.4 MMTCO₂e (2023), the lowest in the 2000–2023 series**. The 2020 goal (431 MMTCO₂e = 1990 levels) was met in 2016, four years early. Emissions fell 21% from 2000–2023 while gross state product grew 81% (CARB inventory trends, https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2025-11/nc-2000_2023_ghg_inventory_trends.pdf).
- The 2017 Scoping Plan projected 2030 BAU at 389 MMTCO₂e vs. a 260 MMTCO₂e limit, with cap-and-trade expected to deliver ~60 MMTCO₂e of the gap (CARB 2022 AB 32 report, https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2022-05/2022%20Annual%20AB%2032%20Report%20to%20JLBC%20-%20Remediated.pdf).
- **Attribution problem:** CRS R48314 notes the cap-and-trade share of statewide reductions cannot be cleanly isolated from the LCFS, RPS, and vehicle standards. GGRF-funded projects claim ~97–110 MMTCO₂e cumulative reductions, but those are expenditure outcomes, not cap effects.
- **Surplus warning:** IEMAC's 2024 report finds current budgets contain more allowances through 2030 than covered entities are expected to need; CARB is weighing removal of **115–390 million allowances** by 2030 and analyzing a 48%-below-1990 cap.

### China — intensity gains, no absolute constraint

- An academic unit-level study of the first compliance cycle (2019–20) found carbon-intensity reductions of **2.46–3.13%** and absolute emission reductions of ~0.86% despite 1.63% production growth; abatement came from efficiency (57%), fuel quality (31%), and unit retirements (12%).
- MEE reports power-generation carbon intensity **down 8.78%** since the ETS opened (https://english.www.gov.cn/news/202503/27/content_WS67e487ddc6d0868f4e8f1358.html).
- Because benchmarks are output-based, total covered emissions can rise with output: national CO₂ emissions continued growing to ~12.6 Gt (2023), with coal still ~51% of electricity supply in 2025. The system's 2020–2024 function was institution-building (MRV, trading infrastructure), not absolute reduction.

---

## 4. Revenue Generation and Allocation

### California — ~$28–30 billion, statutorily earmarked

Cumulative GGRF proceeds reached **~$28 billion by May 2024 (CRS) and ~$30.4 billion by late 2024**. Annual deposits rose with prices, from ~$2.1–2.6 billion (FY2019-20/2020-21) to roughly **$4–5.1 billion annually in FY2021-22 through FY2023-24** (CARB proceeds summary, https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2020-09/proceeds_summary.pdf; LAO, https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4730).

Allocation is unusually prescriptive: **~65% continuously appropriated** — 25% High-Speed Rail, 20% Affordable Housing & Sustainable Communities, 10% Transit & Intercity Rail Capital, 5% Low Carbon Transit Operations, 5% (up to $130M) Safe & Affordable Drinking Water — plus $200M/year for forest health/wildfire prevention from FY2022-23. The remaining ~30% is legislatively appropriated. SB 535 requires ≥35% of investments to benefit disadvantaged and low-income communities. Through 2023, $27.5B had been appropriated to 90 programs across 24 agencies; the 2023 California Climate Investments report counts ~$23B provided, ~$9B implemented, **>70% of implemented funds benefiting priority populations**, and ~97 MMTCO₂e expected cumulative reductions (https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/sites/default/files/auction-proceeds/cci_annual_report_2023.pdf).

### EU ETS — €43.6B peak year, >€250B cumulative, ~76% to climate/energy

| Year | Auction revenue | Key allocations |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 | ~€14–22B (COVID-depressed) | — |
| 2021 | €31B | — |
| 2022 | €38.8B | Modernisation Fund €5.4B |
| 2023 | **€43.6B** | €33B to Member States (€30.9B subject to Art. 10(3) climate-spending rule; €22.2B reported disbursed); €7.4B Innovation + Modernisation Funds; €2.8B REPowerEU/RRF |
| 2024 | **€38.8B** | €24.4B Member States; ~€3B Innovation Fund; ~€6.3B Modernisation Fund; €5.6B REPowerEU |

Sources: Commission carbon-market reports (https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/92ec0ab3-24cf-4814-ad59-81c15e310bea_en; https://climate.ec.europa.eu/document/download/ddc1b1de-652b-49ed-8f15-d9fa8badd39f_en); EEA revenue-use indicator (https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/indicators/use-of-auctioning-revenues-generated). Cumulative revenue since 2013 exceeded €200B by end-2023 and ~€258B by 2025. Member States report spending **~76% on climate and energy** (consistent with the 2013–2020 average of 75%); ~25% is earmarked for specific actions, ~27% flows to dedicated environmental funds, and ~48% enters general budgets. The **Innovation Fund** (~€38B endowment at prevailing prices; €7.35B granted through 2024, mobilizing €12.9B) and **Modernisation Fund** channel ETS revenue to breakthrough decarbonization and lower-income Member States; a **Social Climate Fund** begins in 2026.

### China — zero fiscal revenue by design

With 100% free allocation, the state collects nothing. Market turnover (private transfers) reached ¥24.92B by end-2023 and **¥43.03B by end-2024** (~¥46.2B by mid-2025) (MEE 2024 Progress Report, https://www.mee.gov.cn/ywdt/xwfb/202407/W020240722528850763859.pdf). Second-cycle trading (263 Mt, ¥17.26B) exceeded the first cycle (179 Mt, ¥7.66B) by 19% in volume and 89% in value. Auctioning is planned only in later phases.

---

## 5. Compliance Rates

- **China (most granular reporting):** 99.5% of allowances surrendered in cycle 1 (2019–20 emissions; 2,162 entities by the 31 Dec 2021 deadline) — though only ~94% of entities were fully compliant by count, with provincial rates from 82.9% to 100%. Cycle 2 improved to **99.61% (2021) and 99.88% (2022)**; the 2023 cycle reached ~99.99%. In the 2024 cycle covering new sectors, all 1,291 steel/cement/aluminum entities complied on time and only 1 of 2,087 power entities failed to surrender. Trading participation rose to 82% of entities (+50% vs. cycle 1). *Enforcement weakness:* average penalties were only **~¥0.105/t** — versus **€100/tCO₂e plus make-up obligation in the EU** — though the May 2024 Interim Regulations strengthened MEE's penalty authority (Asia Society, https://asiasociety.org/policy-institute/ets-status-china; MEE report above; Springer, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43979-022-00035-3).
- **EU ETS:** consistently >95–99%; all installations completed verified 2020 emissions reporting by September 2021 (ETC-CME Report 9/2021). The €100/t inflation-indexed penalty plus next-year make-up sustains near-universal surrender.
- **California:** effectively universal compliance through the triennial compliance structure; no mass non-compliance events in 2020–2024. Cost-containment design (floor, ceiling, reserves, 4% offset limit) kept obligations manageable.

---

## 6. COVID-19 Disruption and Recovery

### California — shock absorbed by the floor and self-ratcheting; no rule changes

The May 2020 auction was the stress test: **only 37% of allowances sold (21.2M of 57.5M), generating ~$25M versus a typical $600–850M quarterly haul**. August recovered partially ($474M, 83% sold); November fully ($587M, sellout). The program's self-ratcheting mechanism withheld **32 million unsold allowances**, permanently removing those unsold after 24 months. CARB made no changes to the cap trajectory, banking rules, or compliance deadlines; the Auction Reserve Price prevented structural collapse even as secondary prices briefly breached the floor in March 2020. The episode exposed revenue volatility as a structural vulnerability of funding climate programs from auctions.

### EU ETS — the Market Stability Reserve passed its first real test

Prices crashed from ~€24 to ~€15.25 in March 2020 but recovered within about two months — a decisive contrast with the post-2008 decade of sub-€10 prices. The difference was the **MSR (operational since January 2019)**: when the Total Number of Allowances in Circulation (TNAC) exceeds 833 million, 24% of the surplus is withdrawn from auctions (the doubled 2019–2023 intake rate); below 400 million, 100 million is released. No discretionary COVID intervention was needed — a marked contrast with the 2009–2013 "backloading" of 900 million allowances. Analysts (CEPS, https://www.ceps.eu/ceps-publications/can-the-eu-ets-weather-the-impact-of-covid-19/) had warned even the 24% intake might prove insufficient; in practice, the rebound was so strong that the EU *tightened* the system mid-recovery via Fit for 55 (LRF to 4.3%, rebasing, maritime inclusion, ETS-2). From 2023, MSR holdings above the threshold were invalidated — Directive 2023/959 fixed that threshold at 400 million from 2024 — and the first automatic cancellations executed in 2024, contributing to **~3.2 billion allowances permanently cancelled** cumulatively. TNAC still stood at ~1.11 billion at end-2023 (271 million absorbed that year), a residual overhang. Separately, the 2022 REPowerEU plan mobilized additional auctions (including 27 million MSR allowances) to finance Russian-fossil-fuel substitution.

### China — backloaded compliance cycles as pandemic accommodation

The ETS launched mid-pandemic (July 2021) and sequenced compliance to absorb COVID disruption: cycle 1 covered 2019–2020 emissions with surrender only by 30 December 2021; cycle 2 bundled 2021–2022 into one two-year block with inter-year flexibility; **flexible compliance mechanisms (including CCER offsets) rescued 202 distressed entities**; gas-fired units and large-deficit entities received exemptions. From 2023, the system shifted to annual cycles — producing "tidal" trading, with ~79% of Q4-2024 volume clustered near the deadline.

---

## 7. Interaction with Complementary Policies

### California — cap as backstop beneath a dense policy stack, with waterbed effects

Cap-and-trade overlaps the **RPS (60% renewables by 2030; SB 100's 100% clean electricity by 2045)**, the **LCFS** (renewable diesel/biodiesel reached 56% of on-road diesel by 2023, driving a 17% drop in heavy-duty truck emissions), **Advanced Clean Cars II** (100% ZEV sales by 2035), and building electrification. Complementary measures shrink allowance demand, depressing the carbon price — IEMAC's 2024 surplus warning and the 2024 price slide from $41.76 to ~$30 reflect exactly this "waterbed effect," amplified by the 2022 federal Inflation Reduction Act. Research (Scott, ECR 2023) finds LCFS–cap interaction can even *raise* total emissions and abatement costs by incentivizing upstream fuel production outside the cap, except when the floor/ceiling binds (https://blogs.ubc.ca/jajanmaat/files/2023/05/ScottWilliam_ECR2023.pdf). The carbon price thus sets the marginal cost of *residual* abatement conditional on mandates; CARB's pending decision to remove 115–390 million allowances is the key reform lever.

### EU — from "complementary policies did the work" to genuine price-driven switching

The 2021 State of the EU ETS Report candidly concluded that pre-2021 power-sector reductions "were not [driven by] the ETS price signal... but other policies." That changed as prices exceeded €50: the JRC attributes the **39% power-sector emissions fall between 2018 and 2023** (and −47% from 2013–2023) to renewables build-out *interacting with* the carbon price, which made coal uneconomic and drove coal-to-gas switching (temporarily reversed during the 2021–22 gas crisis) (https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC138215/JRC138215_01.pdf). The record 2023 decline combined RED-driven renewables (revised target: 42.5% by 2030, aspiring to 45%), member-state coal phase-outs (Germany 2038, with 2030 ambition; Poland ~2049), REPowerEU acceleration, demand destruction, and sustained €80+ prices. Fit for 55 then raised the LRF, rebased the cap, added maritime (2024), and created ETS-2 (2027) — layering pricing onto nearly all fossil demand.

### China — ETS as efficiency incentive within a dual-carbon framework

The ETS sits atop "dual carbon" goals (peak before 2030; neutrality by 2060), record renewables deployment, and — contradictorily — continued new coal approvals (coal ≈51.1% of 2025 electricity). The 2023–2024 allocation plan tightened benchmarks across four coal categories and gas heat, and the 2024–2026 "implementation phase" for steel/cement/aluminum retains free intensity-based allocation, with tightening deferred to a "deepening phase" from 2027 (https://chinaenergyportal.org/en/work-plan-for-a-national-carbon-emissions-market-covering-the-cement-steel-and-electrolytic-aluminum-sectors-draft-for-comments/). The planned post-2025 shift of "dual control" from carbon *intensity* to *total* carbon emissions would ultimately force conversion to an absolute cap (Carbon Brief, https://www.carbonbrief.org/explainer-chinas-carbon-market-to-cover-steel-aluminium-and-cement-in-2024). At $11–14/t with free allocation, the price alone cannot drive fuel switching; complementary mandates carry the absolute-reduction burden. The CCER voluntary offset market (relaunched 2023) provides limited compliance flexibility.

---

## 8. Carbon Leakage: Evidence and Border Mechanisms

### EU — the world's first operational carbon border adjustment

Leakage protection historically ran through free allocation: 63 sectors on the carbon-leakage list (~94% of industrial ETS emissions) received **528 million free allowances in 2023, covering ~84% of industrial emissions**. The **CBAM (Regulation (EU) 2023/956, in force May 2023)** begins the transition: transitional reporting-only phase from **1 October 2023 through 2025** (first quarterly reports due 31 January 2024; rules in Implementing Regulation 2023/1773) covering **cement, iron & steel, aluminum, fertilizers, hydrogen, and electricity**; from **January 2026**, importers must buy CBAM certificates priced off EU ETS auctions, with free allocation to the same sectors phased out over **2026–2034** (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R0956; FAQ: https://taxation-customs.ec.europa.eu/system/files/2023-11/CBAM%20Frequently%20Asked%20Questions_November%202023.pdf). Early evidence: a December 2024 Centre for European Reform analysis found **no visible disruption to trade flows** in the first transitional year — importers absorbed administrative costs. Academic assessment remains skeptical that leakage was ever large (Cambridge 2024: "empirical evidence for carbon leakage remains sparse"), but CBAM's **policy-diffusion effect** is already measurable: multiple jurisdictions are adopting domestic pricing partly to retain carbon revenue at home.

### California — documented intra-US leakage, no border instrument

California relies solely on output-based free allocation (~50% of allowances). The empirical record for 2020–2024 shows real, if subtle, leakage:
- *Journal of Financial Economics* (2021): **financially constrained firms shift emissions and output from California to underutilized plants in other states**, increasing total firm emissions — "undermining the effectiveness of the policy" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X21002853).
- *Regional Studies* (2023): no detectable reduction in regional emissions or growth, but **parent-level concentration of emissions changes consistent with regulatory arbitrage** across multi-state firms (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00343404.2023.2194315).
- Norges Bank WP 18/2024: **supply-chain rewiring** — exposed customers show *rising* supply-chain emission intensity (https://www.norges-bank.no/contentassets/6d8edc6711a242ec9a5f59d7584d9a78/wp-18-2024--rewiring-supply-chians.pdf).
- Ex-ante estimates (RFF DP-16-17) had projected up to 17% output loss in glass containers and 11–14% in paperboard, autos, iron & steel, and poultry at ~$10/t without output-based rebating — the mitigation California adopted.

Modest prices ($20–40) plus free allocation have contained — but not eliminated — leakage, which manifests as intra-firm reallocation rather than plant closures.

### China — implicit protection; expansion partly *because of* CBAM

No border mechanism exists;
