## 6. First-Time vs. Experienced Shoppers × High-/Low-Context: Documented Interaction Effects

**Payment reversal.** Among **first-time shoppers in high-context cultures** (Japan, Brazil), reversal architecture functions as a *pre-purchase* confidence signal, not merely a post-purchase remedy: 60% of Japanese consumers check cancellation/modification policies *before* purchasing, and 63% want cancellation possible "until the item ships" — yet 50.5% proceed even when told cancellation is impossible, provided the policy is transparent ([jiji.com](https://jiji.com)). Transparency of the rule matters more than its generosity — a high-UAI signature. In Brazil, Decreto 7.962/2013's same-channel undo mandate plus Compra Garantida's instant refunds create the pre-commitment assurance that substitutes for Rakuten-style in-flow steps. Among **experienced** users everywhere, reversal fades as a decision factor; Mercado Livre's two-tier design (visible confirmation for new users, biometric one-click for returning) is the clearest operationalization of the experience gradient.

**Order modification windows.** Short, bright-line windows (Rakuten's and Otto Marketplace's identical 30 minutes) work in high-UAI Japan because the rule is *known and consistently enforced* — predictability, not generosity, is what high-UAI users price in. Otto's explicit "modifications are impossible after order completion; the order must be cancelled" converts ambiguity into a procedure. In low-context Germany, the 14-day Widerruf plus invoice payment makes the modification window nearly moot for experienced users — the money hasn't moved. The documented failure mode is *silent* windows: Amazon Japan's invisible 5-minute grace period generated the consumer-affairs complaints.

**Mistake acknowledgment.** The cultural signature is sharpest here. Internal-attribution apology ("our mistake") significantly outperforms denial in trust repair for high-UAI-adjacent users (743-observation US–Korea study). Rakuten's お手数 phrasing, its pre-emptive anti-duplicate guidance, and Otto's AGB clause waiving consequences for late defect reports are three formally different mechanisms — apology, pre-emption, liability waiver — achieving the same end: removing the user's fear that *their* error will be punished. Brazilian copy achieves it relationally ("Não se preocupe! … devolvemos 100% do seu dinheiro").

**Confidence and repeat purchase.** Documented chain: 80% of Japanese consumers have experienced checkout dissatisfaction, and ~70% of those say they would not buy from that shop again ([commercepick.com](https://commercepick.com)) — in a high-UAI, high-context market, a single error-handling failure is a churn event, consistent with UAI moderating the satisfaction→reuse link. Japan's 63.2% abandonment (APAC's lowest) and Rakuten's category-leading 3.8% conversion align with confirmation-heavy UX *serving* its population. # Legal Research Brief: Slavery Statutes and Trade Law in the 1730s British Empire

## The Most Important Finding First

**One correction that will save you from a factual error in the novel: the Molasses Act (1733) contains no language classifying enslaved people as property or chattels.** It is purely a customs statute. The explicit "chattels" language you want lives in three other places:

1. **The colonial slave codes** — above all South Carolina's Negro Act of 1740 (which codified 1730s practice), Barbados's 1661 code and 1668 "Real Estate" Act (both still in force in the 1730s), and Jamaica's 1696 code (the governing statute of your decade).
2. **The imperial statute that actually did what you're imagining the Molasses Act did**: the **Colonial Debts Act of 1732 (5 Geo. II, c. 7)**, which made enslaved people seizable as "goods" for debts across the colonies. Holly Brewer's 2021 article (below) identifies this — passed one year before the Molasses Act — as Parliament's decisive intervention on slave property in your decade.
3. The most quotable single passage, bar none, is **Section I of the South Carolina Negro Act of 1740**, which packs both "subjects of property" and "chattels personal... to all intents, constructions and purposes whatsoever" into one sentence.

**Where the texts live:** Your assumption is partly right. The enrolled original of the Molasses Act is at The National Archives, Kew (under 6 Geo. II, c. 13), but it is not freely digitized; the canonical print text is Pickering's *Statutes at Large*, vol. XVI, pp. 374–379. Colonial acts survive as session laws and in the Colonial Office records at Kew (CO 30/2 for Barbados, CO 137 for Jamaica), and — most usefully for you — in the **Laws of Enslavement and Freedom database at the University of New Brunswick** (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/), which is searchable by colony and year and covers Jamaica and Barbados well. South Carolina's acts are in Thomas Cooper and David J. McCord, eds., *Statutes at Large of South Carolina* (10 vols., 1836–1841), vol. VII.

---

## 1. The Statutory Language

### A. The Molasses Act, 1733 (6 Geo. II, c. 13)

Long title: **"An act for the better securing and encouraging the trade of his Majesty's sugar colonies in America."** Royal assent 17 May 1733; duties effective 25 December 1733. The operative text (Pickering's version, as transcribed at https://statutes.org.uk/site/the-statutes/eighteenth-century/1733-6-george-2-c-13-the-molasses-act/ and https://www.originalsources.com/Document.aspx?DocID=IAFKKB9RUXAN3CV):

> "WHEREAS the welfare and prosperity of your Majesty's sugar colonies in America are of the greatest consequence and importance to the trade, navigation and strength of this kingdom: and whereas the planters of the said sugar colonies have of late years fallen under such great discouragements, that they are unable to improve or carry on the sugar trade upon an equal footing with the foreign sugar colonies, without some advantage and relief be given to them from Great Britain: for remedy whereof … be it enacted … That from and after the Twenty-fifth Day of December, One thousand seven hundred and thirty three … there shall be raised, levied, collected and paid, unto and for the use of his Majesty … upon all rum or spirits of the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies or plantations in America, **not in the possession or under the dominion of his Majesty** … the sum of **nine pence**, money of Great Britain, for every gallon thereof … and upon all molasses or syrups of such foreign produce or manufacture as aforesaid … the sum of **six pence** of like money for every gallon thereof … and upon all sugars and paneles of such foreign growth, produce or manufacture as aforesaid … a duty after the rate of **five shillings** of like money, for every hundred weight Avoirdupois."

Note the vocabulary: duties, gallons, hundredweight, "foreign produce." Nothing about persons. If a character in your novel needs an *imperial* statute that treats human beings as merchandise, use the **1732 Colonial Debts Act**, which Brewer describes as Parliament's ratification of the principle that in the colonies "people could be simple property and recoverable like 'goods' for debts."

### B. South Carolina: The Negro Act of 1740 (Act No. 670)

This is the period's most explicit statutory dehumanization, passed in direct response to the **Stono Rebellion of 9 September 1739** — which makes 1739–1740 a natural dramatic pivot for your book. Preamble and Section I:

> "WHEREAS, in his Majesty's plantations in America, slavery has been introduced and allowed, and the people commonly called negroes, Indians, mulatos and mestizos have been deemed **absolute slaves**, and **the subjects of property in the hands of particular persons**, the extent of whose power over slaves ought to be settled and limited by positive laws so that the slaves may be kept in due subjection and obedience …
>
> "Be it enacted … That all negroes, Indians, (free Indians in amity with this government, and negroes, mulattoes and mustizoes, who are now free, excepted,) mulattoes or mustizoes who now are, or shall hereafter be, in this Province, and all their issue and offspring, born or to be born, shall be, and they are hereby declared to be, and remain forever hereafter, **absolute slaves, and shall follow the condition of the mother, and shall be deemed, held, taken, reputed and adjudged in law, to be chattels personal, in the hands of their owners and possessors, and their executors, administrators and assigns, to all intents, constructions and purposes whatsoever**."

(Full text: https://www.scpronet.com/modjeskaschool/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/9-an-act-for-better-ordering-slavecodes1740.pdf; also https://billofrightsinstitute.org/activities/an-act-for-the-better-ordering-and-governing-negroes-and-other-slaves-south-carolina-1740/.)

**Crucial nuance for a 1730–1739 setting:** this language was not yet on the books during most of your decade. South Carolina's operative law was a chain of earlier codes — 1690/91 (No. 57), 1695/6 (No. 141), 1698 (No. 168), 1701 (No. 191a), and 1712 (No. 314) — under which enslaved people were already treated as property "at first by custom and later via statute" (Lee B. Wilson, *Bonds of Empire*, 2021). A novel set in 1738 can have a lawyer character note that the chattel principle is settled practice; a novel set in 1741 can quote the new formula verbatim. The 1740 act also barred enslaved testimony against whites — a detail with obvious courtroom-scene potential.

### C. Barbados: The 1661 Code, the 1668 "Real Estate" Act, and 1730s Amendments

Barbados's foundational statute — **"An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes" (1661)**, the first comprehensive slave code in the English-speaking Americas — remained the governing law of your decade. Its preamble supplies two of the most quoted dehumanizing formulations in the entire corpus:

- The enslaved as **"an heathenish brutish & an unsertain dangerous kind of people"**;
- The statute's protective purpose framed as protecting them **"as we do men's other goods and Chattels."**

The explicit *property classification* was then fixed by **"An Act declaring the Negro Slaves of this Island to be Real Estate" (1668)** and a **1672 declarative act** — enslaved people descended with land, were subject to dower and entail, rather than passing as moveables. Both were still operative in the 1730s. (Index and texts via the UNB database: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1661 and the Barbados location page; the 1661 code is also transcribed at https://slaverylawpower.org/barbados-huntington/; William Rawlin's 1699 *Laws of Barbados* is on EEBO: https://quod.lib.umich.edu/e/eebo2/A30866.0001.001.)

The 1730s Barbadian legislation was amendatory and control-focused, not definitional — useful if you want a character reading "the new act":

- **1731:** *An Act for the punishment of Run-away Slaves, and of Slaves who shall willfully entertain, harbour and conceal any Run-away Slaves*
- **1733 (passed 22 May):** *An Act for the better governing of Negroes; and the more effectual preventing the inhabitants of this island, from employing their Negroes or other Slaves, in selling or bartering* — a restriction on enslaved people's independent economic activity
- **1739:** *An Act for amending … an Act for the Governing of Negroes, and for providing a proper Maintenance and Support for such Negroes, Indians, or Mulattoes as shall be hereafter manumitted or set free* — i.e., pushing the cost of freedpeople onto manumitters

Jerome Handler's 2016 article (below) is essential here: in Barbados, chattel status "was established in custom long before any slave laws were passed," and the three defining features — chattel property, lifetime servitude, hereditary status through the mother — were "implicit in any Barbados law that mentioned slaves" rather than declared in any single clause. That is why the strongest Barbadian "property" quotes are 1661/1668 vintage even for a 1730s story.

### D. Jamaica: The 1696 Code and the 1730s Acts

Jamaica's governing statute through your decade was **"An Act for the Better Order and Government of Slaves" (1696)**. Its most property-explicit surviving language is the recording-of-sales clause (quoted in the preamble of the 1755 revision, https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1755):

> "… the clerks of the peace, or clerks of the vestry … shall keep a distinct book, in which entries shall be made of all slaves sold and disposed of from one party to another … in every of which entries shall be expressed the time of the sale made, with the names of the vender and vendee, the name and mark of the slave or slaves, with the consideration for which sold: which said entry … shall be held, deemed, and adjudged to be a sufficient record and evidence in any court of record…"

Note the ledger-like treatment: name, **mark**, consideration — a slave sale recorded like a land conveyance. Earlier Jamaican law had already grouped the enslaved with livestock: the 1683/1684 acts "labelled enslaved people as 'negroes' and grouped them together with cattle, horses, and 'utensils,'" listing them with "all other goods and chattels."

The 1730s Jamaican statutes give you period-specific color:

- **1725:** *An Act to inflict further and other Punishments on the Transgressors of two several Acts, the one intituled, An Act for the better Order and Government of slaves, and the other intituled, An Act to prevent the enticing or inveigling of Slaves from the Possessors…* (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1725) — the "in-force" punishment statute of the decade.
- **1730:** *An Act to prevent the selling of Powder to rebellious, or any other Negroes whatsoever* — arms control in the Maroon War decade.
- **1735:** An act against hawking and peddling: no "mulatto, Indian, or negro whatsoever, shall hawk or carry about to sell from place to place, or shall sell in any open street or market, any sort or sorts of goods, wares, or merchandises whatsoever."
- **1736 (c. 5), §9:** Regulating debt executions — when "any slave or slaves, taken on any writ or writs of venditioni, shall be exposed to sale," the provost-marshal "shall sell all such slaves singly, **unless in cases of families**." This is a striking scene-ready detail: the law acknowledged families only at the auction block, and only to decide whether to break the lot.
- **1736 (c. 9):** Against "entertaining, concealing, or carrying off … any white men or women servants, or slaves," requiring owners' certificates for hiring enslaved people from vessels.
- **1739 (12 May): The Maroon War Settlement Act**, ending the war with Cudjoe's people — and doing so with revealing property language:

> "… no person whatsoever give any interruption, or presume to seize upon, or detain the said negroes, or any of them, **upon a pretence or claim of property**, or disturb the said negroes in the possessions and privileges granted … by the said articles of agreement…" (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1739)

The treaty only worked by *suspending* the default rule — that any Black person could be seized "upon a claim of property." That default rule is exactly the legal atmosphere of your novel.

A cautionary archival note: the full text of the Barbados 1733 act could not be verified against the UNB database directly; its date and title come from the database index. Before printing any verbatim quotation in a published novel, check it against TNA CO 30/2 or Richard Hall's contemporary compilation, *Acts, Passed in the Island of Barbados. From 1643, to 1762* (London, 1764). For Jamaica, John Lunan's *An Abstract of the Laws of Jamaica Relating to Slaves* is the standard near-contemporary digest.

---

## 2. Parliamentary Law vs. the Colonial Codes on Control and Punishment

The cleanest summary: **in the 1730s, Parliament said what owners *owned*; the colonial assemblies said what enslaved people *could and could not do*.** Five structural differences:

1. **Subject matter.** Imperial law — the 1732 Colonial Debts Act, the **1729 Yorke-Talbot Opinion** (holding that an enslaved person did not become free by reaching Britain or by baptism), King's Bench precedent — regulated the *enforceability of slave property*: debt recovery, cross-jurisdictional status, commercial transactions. The colonial codes regulated *internal discipline*: movement passes, assembly, diet and clothing, manumission, the legal disabilities of free Black people, and capital offenses specific to slavery (arson, poisoning, striking a white person, rebellion, running away).

2. **Mechanism and vocabulary.** Parliament spoke the language of property, contract, and remedy — "goods," debts, duties, plantations. The colonial codes spoke of **"absolute slaves," "chattels personal," "real estate,"** and (Barbados 1661) a "heathenish brutish … kind of people." No 1730s Parliamentary statute prescribed a single plantation punishment; the codes prescribed them in detail.

3. **Punishment severity.** The Barbados 1661 code gave masters near-complete dominion over the life and death of the enslaved: a first offense of striking a Christian meant severe whipping; a second, having "his or her nose slit and … burnt in the face"; a third, death. Theft, arson, rape, and rebellion were capital. The codes authorized branding, mutilation, and burning alive. English law, by contrast, maintained (until *Somerset* in 1772, and even then ambiguously) a legal fiction that slavery was not positively established in England — Parliament legislated *around* slavery, never a unified imperial slave criminal code.

4. **Trial procedure.** Enslaved defendants were tried outside common-law jury trial: in Jamaica by panels of justices and freeholders; in South Carolina (after 1740) by any two justices of the peace plus three freeholders; in Barbados by magistrates with limited appeal. None of these met English common-law criminal standards.

5. **Enforcement machinery.** Colonial codes ran through militias, patrols, and special slave courts; Parliamentary law ran through Vice-Admiralty courts and Privy Council appeal. Formally, colonial statutes could not be "repugnant" to English law and required Crown approval — which is why recent scholarship stresses *continuity*, not divergence, between the two systems.

**The recent scholarly reframing matters for your novel's legal texture.** Lee B. Wilson (*Bonds of Empire*, 2021) argues colonial slave law "was not 'a legal aberration' … it 'was a natural extension' of the English legal system" — colonists built slave law out of English writs, equity procedure, and property categories. Holly Brewer (2021) pushes the point to the metropole: Charles II's judges in the 1660s–1680s created a common law of slavery (people could be "goods" if "infidels," with perpetual, hereditary status), Sir John Holt's post-1688 pushback was itself reversed, and **Parliament's 1732 Colonial Debts Act ratified the whole structure for the colonies**. The Barbados legislators themselves claimed the opposite — that in all the "Lawes of England" there was "noe tract to guide us where to walke, nor any rule sett us, how to governe such Slaves" (1661 preamble). That tension — colonists simultaneously inventing slave law and denying they were inventing it — is a gift for a novelist writing lawyers or planters.

One more mechanism worth dramatizing: litigants in colonial Vice-Admiralty courts "transformed [them] into slave courts by analogizing human beings to ships and cargo," using ordinary English commercial procedure to enforce property in people (see the 2020 chapter "'Negroes Goods and Merchandizes,'" below). Wilson adds the credit dimension: treating the enslaved as pure chattels personal "expand[ed] their credit with British merchants" — the property classification was load-bearing for the entire Atlantic credit system.

---

## 3. Recent Peer-Reviewed Scholarship (2015–2025)

Core works, roughly in order of usefulness for your project:

1. **Holly Brewer, "Creating a Common Law of Slavery for England and its New World Empire," *Law and History Review* 39, no. 4 (Nov. 2021): 765–834.** https://doi.org/10.1017/S0738248021000407. The single most important recent piece for your decade: judges created the common-law infrastructure of chattel slavery, and Parliament's **1732** act confirmed it for the colonies. Directly supports using the Colonial Debts Act as your imperial-era legal anchor.

2. **Lee B. Wilson, *Bonds of Empire: The English Origins of Slave Law in South Carolina and British Plantation America, 1660–1783* (Cambridge UP, 2021).** Book-length treatment of your exact question: how English and colonial slave law interlocked. Reviewed favorably in *William and Mary Quarterly* (2022, https://doi.org/10.1353/wmq.2022.0029) and elsewhere. Strongest on how categorization itself dehumanized: colonists "rendered factual what had been a mere supposition: that Africans were less than human."

3. **Jerome S. Handler, "Custom and Law: The Status of Enslaved Africans in Seventeenth-Century Barbados," *Slavery & Abolition* 37, no. 2 (2016): 233–255.** https://doi.org/10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436. Chattel status preceded codification; the three features (chattel property, lifetime servitude, maternal inheritance) were "part of the culture of the Euro-Atlantic world" before any statute said so.

4. **John Samuel Harpham, "Two Concepts of a Slave in the South Carolina Law of Slavery," *Slavery & Abolition* 39, no. 1 (2018): 101–122.** https://doi.org/10.1080/0144039X.2017.1323704. The slave in S.C. law was simultaneously legal person and property; neither conception reduced to the other, and "both were essential to a legal regime intended at root to establish and preserve white control." Traces the shift into and out of the 1740 chattels-personal formula.

5. **"'Negroes Goods and Merchandizes': Legal Language and the Dehumanization of Slaves in British Vice Admiralty Courts, 1700–1763," in *Slavery, Law, and Power* (2020).** https://doi.org/10.1108/S1059-433720200000083005. Your period exactly; how admiralty procedure made chattel status routine.

6. **"A 'Manifest Violation' of the Rights of Englishmen: Rights Talk and the Law of Property in Early Eighteenth-Century Jamaica," *Law and History Review*.** https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-history-review/article/abs/manifest-violation-of-the-rights-of-englishmen-rights-talk-and-the-law-of-property-in-early-eighteenthcentury-jamaica/05CB34BAA228CCA4D699C64054DD25E8. A 1706 Jamaican escheat case over "the Negro Woman Slave Commonly Called Catalina" and her "Seaven Pickaninny" — colonial courts treating the enslaved as recoverable, alienable property subject to royal prerogative, a generation before your setting.

7. **Bridget Brereton, "Perceptions of French and Spanish Slave Law in Late Eighteenth-Century Britain," *Journal of British Studies* 57, no. 1 (2018).** Useful comparative framing — British commentators believed French and Spanish codes more "humane," which tells you how Britons thought about their own codes.

8. **Padraic X. Scanlan, "Slaves and Peasants in the Era of Emancipation," *Journal of British Studies* 59, no. 3 (2020): 495–520.** https://doi.org/10.1017/jbr.2020.39. Later period, but on how "peasantry" rhetoric competed with chattel framing.

9. **Patricia Hagler Minter, "'The State of Slavery': *Somerset*, *The Slave, Grace*, and the Rise of Pro-Slavery and Anti-Slavery Constitutionalism," *Slavery & Abolition* 36, no. 4 (2015): 603–617.** How the eighteenth-century status quo was re-litigated after 1772.

10. **Justine K. Collins, "The Impact of British Parliamentary Legislations on Enslaved Women of the British Caribbean," *Australian Feminist Law Journal* 47, no. 1 (2021): 85–103.** Identifies the three legal transformations: defining the enslaved as property, establishing control, and legally constructing race.

Two slightly older but indispensable items in your target journals: **Edward B. Rugemer, "The Development of Mastery and Race in the Comprehensive Slave Codes of the Greater Caribbean during the Seventeenth Century," *William and Mary Quarterly* 70, no. 3 (2013): 429–458** (traces the borrowing chain Barbados 1661 → Jamaica 1664/1684 → South Carolina 1691), and James Robertson on a mid-1740s Jamaican pamphlet, *Slavery & Abolition* 33, no. 1 (2012). Also note the 2022 *Law and History Review* response piece to Brewer, "Slavery, Law, and Race in England and its New World Empire," which complicates her thesis with a racial-formation lens — worth reading so your legal scenes don't lean on one scholar uncontested.

---

## 4. The Molasses Act Debate: What Recent Scholars Actually Argue

Your framing contains a premise worth correcting before it gets into the book: **no recent scholar seriously argues the Molasses Act was about slave control.** The live debate is between two older positions, with a newer third strand recontextualizing both:

**Position A — Protective tariff.** The standard view (Albert Southwick's classic 1951 *WMQ* piece; Jacob Price, "The Molasses Act and the Market Strategy of the British Sugar Planters," *Journal of Economic History*): the duties were **prohibitive by design, not revenue-raising**. The West India sugar lobby — one of the era's most effective lobbies (see William Pettigrew's work on the "West India Lobby, 1714–60") — pushed the act through to stop New England merchants buying cheaper French, Dutch, and Spanish molasses after France liberalized its colonial trade in 1717. The duty was set at 6d per gallon precisely so it would *never be collected*; deterrence was the point. The preamble's own language ("unable to improve or carry on the sugar trade upon an equal footing with the foreign sugar colonies") supports this reading.

**Position B — Revenue measure in disguise, and precedent for parliamentary taxation.** Associated with Bailyn and revisionist imperial historians: the act's wording was deliberately ambiguous — "a trade regulation in the form of a revenue act" — and its preamble used taxation language ("given and granted unto your Majesty"). After 1763, British officials cited it as precedent that Parliament *could* tax America; Americans insisted it was a mere trade regulation. This reading matters less for the 1730s than for your characters' grandchildren in 1765.

**Position C — The recent synthesis: trade regulation inseparable from the slave economy.** Newer scholarship (e.g., Eva Landsberg's 2024 Yale dissertation, "The Politics of Sugar: Caribbean Roots of the American Revolution") reframes the question: the act did not regulate *slavery*, but everything it touched *was* slavery. The New England–foreign Caribbean trade it taxed carried the provisions (fish, lumber, grain, livestock) that fed enslaved plantation populations; the molasses was grown by enslaved people; the rum distilled from it was the currency of the African slave trade — by 1772 roughly **75 percent of rum exported to Africa came from Boston and Rhode Island**. Landsberg frames the century-long conflict as "commercial, settler-colonial societies" versus "extractive, plantation-based monocultures." On this view, "trade regulation vs. slave control" is a false binary for the 1730s: the act was presented as a tariff, functioned as a subsidy to British slave-plantation competitiveness, and intervened at a critical node of the triangular trade — without ever mentioning a human being.

**For the novel:** a well-informed character in 1734 would argue about French competition, planter lobbying, and New England smuggling (the act was notoriously under-enforced — "salutary neglect"). No one would describe it as a slave law. If a scene requires an imperial statute that legally *thingifies* a person in 1732–1739 London, the Colonial Debts Act of 1732 is your document.

---

## 5. Practical Recommendations

- **Best single quotation:** South Carolina 1740, §I (preamble + "chattels personal … to all intents, constructions and purposes whatsoever"). If your book ends before mid-1740, either set the final act after Stono (September 1739) and let the new code arrive as a plot event — the rebellion genuinely terrified the lowcountry into legislative action — or use the pre-1740 acts and have a character remark that everyone already treats enslaved people as chattels "by custom."
- **Jamaica, 1730s:** quote the 1696 recording-of-sales clause for property status; the 1725 act for punishment; the 1736 "sell all such slaves singly, unless in cases of families" clause for an auction or debt-execution scene; the 1739 Maroon Settlement for the revealing phrase "upon a pretence or claim of property."
- **Barbados, 1730s:** the 1661 preamble ("heathenish brutish…"; "as we do men's other goods and Chattels") and the 1668 "Real Estate" act for property status — both still governing law; the 1731 and 1733 acts for "current legislation" texture.
- **Imperial contrast:** pair any colonial code with the 1732 Colonial Debts Act (Brewer 2021) and the 1729 Yorke-Talbot Opinion to show how Westminster enabled slave property without ever writing a slave code.
- **Verification before publication:** confirm the Barbados 1733 and Jamaica 1725 texts against TNA originals (CO 30/2; CO 137) or the period compilations (Hall for Barbados, 1764; the *Laws of Jamaica* and Lunan's *Abstract*), since digital transcriptions of those two acts could not be fully cross-checked here. The Molasses Act, South Carolina 1740, Barbados 1661/1668, and Jamaica 1696 texts above are corroborated across multiple independent reproductions and are safe to quote.

**Bottom line:** the legal architecture of your novel's world is a two-story structure — colonial codes below, prescribing whipping, mutilation, and death in granular detail, and imperial law above, silently guaranteeing that the people subjected to those codes could be bought, sold, mortgaged, and seized for debt like any other merchandise. The Molasses Act belongs to the second story, and only to the economics of it; the first story is where your chattel language lives.

final.content:
# New Zealand Structural Steel Fabrication Market Analysis, 2018–2024

**Scope note:** This report covers structural/construction steel fabrication only — fabrication of beams, columns, trusses, portal frames and bridge steelwork for buildings and civil structures. Primary steelmaking (New Zealand Steel/Glenbrook; Pacific Steel) is treated as a supply input, not as fabrication market revenue. Reinforcing bar/mesh is excluded from the fabrication market definition except where explicitly noted.

---

## Executive Summary

- New Zealand's structural steel fabrication sector produces a remarkably stable **~100,000 tonnes per annum** (2018–2024, Steel Construction New Zealand), but installed capacity was expanded from ~120,000t to **~150,000t by 2023**, leaving **~41% spare capacity** heading into the 2023–2024 construction downturn.
- The broader metal product manufacturing sector (Stats NZ ANZSIC C21+C22) grew from **~NZ$11.1bn sales in 2018 to a ~NZ$15.0bn peak in 2022**, then contracted to **~NZ$13.3bn in 2024**. IBISWorld sizes the structural steel fabricating sub-sector at **~NZ$1.8bn (2026 estimate, 2.1% CAGR 2021–26)**.
- Import tariffs on raw steel are **low (0–5% MFN) and mostly eliminated to 0% under FTAs**; tariffs are a minor margin driver compared with labour, capacity utilisation, FX and mill pricing.
- Three steel-intensive anchor projects — **City Rail Link (~29,600t structural steel), Auckland Airport's domestic jet terminal (~4,600t+ first-stage contract), and the New Dunedin Hospital (~11,000t)** — sit within a **NZ$204bn National Infrastructure Pipeline** (Dec 2024).
- Key risks: demand cyclicality/overcapacity, import-supply concentration, and embodied-carbon procurement requirements. Key opportunities: the infrastructure pipeline, local-content/SFC quality differentiation, and low-carbon "green steel" positioning via NZ Steel's $300m Electric Arc Furnace.

---

## (a) Market Size and Growth, 2018–2024

### Revenue — official statistics

No single Stats NZ series isolates structural steel fabrication; the closest official aggregates are ANZSIC **C21+C22 (Primary Metal + Fabricated Metal Product Manufacturing)** from the Economic Survey of Manufacturing, and **C2221 (Structural Steel Fabricating)** from Business Demography data.

**Sales of Metal Product Manufacturing (C21+C22), Stats NZ quarterly, aggregated annually (NZ$m, current prices):**

| Year | Annual sales (NZ$m) | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 2018 | ~11,141 | Q1 2,520 + Q2 2,832 + Q3 2,928 + Q4 2,861 |
| 2019 | ~11,472 | |
| 2020 | ~11,930 | COVID year — resilient |
| 2021 | ~13,579 | Construction boom |
| 2022 | ~14,968 | Peak; peak quarter Q3 2022 = $3,937m |
| 2023 | ~14,511 | Downturn begins |
| 2024 | ~13,333 | ~9% below 2023 average quarterly sales |

Source: Stats NZ, Economic Survey of Manufacturing, via Figure.NZ ([chart](https://figure.nz/chart/hbDmsIotoa3duUzT-Dwlp00904TYKse2n)). This overstates the structural-steel subset (it includes all fabricated metal plus primary metal forming). The GDP contribution series for C22 specifically is available via Stats NZ national accounts / [Figure.NZ](https://figure.nz/chart/Ca2YJ0fZPUM3k0NR-sadrd3NXQ6Ox6wTk).

**Sub-sector estimates:**
- **IBISWorld, "Structural Steel Fabricating in New Zealand"** (report release January 2026): market size **~NZ$1.8bn**, **2.1% CAGR 2021–2026** ([ibisworld.com](https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/)).
- **MBIE context**: total construction activity was **NZ$60.8bn in 2023**, forecast to fall to **~NZ$55.1bn in 2025** and recover to NZ$63.7bn by 2029; non-residential building fell from a NZ$13.7bn peak (2023) to ~NZ$11.8bn (2024); infrastructure held steady at ~NZ$13.6bn/yr through 2024–2027 ([MBIE National Construction Pipeline Report 2024](https://www.mbie.govt.nz/dmsdocument/29978-national-construction-pipeline-report-2024)).

**Market indicator — Steel & Tube Holdings (NZX:STU), NZ's largest steel distributor** (a volume proxy, not a pure fabricator):

| FY (June) | Revenue | Volume | YoY signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY22 | NZ$599.1m | ~167,000t | Peak |
| FY23 | NZ$589.1m | 146,409t | Volume −12.4%; NPAT −43.7% |
| FY24 | NZ$479.1m | 115,535t | Revenue −18.7% |
| FY25 | NZ$385.4m | 101,716t | Revenue −~20% |

Sources: [FY23 NZX results announcement, 20 Aug 2023](https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642); [FY23 Annual Report](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/st_file_list/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20-%20FY23%20Annual%20Report2.pdf); [FY24 Results Presentation](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20FY24%20Results%20Presentation.pdf); [FY25 results](https://steelandtube.co.nz/investor/media/2025/steel-tube-fy25-results).

### Employment

Two complementary series:

- **Stats NZ Business Demography, ANZSIC C2221 (Structural Steel Fabricating)**: **4,250 employees (Feb 2018) → 4,600 peak (Feb 2023) → 4,450 (Feb 2024)** → 4,100 (Feb 2025). Enterprise count: 285 (2018) → 294 (2023) → 285 (2024) ([Figure.NZ / Stats NZ](https://figure.nz/chart/tAQeOoJ0aDCZo3ER-k2pX8VwdLmexeE2c)).
- **SCNZ industry estimate**: **~5,000 workers** across the structural steel sector, consistently cited 2019–2023 ([SCNZ Industry Update, Sep 2023](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)).
- Broader structural metal product manufacturing (C222): ~14,550 filled jobs at Q2 2023 peak, easing to ~13,350 by Q4 2024 (Stats NZ LEED via Figure.NZ).

### Tonnage fabricated

Per SCNZ quarterly Industry Updates ([scnz.org](https://scnz.org/steel-construction/structural-steel-industry-updates/)):

| Period | Output (t/yr) | Installed capacity | Spare capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2019–2020 | ~100,000 | 120,000t | 47% (Jun 2020) |
| 2021 | ~100,000 | 120,000t | 34% (Sep 2021) |
| 2022 | ~100,000 | 120,000t | 26% (Dec 2022) |
| 2023 | ~100,000 | **150,000t** | **41% (Sep 2023)** |

Fabricator count grew from ~127 (2021) to ~149 (mid-2022) to **153 (2023)**; ~96% of sector output is now delivered by SFC (Steel Fabrication Certification)-qualified fabricators ([SCNZ Local Industry](https://scnz.org/steel-in-nz/local-industry); [SCNZ IU Sep 2023](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)). Structural steel holds ~50% share of multi-storey construction nationally and >80% in Christchurch (near zero pre-2010 earthquakes).

**Key insight:** Tonnage was flat at ~100,000t/yr across the whole period while firms invested in capacity — meaning the 2021–22 boom was absorbed as margin/utilisation gains, and the 2023–24 downturn immediately translated into overcapacity rather than volume collapse. Implied value-add is roughly NZ$15,000–18,000 per fabricated tonne (sector revenue ÷ tonnage).

---

## (b) Top 5 Structural Steel Fabricators

**Caveat:** No comprehensive disclosed-revenue ranking exists; most NZ fabricators are private. The ranking below anchors on IBISWorld's analyst revenue estimates (the only published revenue-based ranking), cross-checked against capacity, facility and headcount disclosures. Two borderline cases are flagged: **Pacific Steel** (IBISWorld's #2 at ~NZ$71m) is excluded from the top 5 because it manufactures reinforcing bar rather than fabricating structural steelwork; **Steel & Tube** is included with the caveat that ~85% of revenue is distribution.

| # | Company | Ownership | Scale / Revenue | Key sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Culham Engineering Company Ltd** (Whangarei; also Tokoroa, Kawerau) | Private — Rob Kirwan (MD since 2015) and partners took full ownership from the Culham family in 2021; held via Sentinel Equities Ltd (66.67%), J. Kirwan (16.67%), K. Kirwan (16.67%) through Culham Holdings (Whangarei) Ltd | **~NZ$148m** (IBISWorld 2026 est., group incl. heavy engineering/construction); 450+ staff (scalable to ~1,000); 8.3ha Whangarei site; lead installer on NZ Steel's $300m EAF project | [IBISWorld](https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/) (Jan 2026); [culham.co.nz](https://culham.co.nz/who-we-are/); [Business Central, Oct 2024](https://digitalpublications.online/waterfordpress/business-central-october-24/79/) |
| 2 | **Steel & Tube Holdings Ltd** (NZX: STU) | Publicly listed (NZX) | **NZ$589.1m FY23 revenue; 146,409t** sold; ~900 staff, 35 sites. Manufactures purlins, joists, universal beams, ComFlor, mesh, roofing — but identifies primarily as a distributor/processor | [FY23 Annual Report (Aug 2023)](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/st_file_list/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20-%20FY23%20Annual%20Report2.pdf); [NZX announcement 20 Aug 2023](https://www.nzx.com/announcements/416642) |
| 3 | **D&H Steel Construction Ltd** (Henderson, Auckland) | Private (NZBN 9429039599070, est. 1972/87) — M.G. Sullivan 55% (Duthco Trustees), W. Carson 25%, D. Pouwhare 10% | **~NZ$45m** (IBISWorld 2026 est.); in-house **250–400t/week** fabrication; first NZ fabricator with SFC Construction Category 4 + AS/NZS ISO 3834 Part 2; delivering ~4,600t for Auckland Airport terminal and Dunedin Hospital steel (JV with John Jones Steel) | [IBISWorld](https://www.ibisworld.com/new-zealand/industry/structural-steel-fabricating/235/); [Companies Office / OpenCorporates](https://opencorporates.com/companies/nz/347015); [dhsteel.co.nz](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/how-we-do-it/fabrication/); [BusinessDesk, 19 Oct 2022](https://businessdesk.co.nz/article/property/prices-are-stable-but-residential-market-has-stopped-dh-steel) |
| 4 | **Grayson Engineering Ltd** (Manukau, Auckland) | Private | **Revenue >NZ$55m; >10,000 t/yr** finished product; ~200 staff; 12,000m² purpose-built plant; market leader in buckling-restrained braces (BRBs) | [grayson-brb.co.nz](https://grayson-brb.co.nz/about-us/); [Easysteel case study](https://www.easysteel.co.nz/web/assets/Easysteel-Case-Study-Grayson-Engineering.pdf) |
| 5 | **John Jones Steel Ltd** (Christchurch + Timaru) | Private (Van Schaijik family, founded 1964) | Two sites totalling **19,300m²**; **~8,000 t/yr** capacity; among NZ's most automated shops; JV partner with D&H on the 11,000t New Dunedin Hospital package | [jjsteel.nz](https://jjsteel.nz/about-us/); [Peddinghaus profile, 13 Sep 2019](https://www.peddinghaus.com/john-jones-steel-blasts-production-timetables/videos/91); [Health NZ, Jul 2026](https://www.healthnz.govt.nz/news-and-updates/new-dunedin-hospital-inpatient-building-begins-to-rise-from-the-ground) |

**Next tier:** **Calder Stewart Steel** (Stewart family group; 10,500m², $14m Milton, Otago facility; SFC Cat 3 — [bizdb](https://www.bizdb.co.nz/company/9429041501498/), [SCNZ Steel Futures 2015](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Steel-Futures-Feb-2015.pdf)); **Eastbridge Ltd** (Napier; ~6,000t/yr; 8,000m² workshops; bridge specialist — supplied 1,300t Karapiro Viaduct, [Scoop, 26 Mar 2014](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/BU1403/S00881/napier-firm-wins-waikato-expressway-steel-bridge-contract.htm)); **Red Steel** (Hawke's Bay); **Steltech Structural** (BlueScope/NZ Steel subsidiary supplying welded beams — [steltech.co.nz](https://www.steltech.co.nz/about-steltech/)). Excluded on scope: **Pacific Steel (NZ) Ltd** (~NZ$71m IBISWorld est.; wholly owned by BlueScope Steel since its 2014 NZ$120m acquisition from Fletcher Building — [Commerce Commission clearance, 2014](https://www.comcom.govt.nz/news-and-media/news-and-events/2014/bluescope-steel-cleared-to-buy-steel-production-assets-of-pacific-steel/)) — a reinforcing-bar manufacturer, not a structural fabricator.

---

## (c) Import Tariffs on Raw Steel (HS 7207–7216) and Margin Impact

### MFN tariff rates (NZ Customs Working Tariff Document, Chapter 72; MBIE summary)

MBIE confirms: "Most goods imported into New Zealand have no import tariffs. Tariffs of 5 or 10 per cent apply to some imported goods including some textiles, footwear, processed foods, machinery, **steel**, and plastic products" ([MBIE — Tariffs in New Zealand](https://www.mbie.govt.nz/business-and-employment/business/trade-and-tariffs/tariffs-in-new-zealand)).

| HS code | Product | MFN ("Normal") rate | FTA rate (CPTPP etc.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **7207** | Semi-finished iron/non-alloy steel (blooms, billets, slabs) | **Free (0%)** | 0% |
| **7208** | Flat-rolled ≥600mm, hot-rolled (e.g., 7208.10) | **5%** | 0% at entry into force |
| **7209** | Flat-rolled ≥600mm, cold-rolled | **5%** | 0% |
| **7210** | Flat-rolled, clad/plated/coated | **5%** | 0% |
| **7211** | Flat-rolled <600mm, not clad | **5%** | 0% |
| **7212–7215** | Other flat; bars & rods | 0–5% | 0% |
| **7216** | Angles, shapes & sections: hot-rolled U/I/H/L/T (7216.10–7216.50) | **Free (0%)** for standard hot-rolled sections; small/cold-formed sub-headings (7216.21 2.5%; 7216.61–7216.99) **up to 5%** | 0% |
| **7308** (fabricated structures — bridges, columns, beams) | Structures & parts of structures | **5%** | 0% EIF for CPTPP parties |

Sources: NZ Customs Working Tariff Document ([customs.govt.nz](https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/it3lql10/introduction.pdf)); sub-heading verifications via [HS 7208.10 (5%)](https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7208-10/), [HS 7216.21 (2.5%)](https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-21/), [HS 7216.22 (0%)](https://hscodedb.com/nz/hs-code/7216-22/); NZ CPTPP tariff elimination schedule ([text](https://wikileaks.org/tpp-final/2-D-New-Zealand-Tariff-Elimination-Schedule/page-132.html)); NZ–EU FTA schedule ([MFAT](https://www.mfat.govt.nz/assets/Trade-agreements/EU-NZ-FTA/Annexes/Appendix-2-A-2-Tariff-Schedule-of-New-Zealand.pdf)).

### Effective tariff impact on fabricator margins — minimal

1. **FTA erosion:** NZ's principal steel origins — Australia (CER duty-free), Japan, Korea, Vietnam (CPTPP/AANZFTA), China (NZ–China FTA), EU and UK (new FTAs) — face **0% on virtually all lines**. NZ Customs OIA 25-677 (data extracted 2 Sep 2025) shows 2020–2024 imports of HS 7208/7211/7216 dominated by Australia, China, Indonesia, Japan, Korea and Thailand ([OIA document](https://www.customs.govt.nz/media/yyshc4tn/oia-25-677-iron-and-non-alloy-steel-imports-2020-to-2024.pdf)).
2. **Structural sections enter duty-free anyway:** the core fabricator input — hot-rolled H/I/U sections under 7216.10–7216.50 — is 0% even at MFN. Only flat-rolled feedstock (7208–7211) carries 5% MFN, worth roughly **NZ$75–110/t** on a ~$1,500–2,200/t landed price — a 3–5% input-cost wedge only where FTA preference is not claimed.
3. **Pass-through contracting:** raw steel is typically 35–55% of project cost and is passed through to clients in NZ construction contracts; fabrication value-add ($4,000–8,000/t at multi-storey pricing) dwarfs the duty wedge.
4. **Residual protection is eroding:** the 5% MFN duty on *imported fabricated* steelwork (HS 7308) is the only tariff that directly protects local fabrication — and it is 0% for CPTPP origins, meaning offshore-fabricated competition (e.g., pre-assembled modules) faces little duty barrier.

**Net:** labour cost, capacity utilisation, NZD/USD, and mill price cycles are materially larger margin drivers than tariffs. Steel & Tube's FY23 commentary — "elevated pricing from steel mills almost offset[ting] softer volumes" ([FY23 Annual Report](https://steelandtube.co.nz/sites/default/files/st_file_list/Steel%20%26%20Tube%20-%20FY23%20Annual%20Report2.pdf)) — captures the real dynamic.

---

## (d) Three Major Infrastructure Projects

### 1. City Rail Link (CRL), Auckland — NZ$5.5bn+, completion 2026
- **Scope:** 3.45km twin-bore underground rail with new Te Waihorotiu (Aotea) and Karanga-a-Hape stations.
- **Steel demand:** **29,595 tonnes of structural steel** across project structures, with associated embodied carbon of **40,234 tCO₂e** ([SESOC 2023 conference paper](https://www.sesoc.org.nz/static/Documents/Conference/2023/SESOC2023-0043-Page-43-98-Page-Ethan-43-98-Page-Ethan.pdf)); **~25,000 tonnes of locally made reinforcing bar** over 3–4 years supplied by Pacific Steel ([NZ Steel release](https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/local-steel-for-aucklands-city-rail-link/)); 1,500t epoxy-coated rebar via Steel & Tube (Nov 2019); >1,100t of rail/track steel in the final tracklaying programme ([CRL media release, Feb 2024](https://www.cityraillink.co.nz/media-releases-2024)). **Total steel ~28,000–30,000t+.**
- **Timeline:** practical completion target November 2025; public opening **2026** ([NZ Herald, Dec 2024](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/fresh-concerns-about-completion-date-of-aucklands-55b-city-rail-link/LCYPSJ4Z35BPPEXO46S657BLF4/)).

### 2. Auckland Airport Domestic Jet Terminal — NZ$2.2bn programme; peak construction 2025–2028
- **Contract:** NZ$800m build awarded to Hawkins ([Auckland Airport, Sep 2024](https://corporate.aucklandairport.co.nz/news/latest-media/2024/building-for-the-long-haul-auckland-airport-to-partner-with-hawkins)).
- **Steel demand:** **~4,600 tonnes disclosed for the first construction stage** — 1,600t of column steel (190 columns up to 21m tall, up to 12t each) plus ~3,000t of floor beams, lift shafts, roof and façade structures — fabricated by **D&H Steel** with 50 workers on two 10-hour shifts, scaling to 200+ staff on the project ([Auckland Airport, Feb 2025](https://corporate.aucklandairport.co.nz/news/latest-media/2025/new-heights-vertical-construction-begins); [D&H Connexions, Autumn 2025](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/2731_DH_Steel_newsletter_Autumn_21Mar25_WEB.pdf)). Full-programme steel likely **8,000–12,000t+**.
- **Timeline:** vertical construction began February 2025; on-site workforce peaks at ~2,500 by end-2027.

### 3. New Dunedin Hospital (Project Whakatuputupu) — steel erection 2026–2030
- **Steel demand:** **~11,000 tonnes of structural steel**, delivered in ~550 truckloads; **15,200+ individual components**; an estimated **330,000 fabrication hours**, fabricated in New Zealand by the **D&H Steel / John Jones Steel joint venture** ([Health NZ, Jul 2026](https://www.healthnz.govt.nz/news-and-updates/new-dunedin-hospital-inpatient-building-begins-to-rise-from-the-ground); [CPB Contractors](https://www.cpbcon.com.au/news-and-media/2026/milestone-new-dunedin-hospital); [D&H newsletter, May 2022](https://www.dhsteel.co.nz/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/2542_DH_Steel_newsletter_4pp_FA_4May22_EML2.pdf)).
- **Timeline:** 13-storey base-isolated inpatient building; steel erection commenced July 2026; practical completion **late 2030**, first patients 2031.

**Pipeline context:** Te Waihanga's National Infrastructure Pipeline grew from **NZ$121.2bn (Mar 2024)** to **NZ$204bn across 7,600+ projects (Dec 2024)**, of which NZ$107.9bn is funded/confirmed; forecast spend NZ$12.1bn in 2024 ([Pipeline Snapshot Mar 2024](https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/1oukkaqh/pipeline-snapshot-march-2024.pdf); [Dec 2024](https://media.umbraco.io/te-waihanga-30-year-strategy/bysgbmlz/pipeline-snapshot-december-2024.pdf); [Beehive, 19 Jun 2024](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/national-infrastructure-pipeline-worth-over-120-billion)). Transport dominates (~NZ$61.9–131.6bn depending on scope), with the Roads of National Significance programme (Whangārei–Port Marsden, Brynderwyns alternative, Warkworth–Wellsford, Ōtaki–north of Levin, second Waitematā Harbour crossing) in the [NZTA State Highway Investment Proposal 2024–34](https://nzta.govt.nz/assets/resources/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34/state-highway-investment-proposal-2024-34.pdf). The NZ$280m Mt Messenger Bypass (two bridges to ~125m + 235m tunnel, completion ~2027) implies a further ~1,500–2,500t of bridge steel ([ConsultANZ, 16 Apr 2024](https://www.consultanz.com.au/list-major-infrastructure-projects-new-zealand-2021/)).

---

## (e) Top 3 Strategic Risks and Opportunities

### Risks

**1. Demand cyclicality and structural overcapacity.** Sector output is flat (~100,000t) against 150,000t installed capacity — **41% spare capacity at Sep 2023** ([SCNZ](https://scnz.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/SCNZ-IU-SEP2023_Web.pdf)) — as the market entered a downturn: Steel & Tube volumes fell 12.4% (FY23), then revenue −18.7% (FY24) and ~−20% (FY25); Stats NZ C21+C22 sales fell ~9% in 2024; MBIE forecasts total construction activity dropping from NZ$60.8bn (2023) to NZ$55.1bn (2025), with local-government infrastructure starts projected to fall 51% from their 2025 peak by 2027 ([MBIE Pipeline 2024](https://www.mbie.govt.nz/dmsdocument/29978-national-construction-pipeline-report-2024)). Fabricators face a fixed-cost absorption squeeze until the RoNS/health/airport pipeline ramps.

**2. Supply-chain concentration and import dependency.** NZ has one flat-steel producer (NZ Steel/Glenbrook) and one rebar producer (Pacific Steel); virtually all structural sections are imported from a handful of Asian/Australian mills (Customs OIA 25-677). As Asmuss Group's CEO put it, "Most of New Zealand's structural steel needs are met by overseas suppliers" ([Engineering News NZ, 20 Nov 2024](https://engineeringnews.co.nz/2024/11/20/infrastructure-boost/)). Exposure runs to shipping disruption, FX, mill consolidation, and any FTA-preference or trade-remedy shifts — compounded by the erosion (to 0% under CPTPP) of the 5% HS 7308 duty that is the only tariff protecting local *fabrication* against imported pre-fabricated steelwork.

**3. Decarbonisation and procurement-compliance barriers.** Embodied-carbon assessment is now embedded in major tenders — CRL's 29,595t of steel carries a disclosed 40,234 tCO₂e footprint (SESOC 2023) — and quality/whole-of-life-carbon credentials are becoming pre-qualification gates. With only ~57–65 of ~153 fabricators SFC-certified (albeit covering 92.5–96% of output), non-certified shops risk exclusion from public panels. Skilled-labour scarcity (90% of construction firms reported moderate-to-severe trade shortages at the 2021–23 peak; infrastructure workforce needs to grow from ~40,000 toward 97,000 over 30 years — [MBIE Sector Trends 2023](https://www.mbie.govt.nz/assets/building-and-construction-sector-trends-annual-report-2023.pdf)) will re-bind quickly when the pipeline ramps.

### Opportunities

**1. Generational infrastructure pipeline.** NZ$204bn in the National Infrastructure Pipeline (Dec 2024), NZ$107.9bn funded, ~NZ$33bn in government transport commitments and NZ$6bn of project starts flagged before Christmas 2025. Disclosed steel packages already contracted — CRL (~29,600t), Auckland Airport (4,600t+), Dunedin Hospital (11,000t, 330,000 local fabrication hours) — plus bridge-heavy RoNS projects give multi-year forward cover that favours certified local fabricators.

**2. Local-content preference and quality differentiation.** SFC certification, seismic performance (structural steel's Christchurch share rose from near-zero to >80% post-quake), ECI procurement models, and buy-local policy signals (e.g., Eastbridge's 2014 Karapiro win explicitly credited local economic benefit) create a defensible moat against imported fabricated steelwork despite the 0% HS 7308 FTA rate. Higher-margin niches — welded plate beams (Steltech), buckling-restrained braces (Grayson), base-isolation steelwork (Dunedin Hospital) — reward engineering capability over price.

**3. Green-steel supply chain and Construction 4.0.** NZ Steel's **NZ$300m Electric Arc Furnace** (installed by Culham Engineering) cuts Glenbrook emissions **>45% (~1Mt CO₂/yr)** and recycles ~300,000t/yr of domestic scrap ([NZ Steel EAF](https://www.nzsteel.co.nz/news-and-media/electric-arc-furnace-announcement/); [Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/nz%E2%80%99s-biggest-ever-emissions-reduction-project-hits-milestone)) — enabling fabricators to market among the world's lowest-carbon structural steel chains as embodied-carbon limits tighten. Complementary investment is flowing into logistics (Asmuss's $25m, 15,400m² Drury South facility holding 12,000t+ of steel) and into automation/robotic welding R&D (HERA's $10.3m Construction 4.0 Endeavour programme — [HERA Annual Report 2023](https://hera.org.nz/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/AnnualReport_2023_FINAL_SPREAD.pdf)), while the downturn creates consolidation opportunities among the ~150 small fabricators.

---

## Data-Quality Caveats

1. **Scope mismatch:** Stats NZ C21+C22 (~$13.3bn in 2024) covers all metal manufacturing; the structural-steel fabrication sub-sector is ~NZ$1.8bn (IBISWorld). The two series cannot be directly reconciled.
2. **Company revenues:** IBISWorld estimates (2026 release) are modelled, not audited filings; private-company figures (Grayson >$55m, John Jones Steel ~8,000t/yr) are latest disclosed values, not necessarily 2023/24 actuals.
3. **Tariff verification:** headline rates above are from the NZ Customs Working Tariff Document and MBIE; specific statistical keys (e.g., 7216.32/7216.40) should be confirmed against the current chapter reprint before use in tender pricing.
4. **Project tonnages:** CRL, Auckland Airport and Dunedin Hospital tonnages are disclosed figures; Mt Messenger is an engineering estimate by bridge analogy.
5. **SCNZ tonnage history:** quarterly Industry Updates are fully public only from ~2020/22 onward; the ~100,000t/yr figure for 2018–2019 is the stable descriptor carried across later issues rather than a precise annual series.

# Array Technologies Segment Portfolio Strategy: The Legacy–STI Gross Margin Divergence (Q1 2023 – Nine Months Ended September 2024)

## Direct Answer

The gross margin differential between Array Legacy Operations and STI Operations is **not a temporary, cyclical phenomenon — it is a structurally persistent and widening gap**. In the nine months ended September 30, 2023, the two segments ran at essentially identical economics (Array Legacy 26.9% gross margin vs. STI 26.6%, a differential of just +33 basis points). By the nine months ended September 30, 2024, that gap had exploded to **+2,671 basis points** (Legacy 41.8% vs. STI 15.1%) — a swing of more than 2,600 bps in twelve months. The divergence is driven by a regulatory asymmetry (U.S.-only Section 45X manufacturing credits and the IRA domestic-content adder accrue almost entirely to Legacy) colliding with international headwinds concentrated in STI (Brazilian real devaluation, ASP pressure, and no access to U.S. incentives). The strategic consequence is that Array's portfolio has effectively become a **one-segment value-creation story**: in 9M 2024, Legacy generated roughly 88% of consolidated gross profit from ~72% of revenue, while STI contributed only ~12% of gross profit from ~28% of revenue. The **$162 million non-cash goodwill impairment recorded against the STI Operations reporting unit in Q3 2024** is the accounting confirmation that the January 2022 STI acquisition (~$891M consideration) has not delivered on its margin thesis, and it reframes Array's integration priorities decisively around U.S. domestic content.

---

## I. The Quantitative Record: Segment Gross Margins by Quarter

All figures are segment revenue and gross profit (in $ thousands) as reported in Array Technologies' SEC filings (Forms 10-Q and 10-K); gross margin = segment gross profit ÷ segment revenue. Sources: [Q1 2024 10-Q segment note (R64)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000049/R64.htm), [Q2 2024 10-Q segment note (R35)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000062/R35.htm), [Q3 2024 10-Q segment note (R21)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R21.htm), [Q3 2023 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072123000171/arry-20230930.htm), [FY 2023 10-K segment note (R47)](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000011/R47.htm).

### Array Legacy Operations

| Period | Revenue ($K) | Gross Profit ($K) | Gross Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 2023 | 305,204 | 79,835 | **26.2%** |
| Q2 2023 | 345,261 | 102,950 | **29.8%** |
| Q3 2023 | 244,857 | 58,233 | **23.8%** |
| Q4 2023¹ | 277,505 | 76,586 | **27.6%** |
| Q1 2024 | 114,381 | 49,086 | **42.9%** |
| Q2 2024 | 185,160 | 77,306 | **41.8%** |
| Q3 2024 | 160,266 | 65,726 | **41.0%** |

### STI Operations

| Period | Revenue ($K) | Gross Profit ($K) | Gross Margin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 2023 | 71,569 | 17,705 | **24.7%** |
| Q2 2023 | 162,464 | 43,452 | **26.7%** |
| Q3 2023 | 105,581 | 29,146 | **27.6%** |
| Q4 2023¹ | 64,110 | 7,643 | **11.9%** |
| Q1 2024 | 39,022 | 6,004 | **15.4%** |
| Q2 2024 | 70,606 | 8,647 | **12.2%** |
| Q3 2024 | 71,140 | 12,589 | **17.7%** |

¹ Q4 2023 is derived: FY 2023 segment totals minus nine-month figures from the [FY 2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000011/R47.htm) and [Q3 2024 10-Q comparative tables](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R65.htm).

### The Differential (Legacy minus STI)

| Period | Legacy GM | STI GM | Gap (pp) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 2023 | 26.2% | 24.7% | **+1.4** |
| Q2 2023 | 29.8% | 26.7% | **+3.1** |
| Q3 2023 | 23.8% | 27.6% | **−3.8** (STI higher) |
| Q4 2023 | 27.6% | 11.9% | **+15.7** |
| Q1 2024 | 42.9% | 15.4% | **+27.5** |
| Q2 2024 | 41.8% | 12.2% | **+29.5** |
| Q3 2024 | 41.0% | 17.7% | **+23.3** |
| **9M 2023** | **26.9%** | **26.6%** | **+0.3** |
| **9M 2024** | **41.8%** | **15.1%** | **+26.7** |
| FY 2023 (context) | 27.1% | 24.3% | +2.8 |
| FY 2024 (context) | 40.8% | 10.9% | +29.9 |

### Magnitude and Persistence

Three features of the data establish that this is a structural break rather than noise:

1. **The 2023 baseline was parity.** Across 9M 2023 the segments were economically interchangeable (26.9% vs. 26.6%), and in Q3 2023 STI actually *outearned* Legacy by 382 bps. STI was the larger revenue contributor in Q2 and Q3 2023 (~30–32% of consolidated revenue). There was nothing structurally inferior about STI's economics as recently as mid-2023.

2. **The 2024 divergence is symmetric and present in every quarter.** Year-over-year bridges by quarter:
   - Q1 2024: Legacy **+1,676 bps** (26.2% → 42.9%); STI **−935 bps** (24.7% → 15.4%)
   - Q2 2024: Legacy **+1,193 bps** (29.8% → 41.8%); STI **−1,450 bps** (26.7% → 12.2%)
   - Q3 2024: Legacy **+1,723 bps** (23.8% → 41.0%); STI **−991 bps** (27.6% → 17.7%)

   Both segments moved simultaneously in opposite directions — Legacy up ~1,200–1,700 bps and STI down ~900–1,500 bps in every quarter — which is the signature of a structural driver (a policy/mix change affecting one segment) rather than shared market cyclicality.

3. **The gap persisted and compounded in dollar terms.** In 9M 2024, Legacy's gross profit *grew in margin terms* despite a ~49% revenue decline ($192.1M gross profit on $459.8M revenue), while STI's gross profit **collapsed ~70%** (from $90.3M in 9M 2023 to $27.2M in 9M 2024) on a ~47% revenue decline. STI's share of consolidated gross profit fell from 27.3% to 12.4% even as it still produced 28.2% of consolidated revenue — meaning one segment is now subsidizing consolidated profitability while the other dilutes it.

---

## II. Anatomy of the Divergence: Three Phases

**Phase 1 — Rough parity (Q1–Q3 2023).** Cumulative differential of only +0.3 pp. Both segments benefited from the 2023 industry-wide tailwinds (falling steel and logistics costs, strong U.S. utility-scale demand), and STI proved it could match or exceed Legacy margins (Q3 2023: 27.6% vs. 23.8%).

**Phase 2 — Inflection at STI (Q4 2023).** The decisive break occurred *before* 2024: STI's gross margin plunged to **11.9%** in Q4 2023 — a ~16 pp sequential collapse — while Legacy held at 27.6%. STI Q4 revenue fell to $64.1M (from $105.6M in Q3), signaling volume compression, adverse project mix, and emerging price pressure in Brazil and Spain. This +15.7 pp Q4 gap was the early-warning indicator that the 2024 divergence was coming.

**Phase 3 — Sustained structural gap (Q1–Q3 2024).** Legacy margins **stabilized above 40%** in all three quarters (42.9% / 41.8% / 41.0%) while STI remained trapped in a **12–18% band** (15.4% / 12.2% / 17.7%). Persistence across three consecutive quarters, with no quarter of convergence, rules out one-time items as the explanation.

---

## III. Drivers of the Divergence

### A. Legacy's expansion is overwhelmingly a Section 45X story

The Inflation Reduction Act's **Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit** pays credits for U.S.-manufactured solar components, including torque tubes and structural fasteners — precisely the components Array produces. Per the FY 2024 10-K, 45X vendor rebates and direct credits totaled **$173.6 million in 2024 versus only $9.3 million in 2023** — an incremental ~$164M flowing through Legacy's cost of revenue. Key reinforcing developments:

- The U.S. Treasury/IRS **final regulations issued October 24, 2024** confirmed the statutory definitions of torque tube and structural fasteners, locking in eligibility of Array's components.
- Array began **direct manufacturing in Q2 2024 at a new Albuquerque, New Mexico facility**, allowing it to claim credits on its own production rather than relying solely on vendor rebates ([Q3 2024 press release](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2024/11/07/2977200/0/en/array-technologies-inc-reports-financial-results-for-the-third-quarter-2024-delivers-exceptional-gross-margin-growth-and-continued-operational-momentum.html); [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R9.htm)).
- On the Q3 2024 earnings call, CEO Kevin Hostetler explicitly tied the consolidated adjusted gross margin of 35.4% to "the realization of torque tube and structural fastener 45X benefits."
- Because STI earns revenue primarily outside the U.S. (Spain, Brazil), it **cannot claim 45X credits**, and the 10% domestic-content bonus under Notice 2024-41 accrues only to U.S.-manufactured projects. This regulatory asymmetry is the single largest structural driver of the gap.

### B. STI's compression is multi-causal and international in nature

1. **Volume and ASP pressure:** STI 2024 revenue fell ~37% YoY on a ~12% volume decline plus price reductions; Q1 2024 STI revenue of $39.0M was nearly half the level of any 2023 quarter.
2. **Brazilian real devaluation:** On the Q3 2024 call, CFO James Zhu attributed guidance narrowing to "a significant devaluation of the Brazilian real" — even with stable local-currency volume and pricing, USD-translated revenue and margin deteriorate.
3. **Project mix:** STI serves large international utility-scale projects with more competitive pricing and greater FX exposure, and limited pass-through of cost increases.
4. **No domestic-content premium:** Trackers sold outside the U.S. cannot capture the IRA's 10% domestic-content adder, removing the pricing umbrella that protects Legacy.

**Methodology note (apples-to-apples comparability):** Two reporting changes do *not* distort the comparison. First, the Brazil ICMS value-added tax benefit ($19.9M in 9M 2023) was reclassified between revenue and cost lines in 2024 with **no effect on gross profit**. Second, segment gross profit as restated in the 2024 filings includes amortization of developed technology in cost of revenue (~$3,639K per quarter, allocated to Legacy); using the restated figures keeps all periods on the same basis.

---

## IV. What the Differential Reveals About Strategic Value and Operational Efficiency

### Array Legacy: the structurally advantaged profit engine

With ~72% of consolidated revenue producing ~88% of consolidated gross profit in 9M 2024, Legacy has become an exceptionally efficient value driver:

- **Profit resilience despite volume decline:** FY 2024 revenue fell ~44% YoY, yet gross profit dollars declined only ~15% ($317.6M → $270.0M) because margin expansion (27.1% → 40.8%) absorbed most of the volume shock.
- **A stacked advantage set:** (i) a U.S. manufacturing footprint inside the most generous solar incentive regime globally (45X + the 10% domestic-content adder); (ii) certified 100% domestic-content availability for U.S. customers announced for H1 2025; (iii) the flagship DuraTrack HZ v3 platform extended by OmniTrack™ for challenging terrain; and (iv) a ~$2.0B orderbook with roughly 20% of orders evaluating domestic content. Adjusted gross margin reached 35–38% in 2024 per quarterly releases (38.3% in Q1 2024, inclusive of a ~$4M one-time item, per the [Q1 2024 earnings call](https://equibles.com/stocks/arry/calls/2024-q1)).
- **Caveat on quality of earnings:** A ~42% gross margin is substantially a policy-derived margin. Its persistence depends on IRA/45X legislative durability — a genuine risk factor (discussed in Section VII).

### STI: a structurally disadvantaged, value-eroding asset

The evidence that STI's strategic value has materially eroded is unambiguous:

- **$162.0M non-cash goodwill impairment in Q3 2024**, taken specifically against the STI Operations reporting unit (estimated fair value $455.9M vs. a higher carrying value) — a formal acknowledgment that the business is worth materially less than its acquisition-date carrying value ([Q3 2024 10-Q, Goodwill note](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1820721/000182072124000076/R12.htm)).
- **Segment assets fell from $838.0M (FY 2023 10-K) to $407.5M (FY 2024 10-K)** — a ~51% reduction driven by the goodwill write-down and FX translation. (One panel of researchers also reported a further ~$166M of Q4 2024 impairments/write-downs; this figure appears in only one source and should be verified against the FY 2024 10-K before being relied upon.)
- **Dilutive economics:** a 28% revenue share generating only 12% of gross profit means STI consumes working capital, SG&A, and management attention at margins roughly one-third of Legacy's, dragging consolidated GAAP gross margin (34.2% in 9M 2024) well below what Legacy alone would produce.

The original rationale for the January 11, 2022 acquisition — "accelerating international expansion" — has thus inverted: the international asset is now the portfolio's margin laggard, while the domestic business it was meant to complement has become the overwhelming source of value.

---

## V. Competitive Positioning Implications

The contrasting margin trends reveal a **bifurcated competitive position**:

**In the U.S., Array Legacy has widened a policy-reinforced moat.** As one of the few tracker manufacturers able to certify U.S. domestic content, Array can offer developers the incremental 10% ITC/PTC adder — a differentiator competitors without U.S. manufacturing cannot replicate. The 45X + domestic-content flywheel is visible in ~20% domestic orderbook growth even amid industry-wide U.S. headwinds (interconnection queues, permitting delays, AD/CVD tariff uncertainty). Legacy's ~42% gross margin is, in effect, the market pricing of this regulatory moat.

**Internationally, Array (via STI) competes as a price-taker.** In Spain and Brazil, STI faces regional tracker OEMs with no U.S. incentive umbrella to soften pricing, plus direct FX exposure (Brazilian real, euro) that Legacy does not share. STI's margin floor in the 12–18% range is the observed result. Its competitive levers — terrain-following technology (OmniTrack™), local manufacturing presence, project execution track record, and southern-hemisphere seasonality offset — support revenue retention but have demonstrably *not* produced margin expansion. Whether 15% gross margin is Array-specific underperformance or the sector-typical floor for international tracker markets cannot be determined from Array's filings alone; no public segment-comparable data from private competitors (e.g., PVHardware, Soltec) was available in the record reviewed, which is a genuine analytical gap.

**Net positioning effect:** the U.S. moat is widening exactly where incentives are richest, while the international franchise is exposed exactly where they are absent. The portfolio's margin structure now *is* its competitive map.

---

## VI. Implications for Acquisition Strategy and Integration Priorities

The sustained 2,600+ bps gap, together with the impairment, supports four conclusions about Array's M&A and integration posture:

**1. The portfolio's center of gravity has decisively shifted to U.S. domestic content.** Every major 2024 value-creation lever — 45X credit maximization (~$164M incremental benefit), the Albuquerque plant, domestic-content certification, OmniTrack™ adoption, orderbook growth — accrues exclusively to Legacy. The margin differential is effectively a measurement of this strategic tilt: management attention and capital have followed the policy-driven returns.

**2. Integration priorities have favored Legacy margin harvesting over STI cost repair.** There is no evidence in the record of a comparably aggressive program to close STI's margin gap (supply-chain re-sourcing, mix shift, pricing discipline, or restructuring). Economically this prioritization is rational — returns on incremental U.S. investment clearly dominate — but it signals that management does not expect STI to approach Legacy-level margins in the foreseeable future, and that STI is being carried while the U.S. business compounds.

**3. The acquisition framework itself needs recalibration.** The STI experience demonstrates that **regulatory and incentive asymmetry can overwhelm geographic-diversification logic**. A diversification rationale that looked sound in January 2022 was overwhelmed within three years by a U.S. policy regime (IRA/45X, domestic content) that rewards domestic manufacturing concentration. Future M&A screening should weight incentive-jurisdiction exposure — i.e., whether a target's revenue can capture U.S. content-linked economics — at least as heavily as market-access diversification. Market behavior corroborates the lesson: Array's stock hit a 52-week low during Q3 2024, coinciding with the STI goodwill write-down, indicating investors no longer credit the international-diversification thesis at STI's prior carrying value.

**4. STI is a hold-and-fix, not yet a divestiture candidate — but the burden of proof has shifted.** With $407.5M of remaining segment assets (international PP&E, intangibles, and working capital in Spain and Brazil) and a stated strategic role in "expanding our presence in Brazil and other southern hemisphere markets to mitigate seasonal revenue fluctuations" (FY 2024 10-K), near-term divestiture is unlikely. However, persistent sub-18% gross margins plus the impairment create explicit pressure to either (a) demonstrate a credible 2025–2026 margin-recovery path, or (b) rationalize the carrying value further. The strategic question is no longer whether STI is dilutive — it demonstrably is — but whether its remaining asset base earns an adequate return versus sale proceeds or restructuring.

---

## VII. Risks, Caveats, and Forward Indicators

**Sustainability of Legacy's margin.** Legacy's ~42% gross margin is not purely operational; a large share is 45X-derived. Legislative repeal, modification, or a shift to technology-neutral credit structures would compress Legacy margins toward their underlying operational level. Conversely, 45X is currently statutory through the IRA's phase-out schedule, and the October 2024 final regulations reduce near-term interpretive risk. Forecasts should treat Legacy's margin as policy-sensitive, not permanent.

**Verification items.** (i) The reported additional ~$166M of Q4 2024 STI-related write-downs (beyond the confirmed $162M Q3 goodwill impairment) should be confirmed in the FY 2024 10-K. (ii) Segment-level capex, R&D, and SG&A allocations — which would quantify integration priorities in dollars — are not disclosed at the granularity needed and remain an analytical blind spot. (iii) STI's customer concentration, FX hedging effectiveness, and working-capital drag are not separately disclosed and limit a full cost-of-carry assessment.

**KPIs to monitor for 2025–2026:**
- STI quarterly gross margin: sustained recovery above ~20% would signal credible repair; continued sub-15% readings raise the probability of further impairment.
- Any restructuring, divestiture, or strategic-review language regarding STI in 10-K/10-Q risk factors and MD&A.
- Legacy margin excluding 45X benefits (disclosed adjusted-margin bridges) — the true operational trajectory underneath the policy benefit.
- Domestic-content order share (currently ~20% of the ~$2.0B orderbook) as the leading indicator of moat monetization.
- Brazilian real trajectory and STI's USD-translated ASPs, the proximate drivers of the 2024 compression.

---

## Summary Verdict

From Q1 2023 through the nine months ended September 2024, the Legacy–STI gross margin differential evolved from **+33 bps (parity) to +2,671 bps (a chasm)** — with Q4 2023 (STI at 11.9%) as the inflection point and 2024 as structural confirmation. The gap is driven by asymmetric policy economics (45X credits of $173.6M in 2024 vs. $9.3M in 2023, plus the domestic-content adder, accruing only to U.S. operations) and asymmetric market exposure (Brazil FX, international price competition, hitting only STI). The result: Legacy is a high-margin, policy-fortified profit engine generating ~88% of gross profit on ~72% of revenue; STI is a lower-margin international platform whose $162M goodwill impairment and ~51% segment-asset reduction formally validate its diminished strategic value. For portfolio optimization, Array's rational course is to keep compounding Legacy's domestic-content advantage, run STI for cash and seasonal diversification while demanding a measurable margin-recovery path, and re-weight future acquisition criteria toward incentive-jurisdiction alignment — because the last three years have demonstrated that in solar tracking, *where* you manufacture now matters more to margins than *where* you sell.
