# Suggestion Timing, Flow State, and Trust in AI Code Completion: A Research Synthesis for Enterprise Interface Design

## 1. Direct Answer: What the Evidence Supports

Five findings carry the most design weight and are corroborated across independent sources:

1. **Latency has two distinct regimes, not one.** For inline ghost-text completion, 85% of 599 surveyed practitioners expect results within **200 ms**, and the practical ceiling is ~500 ms before friction becomes perceptible. For statement-level and multi-line completion, developers tolerate up to **~2 seconds** — provided a progress indicator is shown. For on-demand generation (comment-to-code, chat), multi-second waits are tolerated and can even be perceived as model "deliberation" ([Xia et al., arXiv:2301.03846](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.03846v1); [arXiv:2604.06183](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06183)).

2. **When a suggestion appears matters more than how fast the model is.** The strongest direct evidence is a two-month adaptive-timing deployment: shifting from immediate display to state-aware delays raised acceptance from **4.9% to 18.6%** (a 3.8× improvement) and cut "blind rejections" (suggestions dismissed unread) from 8.3% to 0.36% — a 23× reduction — while eliminating **75% of wasted inference calls**. Optimal delays differ by task: **1.1 s base (range 0.8–1.4 s) during implementation vs. 1.3 s base (range 1.0–1.6 s) during debugging**, derived from the 97th percentile of observed inter-keystroke intervals ([Al Awad et al. 2025, arXiv:2511.18842](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18842v1)).

3. **Debugging and feature development require different timing policies.** Acceptance rates run meaningfully higher during new feature development (~40–44%) than during algorithm-heavy or debugging-adjacent work (~31–34%), and proactive interventions at workflow boundaries (e.g., post-commit) achieved **52% engagement vs. 62% dismissal for mid-task interventions** in the JetBrains ProAIDE field study ([arXiv:2404.12000](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.12000v2); [arXiv:2601.10253](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.10253v1)).

4. **Less experienced developers accept more and gain more — with an important exception.** Juniors accept ~31.9% of Copilot suggestions vs. ~26.2% for the most experienced developers, and Microsoft's controlled and field experiments show larger junior gains. But on deeply familiar codebases, highly experienced maintainers were measured **19% slower** with AI assistance (METR 2025). The effect is task-complexity- and codebase-familiarity-dependent, not a simple seniority gradient ([IT Pro/GitHub data](https://www.itpro.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/github-30-of-copilot-coding-suggestions-are-accepted); [METR](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)).

5. **Explanations calibrate trust only when accurate and adaptive.** Full explanations raise both trust and appropriate agreement, but low-quality explanations **impaired correctness judgment (OR = 0.58, p = 0.037) while simultaneously raising confidence** (3.99 → 4.25 on a 5-point scale) — a miscalibration hazard. Adaptive, expertise-adjusted explanations increased error detection by up to 16%. Meanwhile, only ~30% of developers trust AI output, trust declines with seniority, and **only ~52% of accepted suggestions survive unedited** — acceptance telemetry overstates true trust ([ICSE 2025 trust study](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199); [arXiv:2607.08885](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.08885); [Tech Science Journal](https://www.techscience.com/jai/v7n1/64684/html)).

A methodological caveat up front: **no published study directly compares Copilot, Tabnine, and CodeWhisperer head-to-head segmented at exactly the 2–5 year vs. 10+ year tenure bands you specified.** The synthesis below triangulates from adjacent evidence; Tabnine in particular lacks large-scale public telemetry, and code-quality outcomes (bug rates, maintainability, security) are under-measured relative to productivity metrics throughout this literature.

---

## 2. Optimal Latency Thresholds (Milliseconds)

### 2.1 Empirically grounded thresholds

| Band | Meaning | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **≤100 ms** | Perceived as instantaneous; continuous with the developer's own typing | Card–Moran–Newell perceptual frame via [feelsfast.fyi](https://feelsfast.fyi/scenarios/ai-inline-completion); developer at 60 wpm strikes a key ~every 200 ms ([Pavel Fatin](https://pavelfatin.com/typing-with-pleasure/)) |
| **≤200 ms** | Token-level inline expectation: 85% of 599 practitioners expect completion within this window; 79% satisfied if correct token is in top 3 | [Xia et al., arXiv:2301.03846](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.03846v1); 200 ms is also the measured average latency of a research-grade plugin (Code4Me V2, [TU Delft](https://pure.tudelft.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/314846873/3774748.3787616.pdf)) |
| **~400–500 ms** | Doherty productivity threshold (~400 ms); below ~500 ms most users do not consciously notice delay. Practical hard ceiling for inline ghost text | [feelsfast.fyi](https://feelsfast.fyi/scenarios/ai-inline-completion) (practitioner synthesis of HCI literature) |
| **750 ms** | Meta CodeCompose's minimum display duration for a suggestion to count as "seen" — anything shorter is dismissed by the next keystroke before being read | [arXiv:2402.04141](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141) |
| **~1 s** | Meta's field finding: developers tolerate suggestions appearing within 300–500 ms but **not beyond 1 second** for inline multi-line | [DX Newsletter on CodeCompose](https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/ai-assisted-code-authoring-at-scale) |
| **≤2 s** | Statement/multi-line tolerance ceiling ("most favored latency: no more than 2 seconds") | [Xia et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2301.03846v1) |
| **0.8–1.4 s (base 1.1 s)** | Adaptive post-pause delay when **implementing** | [Al Awad et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18842v1) |
| **1.0–1.6 s (base 1.3 s)** | Adaptive post-pause delay when **debugging** | [Al Awad et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18842v1) |
| **9–20 s** | Tolerable for on-demand/chat generation; in a 240-participant study, 2-second responses were rated *less thoughtful and less useful* than 9- or 20-second ones — moderate delay is attributed to AI deliberation | [arXiv:2604.06183](https://www.arxiv.org/pdf/2604.06183) |

### 2.2 Reconciling the apparent tension (200 ms vs. ~1.1 s)

These are **different knobs**. The 200 ms figure governs *render latency once a completion point is reached* — the perceived responsiveness of the editor. The ~1.1–1.3 s figures govern *deliberate debounce delay after a typing pause is detected* — withholding the suggestion until the developer is cognitively ready to read it. A well-designed system does both: waits ~1 s after a pause to offer, then renders in <200 ms.

### 2.3 Staleness dominates raw speed

A completion that arrives after the user's cursor or edit state has moved is *perceived as wrong even if the model output was correct* — the "haunted suggestion" failure mode documented in practitioner engineering analyses. The required mechanisms are **debouncing** (waiting for a genuine pause), **cancellation** (discarding in-flight requests whose context went stale), and **speculative caching** (keeping a suggestion alive if the user continues along the predicted trajectory) ([Pochi engineering write-up](https://getpochi.hashnode.dev/how-a-code-editor-decides-the-right-moment-to-show-an-llm-generated-code-suggestion); [Sourcegraph](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-lifecycle-of-a-code-ai-completion); [Devin.ai](https://devin.ai/blog/latency-the-ultimate-constraint)). Related behavioral evidence: **predictable delays outperform variable delays** for user performance — a consistent ~150 ms debounce feels better than erratic model-dependent timing ([IJHCS](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2013.12.004)).

### 2.4 Latency investments pay off measurably in acceptance

- **JetBrains**: a 4× latency reduction in its re-architected cloud completion **tripled acceptance rate** ([JetBrains blog](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/10/complete-the-un-completable-the-state-of-ai-completion-in-jetbrains-ides/); [JetBrains announcement](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/jetbrains_how-code-completion-has-improved-activity-7271970271400505344-rcVw)).
- **Meta CodeCompose**: Flash Attention cut first-token latency **2.53×**; CUDA graphs and fused kernels cut median generation latency 29% (p90: 40%); the full optimization stack reduced median latency **74% overall**, producing **+13% display rate and +8% acceptance rate** for multi-line suggestions ([arXiv:2402.04141](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2402.04141)).
- **GitHub Copilot**: the 2023 model update's 13% latency improvement contributed to a +6% relative acceptance-rate gain ([GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/smarter-more-efficient-coding-github-copilot-goes-beyond-codex-with-improved-ai-model/)).
- **Relevance can buy back latency** beyond the token regime: JetBrains' cloud completion runs roughly twice as slow as its local full-line completion yet achieves marginally *higher* acceptance — quality compensates once the sub-500 ms inline constraint is not at stake ([JetBrains](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/10/complete-the-un-completable-the-state-of-ai-completion-in-jetbrains-ides/)).

---

## 3. Acceptance Rates, Interruption Timing, and Task Type

### 3.1 Why timing is expensive: the interruption-cost literature

AI suggestions are interruptions, and interruption costs in programming are severe and asymmetric:

- **Resumption lag**: Developers take **10–15 minutes** to resume editing after an interruption; only **10% of sessions resume within one minute**, and only 7% resume without first navigating to other locations ([Parnin & Rugaber, SQJ 2011](https://www.chrisparnin.me/pdf/parnin-sqj11.pdf)). Broader workplace estimates: ~20 minutes per interruption occurrence-plus-handling, 3–5 interruptions/day, consuming 15–20% of total time ([DeMarco, IEEE Software](https://doi.org/10.1109/52.714843)).
- **Hidden stress cost**: Interrupted knowledge workers completed tasks *faster* (compensatory speed-up) but paid with significantly higher stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort — output metrics alone miss the damage ([Mark, Gudith & Klocke, CHI 2008](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1357054.1357072)).
- **Timing within a task matters**: interruptions at moments of low predicted workload (task/subtask boundaries) cause less resumption lag and annoyance than mid-task interruptions ([Adamczyk & Bailey, CHI 2004](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/985692.985727)); disruptiveness is determined by the problem-state requirements of both tasks ([Borst, Taatgen & Van Rijn, CHI 2015](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2702123.2702156)).
- **Interruptibility is computable from IDE data**: computer-interaction features alone predicted developer interruptibility with **74.8% accuracy** (biometrics: 68.3%; combined: 75.7%) in a two-week field study; the related FlowLight deployment (449 participants) cut in-person interruptions 46% ([Züger et al., CHI 2018](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3173574.3174165)). This is precisely the signal class an AI completion system needs for timing decisions.
- **Self-interruptions are worse than external ones**; contextual factors (interruption type, time of day, task type) dominate task-intrinsic factors ([Abad et al., EASE 2018](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1805.05508): 4,910 recorded tasks, 17 developers, 132-person survey).
- **Debugging is structurally more fragile**: debugging sessions consist of shorter, more frequent episodes (mean **1 min 2 s**) than implementation (2 min 5 s) or refactoring (2 min 13 s) — developers constantly re-engage short memory contexts, so mid-debug interruptions cost more ([Rini et al., ICSE 2019](https://rahulpandita.github.io/files/riniICSE2019.pdf)).
- **Micro-interruptions from the suggestions themselves**: eye-tracking shows ~**half of generated suggestions are never visually examined**; of those examined, over 75% are not used; suggestions are reviewed for only ~0.9 s on average — yet rejected suggestions consume disproportionate cognitive resources ([ICSE 2026 eye-tracking study](https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3744916.3773132)). On-screen, high-dominance interruptions significantly increase time on code-comprehension tasks ([Breaking the Flow, ICSE 2024](https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3597503.3639079)).

### 3.2 Acceptance by task type

Directly measured per-task acceptance rates:

| Task | Copilot | Tabnine | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Algorithm & data structures | 34% | 17% | Lowest-yield context |
| **Management system (new feature) development** | **44%** | **34%** | Highest-yield context |
| Real-world task development | 39% | 19% | — |

([Tan et al., 27 participants, three ACATs, arXiv:2404.12000](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.12000v2)). In the same study, **single-line "edited line" completion was the most accepted suggestion type; comment-triggered and string completions had the lowest acceptance**.

From the CUPS behavioral taxonomy (21 programmers, 3,137 labeled segments, 1,096 suggestions): algorithmic problem-solving 30.6% acceptance, data analysis 29.8%, **data manipulation 24.8%** — the exploratory, understanding-heavy task drew the *least* welcome suggestions ([Mozannar et al., CHI 2024](http://erichorvitz.com/Reading_between_the_lines_CHI_2024.pdf)). For agent-style pull request tasks, the gap widens further: **documentation 82.1% acceptance vs. new features 66.1%** ([arXiv:2602.08915](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.08915v2)).

Survey data aligns: 87.3% of 481 programmers use AI assistants during feature implementation, but only 65.5% during bug triaging ([arXiv:2406.07765](https://arxiv.org/html/2406.07765)).

### 3.3 Debugging vs. feature development: the operational synthesis

The published studies do not cleanly partition acceptance into "debugging vs. new feature" conditions, but five convergent evidence streams support a clear design rule:

1. **Inter-keystroke intervals are longer in debugging** (97th percentile: 1.293 s vs. 1.068 s implementing), so the adaptive controller widens its delay window to 1.0–1.6 s with a stricter 1.0 s floor ([Al Awad et al.](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18842v1)).
2. **Debugging maps to "exploration mode"** in Barke et al.'s grounded theory of Copilot use (20 developers): slow, deliberate, prompt-heavy interaction requiring validation — versus "acceleration mode" for known-plan implementation, where a matching suggestion is nearly free ([arXiv:2206.15000](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2206.15000v3.pdf)).
3. **Debugging is the most verification-intensive CUPS context** (Debugging/Testing ≈ 11.3% of session time, surrounded by verification states), so a wrong suggestion is maximally costly ([CHI 2024](http://erichorvitz.com/Reading_between_the_lines_CHI_2024.pdf)).
4. **Workflow boundaries are the safe proactive moments**: ProAIDE's 5-day field study (15 professional developers, 229 interventions, 5,732 interaction points) found **52% engagement at post-commit boundaries vs. 62% dismissal mid-task**; well-timed proactive suggestions took **45.4 s to interpret vs. 101.4 s for reactive** (p = 0.0016) — proactive at the *right* moment reduces cognitive load rather than adding it; SUS usability 72.8/100 ([arXiv:2601.10253](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.10253v1)).
5. **Suppression beats display**: the CDHF framework (Microsoft Research/MIT; 535 programmers, 168k suggestions) can hide 25% of suggestions while guaranteeing 95% of them would have been rejected, raising acceptance 7.2% and avoiding 13% of generations entirely; modeling the programmer's *latent state*, not just acceptance history, was critical — a minimal version shipped in Copilot ([AAAI 2024](https://www.erichorvitz.com/copilot_display_AAAI.pdf)).

**Design rule**: proactive inline during acceleration-mode implementation; delayed or on-demand during debugging, log inspection, and code comprehension; proactive at natural boundaries (post-commit, after save, between functions).

### 3.4 Context effects beyond task

Acceptance is state-dependent, not purely model-quality-driven: weekend acceptance runs 23.5%, weekday-evening 23%, weekday working hours 21.2% (all p < 0.001) — and the fit to the *user's habitual time regime* matters more than clock time ([Ziegler et al. 2022](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537)).

---

## 4. Experience Level: 2–5 Years vs. 10+ Years

### 4.1 The evidence, including its contradictions

**Juniors gain more (multiple independent sources):**
- Copilot RCT (95 developers, JavaScript HTTP server): **55.8% faster** completion (71.17 vs. 160.89 min; 95% CI [21%, 89%]; p = 0.0017); heterogeneous effects show benefit *decreasing* with years of experience (+8.23 min per year, p = 0.0629) and increasing with daily coding hours ([Peng et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590)).
- Three field RCTs at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune-100 firm (4,867 developers): **26.08% increase in completed tasks (SE 10.3%; computed 95% CI ≈ [5.9%, 46.3%])**, with less experienced developers showing higher adoption *and* greater gains ([Cui et al.](https://demirermert.github.io/Papers/Demirer_AI_productivity.pdf)).
- Telemetry at scale (934,533 users): benefits greatest for less experienced users; ~30% overall acceptance ([arXiv:2306.15033](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.15033)).
- Acceptance by seniority: **31.9% (less experienced) vs. 26.2% (most experienced)**; senior developers 1.8% less likely to accept; long-tenure 4.3% less likely ([IT Pro/GitHub](https://www.itpro.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/github-30-of-copilot-coding-suggestions-are-accepted); [DX Newsletter](https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/copilot-impact-on-productivity)).
- JetBrains April 2024 survey: developers with <2 years' experience save **3–5 hours/week** vs. <1 hour for seniors; overall 49% report improved focus and 46% enter flow more easily ([JetBrains](https://blog.jetbrains.com/ai/2024/04/developers-save-up-to-8-hours-per-week-with-jetbrains-ai-assistant/)).

**Seniors can gain more on the right tasks:** Google's enterprise RCT (96 engineers, complex enterprise task) found ~21% time reduction with **senior developers and high-coding-hours developers significantly faster** in the AI condition — explicitly contrasting with Peng et al., whose sample skewed freelance/junior ([arXiv:2410.12944](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12944)).

**Seniors can be *slowed* on familiar code:** METR's 2025 randomized trial (16 experienced open-source maintainers, 246 real issues on repositories averaging 22k+ stars and 1M+ lines) found AI use **increased completion time 19% — while the developers themselves expected a 24% speedup** ([METR](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/)). Perceived and actual productivity diverge, which is itself design-relevant. Consistent: McKinsey found time savings shrink to **under 10% on high-complexity tasks** ([McKinsey](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/mckinsey-digital/our-insights/unleashing-developer-productivity-with-generative-ai)), and in the three-ACAT controlled study experienced participants sometimes took *longer* with assistance ([arXiv:2404.12000](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.12000)).

### 4.2 Resolution and behavioral mechanisms

The contradiction resolves along **task complexity and codebase familiarity**: juniors gain most on greenfield, boilerplate-heavy, well-specified work; seniors gain on complex enterprise tasks where they can steer the tool; seniors *lose* on deeply familiar maintenance work where verification cost exceeds typing/lookup savings.

Behavioral mechanisms differ by cohort:
- **Novices** exhibit "shepherding" (guiding the AI by reading suggestions) and "drifting" (being pulled off-track by incorrect suggestions), with higher metacognitive difficulty ([Prather et al., ICER 2023](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3617367)); they use AI primarily for debugging and learning.
- **Seniors** spend

# Delta Ranges for the Protective Collar (Long Stock + Short OTM Call + Long OTM Put)

## Direct Answer

```
Sold Call Delta: 0.20 to 0.30 (sweet spot: 0.25–0.30)
  (reason: 0.30 is the codified institutional convention — Cboe's BXMD index
  mechanically selects the SPX call with delta closest to 0.30 — and it
  maximizes the premium available to fund the put; 0.20–0.25 when upside
  retention is the priority. 0.30 delta ≈ ~30% risk-neutral probability of
  expiring ITM, i.e., you keep shares roughly 70% of cycles.)

Bought Put Delta: 0.20 to 0.30 (sweet spot: 0.25–0.30)
  (reason: protective-put literature and institutional practice put standard
  hedges at 5–10% OTM, which is roughly −0.20 to −0.35 delta at 30–90 DTE.
  0.30 buys a tighter floor ~5% OTM; 0.20 is a cheaper floor ~8–10% OTM.
  Below ~0.16 is "crash insurance" only — ordinary −5–10% drawdowns go unhedged.)

Symmetric vs Asymmetric: ASYMMETRIC is the market standard. Equal deltas do
  NOT produce a zero-cost collar because volatility skew makes puts richer
  than equidistant calls (a 0.30-delta put costs ~30–35% more than a 0.30-delta
  call at the same expiry). Two valid asymmetric templates exist depending on
  your binding constraint:
    - Zero-cost (retail default): call delta ≥ put delta, e.g., sell 0.30Δ call
      / buy 0.20–0.25Δ put.
    - Protection-first (institutional default): put delta > call delta, e.g.,
      buy 0.30–0.40Δ put / sell 0.10–0.20Δ call, accepting a net debit.
  Construction rule: pick the put floor first from risk tolerance, then walk
  the call chain to match premium — do not match deltas.

Example Collar:
  Stock: $100 (100 shares), 45–60 DTE, typical single-stock IV ~20–25%
  Sell call: $107 strike, Delta +0.25  (~7% OTM),  premium ≈ $1.10–1.80
  Buy put:   $95 strike,  Delta −0.27  (~5% OTM),  premium ≈ $1.15–1.80
  Net credit/debit: ≈ $0.00 (zero-cost; ±$0.10 depending on skew)
  Max gain: ≈ $700/contract (called away at $107)
  Max loss: ≈ $500/contract (put floor at $95)
  Net position delta: 1.00 − 0.25 − 0.27 ≈ +0.48

Sources: [Cboe BuyWrite Indices Methodology (BXMD 0.30-delta rule);
Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index (CLL) description;
Israelov & Klein, AQR, "Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies" (2016);
LGIM America, "Tailor Your Risk by Buttoning-up with an Equity Collar" (2024);
SpotGamma/Morningstar on JPMorgan JHEQX collar; full list at bottom]
```

---

## 1. Sold Call Delta: 0.20–0.30, with a Codified Anchor at 0.30

**The strongest single piece of evidence is codified, not anecdotal.** Cboe maintains a dedicated benchmark — the **Cboe S&P 500 30-Delta BuyWrite Index (BXMD)** — whose methodology states that when writing the monthly OTM SPX call, "the option with a delta closest to 0.30 is selected" ([Cboe BuyWrite Indices Methodology](https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_BuyWrite_Indices_Methodology.pdf)). A collar's short call leg *is* a covered call, so BXMD is the institutional answer to the question. Since 2002, BXMD has roughly doubled the risk-adjusted performance of BXM (the ATM, ~0.50-delta version), and Nasdaq Dorsey Wright notes "some option sellers find 30 delta to be the sweet spot between generating premium and preserving upside."

Practitioner literature converges on the same band:

| Source | Sold Call Delta |
|---|---|
| Cboe BXMD (codified) | 0.30 exactly |
| Ryan O'Connell, CFA ([ryanoconnellfinance.com](https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/collar-strategy/)) | 0.20–0.30 ("balanced collar") |
| Saxo Bank (Koen Hoorelbeke) | 0.20–0.30 balanced; 0.15–0.20 protective |
| OptionsPilot / QuantWheel | 0.20–0.30 ("keep shares 70–80% of the time"); 0.30 best risk-adjusted in 30-yr SPY backtest (~12.4% annualized vs 11.8% at 0.20, ~28% assignment frequency) |
| Optvana / OptionsDecay | 0.20–0.30 specifically so "call premium exceeds or equals the put cost" |
| Barchart collar screener | −0.25 default |
| Cboe CLL (95-110 index) | 10% OTM monthly call ≈ 0.00–0.20 delta depending on vol regime (AQR measured 0.12 in Dec 2008, ~0.00 in Sept 2014) |

**0.30 vs 0.20 decision rule:** sell 0.30Δ when the goal is funding the put (the economic point of the structure); drop to 0.20Δ (or 0.15Δ) when upside retention dominates — e.g., low cost basis, tax aversion to assignment, or a bullish view. One interpretive caution: 0.30 delta is approximately a 30% *risk-neutral probability of expiring ITM*, not a guaranteed 30% assignment rate — early exercise, dividends, and rolls all intervene.

## 2. Bought Put Delta: 0.20–0.30 for Standard Protection

The put is the insurance leg, and conventions cluster tightly:

| Source | Bought Put Delta | Approx. Strike Distance |
|---|---|---|
| Ryan O'Connell, CFA | −0.20 to −0.30 | 5–10% OTM |
| FinancialTechWiz / Proflex | −0.25 to −0.35 ("the standard hedge") | 5–10% OTM, 60–90 DTE |
| Saxo Bank | 0.20–0.25 balanced; 0.25–0.35 protective | 5–10% OTM |
| Cboe CLL benchmark | 5% OTM quarterly ≈ −0.24 to −0.39 (AQR measured −0.39 at VIX 44.9 in Dec 2008; −0.24 at VIX 12.1 in Sept 2014) | 5% OTM |
| JPMorgan JHEQX (actual Dec 2021 roll, per SpotGamma) | long put **0.30Δ** (short put of spread 0.07Δ) | 5% OTM / 20% OTM |
| Optvana / OptionsDecay (zero-cost variant) | 0.16Δ ("16-delta puts") | further OTM, cheaper |

**Trade-off arithmetic:** a 0.30Δ put typically sits ~3–5% OTM at 30–45 DTE on index vols and floors losses close to spot, but costs the most; a 0.20Δ put sits ~5–8% OTM and is materially cheaper; anything at 0.10–0.16Δ is disaster insurance only. In a *collar* (where the call subsidizes the put), traders often accept a slightly lower put delta than they would for a standalone protective put (0.30–0.40) — the structure trades protection depth for cost efficiency.

## 3. Symmetric vs Asymmetric: Asymmetric Is the Standard — and the Direction Depends on Your Constraint

This is the question where naive intuition (sell 0.30Δ call, buy 0.30Δ put, done) is most wrong. Three findings resolve it:

**a) Skew breaks equal-delta zero-cost.** Equity index options carry persistent negative volatility skew — puts are bid richer than equidistant calls. Quantified with a skew-adjusted Black-Scholes model (S=$100, 45 DTE, IV = 20% − 0.60·ln(K/S), finite-difference-verified deltas):

| Leg | Strike | Delta | Premium | IV |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Call, 0.30Δ | $103.89 (+3.9%) | +0.30 | $1.15 | 17.7% |
| Put, 0.30Δ | $96.68 (−3.3%) | −0.30 | **$1.54** | 22.0% |
| Put, 0.25Δ | $95.41 (−4.6%) | −0.25 | $1.25 | 22.8% |
| Put, 0.20Δ | $93.90 (−6.1%) | −0.20 | $0.97 | 23.8% |

The 0.30Δ put costs **~34% more** than the 0.30Δ call. As OptionsDecay puts it: "On SPY in a normal vol regime, matching deltas usually leaves a small net debit, not a clean zero." The three honest fixes: accept the debit, sell a higher-delta call (~0.35Δ), or **buy a lower-delta put (0.20–0.25Δ)** — the last being the market-standard resolution.

**b) Therefore zero-cost collars are asymmetric with call delta ≥ put delta.** "Zero-cost" is what "typically drives collar portfolio construction" (AQR), and the standard build is: pick the put floor first, then walk the call chain to the strike whose premium matches the put's. Verified example (flat 25% vol, 60 DTE, r=3%): a 5% OTM $95 put costs $1.79 at Δ −0.27; the premium-matched call lands at ≈ **$106.70 (+6.7% OTM, Δ +0.30)** — a ~0.03–0.06 delta gap, not a 0.27/0.27 pair.

**c) But protection-first institutional collars are asymmetric the other way.** The Cboe 95-110 index (5% OTM put / 10% OTM call) is *deliberately* net-debit: AQR measured that CLL "spends roughly $7.50 on put options for every dollar it collects from selling calls." Its measured leg deltas were put −0.39 / call +0.12 (high-vol) and put −0.24 / call ~0.00 (low-vol) — i.e., put delta far exceeds call delta. Institutions buying CLL-style structures are paying for drawdown control, not optimizing to zero premium.

**Reconciliation (state directly):** both templates are asymmetric; symmetric-delta collars are rare outside delta-neutral vol strategies. Choose by objective:
- **You want zero cost** → sell 0.25–0.30Δ call, buy 0.20–0.25Δ put.
- **You want maximum protection and accept a debit** → buy 0.30–0.40Δ put, sell 0.10–0.20Δ call (the institutional/CLL pattern).

One nuance worth preserving: at *equal percentage distance* (e.g., ±5%), the deltas are nearly equal anyway (≈ +0.23 call vs −0.24 put in the model above) — "symmetric by moneyness" and "symmetric by delta" almost coincide; it is the *premium* that is asymmetric. And the strike-distance direction can flip by underlying: indices (negative skew) force the zero-cost call *closer* to spot than the put (JPMorgan's hedged equity fund sells calls 3.5–5.5% OTM to fund a 5% OTM put spread), while single stocks with lognormal right tails often let the call sit *further* OTM at equal premium (NISA, "The Long Right Tail: Asymmetry in Single-Stock Collars").

## 4. Percentage Distance: Useful Label, Poor Specifier

Institutional conventions expressed in % of spot:

| Structure | Put | Call | Tenor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cboe CLL (95-110)** — canonical benchmark since 1986 | 5% OTM (quarterly) | 10% OTM (monthly) | Mixed |
| **Cboe CLLZ** (zero-cost put-spread collar) | Buy 2.5% OTM / sell 5% OTM | Whatever call funds the spread | Monthly |
| **LGIM pension collar** | 10% OTM (90 strike) | 12% OTM (112 strike) — "fully offset the premium" | 1 year |
| **Wells Fargo / UBS monetization collar** | 10% OTM | 20% OTM | 2 years |
| **bfinance UK public-sector pension** | Protection band −10% to −30% (put spread) | Cap +10% | — |
| **ERISA pension example (OIC)** | 7% OTM (93 strike) | 5.3% OTM | 30 days |
| Retail guides (O'Connell, ApexVol) | 5–10% OTM | 5–15% OTM | 30–45 days |

**Critical caveat: delta is the better specifier than fixed percentages.** A 5% OTM put is −0.19 delta at 30 DTE / low IV but −0.35+ at 90 DTE / high IV — verified by direct calculation and by AQR's regime measurements above. A "10% OTM put" on a low-vol utility and on a 40-vol growth name are radically different insurance contracts; a 0.25-delta put is the *same probability of protection* on both. Anchor on delta; treat percentage as the descriptive label.

## 5. What Institutions Actually Do

- **Cboe CLL → Global X XCLR:** passive 95/110 collar, 28.5-year backtest (1986–2014, Szado & Schneeweis via AQR): ~5.2% annualized vs ~7.3% for SPX, with vol ~10.7% vs ~15.7% — about 71% of the return for 67% of the volatility, and **−1.3%/year negative alpha** in AQR's replication. Verdict: it is a funded-status/drawdown tool, not an alpha source.
- **Put-spread collars dominate pension/LDI use.** LGIM explicitly recommends them for DB plans; Cboe CLLZ codifies the monthly version (buy 2.5% OTM put, sell 5% OTM put, sell call to fund). Cost: ~3–6 bps/year static (bfinance). LGIM's case study: an 85% put / 107% call collar later upsized to 91%/105%; their 2022 illustration used a 70–90% put spread with upside capped at ~33% over two years for protection from −10% to −30%.
- **JPMorgan Hedged Equity Fund (JHEQX)** — the largest collar program (~40,000+ contracts per leg, billions in notional, quarterly rolls, "always on, never adjusted"): buys 5% OTM put, sells 20% OTM put, sells 3.5–5.5% OTM call to make the structure zero-cost. The actual December 2021 roll observed by SpotGamma: long put **0.30Δ**, short put **0.07Δ**, short call **0.34Δ** — a real-world confirmation of the 0.30-ish call / 0.30-ish long-put pairing with the cost problem solved via the put spread rather than a lower put delta.
- **Concentrated-stock / insider collars:** UBS and Wells Fargo document 2-year zero-premium 90/120 structures (wide band, also designed around tax constraints); Bettis, Bizjak & Kalpathy found insiders hedge ~30% of holdings on average via zero-cost collars and prepaid forwards.

**Net position delta** across all of these lands around **+0.45 to +0.75** — a collar is a *long-biased* position with a floor and a cap, not a delta-neutral structure. A truly delta-neutral collar is a specialized vol/theta trade, not stock protection.

## 6. Worked Example (verified arithmetic)

Stock $100, 45 DTE, skew-adjusted IVs, r=4.5%, q=1.5% (premiums model-generated; expect one-strike granularity on live chains):

```
Buy  $95 put   Δ −0.24,  $1.16
Sell $104 call  Δ +0.29,  $1.11
Net debit: $0.05/share ($5/contract) ≈ zero-cost

Max gain (called away): (104 − 100 − 0.05) × 100 ≈ $394
Max loss (put floor):   (100 − 95 + 0.05) × 100 ≈ $506
Profit band: $95–$104 (~9% wide)
Net position delta: 1.00 − 0.29 − 0.24 ≈ +0.47
Expiry sanity checks: S=$90 → −10 + 5 − 0.05 = −$5.06/sh ✓
                      S=$110 → +10 − 6 − 0.05 = +$3.94/sh ✓
```

For a wider, single-stock-style band at higher IV (25%, 60 DTE): sell $107 call (Δ +0.30, ≈$1.79) / buy $95 put (Δ −0.27, $1.79) — exact zero cost, $500 max loss, $700 max gain, net delta ≈ +0.43. For a tighter protective version (Saxo's framework): $97 put (Δ ≈ −0.32) / $104 call (Δ ≈ +0.18) for a small net debit of ~$0.30–0.50, buying a higher floor at the cost of a lower cap.

## 7. Caveats That Matter

1. **Delta is not constant across regimes.** AQR measured the same 95/110 CLL structure producing put deltas of −0.24 to −0.39 and call deltas of 0.00 to +0.12 depending on the vol regime. The ranges above are *entry anchors* at 30–60 DTE and normal IV — always confirm the live chain delta at your chosen tenor.
2. **"Zero-cost" is not a free lunch.** AQR: the CLL collar earned −1.3%/yr alpha vs simply holding less equity; you pay in forfeited upside and negative variance premium. Use collars for risk control (funded status, concentration, behavioral discipline), not return enhancement.
3. **Dividends and pin risk** (unaddressed in most conventions): an ITM short call into an ex-dividend date raises early-assignment risk — relevant when choosing between 0.30Δ and 0.20Δ calls on high-yield names.
4. **Rolling protocol matters more than entry delta over time** — institutions roll mechanically (monthly/quarterly, "never adjusted"), which is itself a finding: the discipline, not the delta tuning, drives the outcome.

## Sources

1. **Cboe BuyWrite Indices Methodology** (BXMD 0.30-delta selection rule) — https://cdn.cboe.com/api/global/us_indices/governance/Cboe_BuyWrite_Indices_Methodology.pdf
2. **Cboe S&P 500 95-110 Collar Index (CLL) description** — https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/newcollardescriptionoct1909.pdf
3. **Cboe Insights: Hedging Downside with PPUT, CLL and CLLZ** — https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/benchmark-indices-series-hedging-downside-exposure-with-pput-cll-and-cllz-indices/
4. **Israelov & Klein (AQR), "Risk and Return of Equity Index Collar Strategies," J. of Alternative Investments (2016)** — https://www.aqr.com/-/media/AQR/Documents/Journal-Articles/Risk-and-Return.pdf
5. **LGIM America, "Tailor Your Risk by Buttoning-up with an Equity Collar" (2024)** — https://am.landg.us.com/asset/4994de/globalassets/lgima/insights/whitepapers/tailor-your-risk-by-buttoning-up-with-an-equity-collar.pdf
6. **SpotGamma, "The JPM Collar Trade"** (observed JHEQX deltas) — https://spotgamma.com/jpm-morgan-collar-trade/ ; Morningstar JHEQX analysis — https://www.morningstar.com/funds/xnas/jheqx/analysis
7. **Ryan O'Connell, CFA, "Collar Option Strategy"** — https://ryanoconnellfinance.com/collar-strategy/
8. **OptionsDecay, "The 0.30/0.30 Delta Collar"** — https://www.optionsdecay.com/strategies/intermediate/collar/
9. **Equicurious, "Protective Puts and Collars"** (worked example, net delta +0.58) — https://equicurious.com/learn/derivatives/options-strategies-and-greeks/protective-puts-and-collars
10. **NISA, "The Long Right Tail: Asymmetry in Single-Stock Collars"** — https://www.nisa.com/perspectives/the-long-right-tail-asymmetry-in-single-stock-collars/
11. **Professional Pensions / bfinance (2019)** (UK pension put-spread collar) — https://www.professionalpensions.com/analysis/3069310/-schemes-protect-equity-losses
12. **Wells Fargo / UBS equity risk management guides** (2-year 90/120 monetization collars) — https://onlineservices.ubs.com/staticfiles/pws/adobe/equity_risk_management.pdf

**Bottom line:** sell the call at **0.20–0.30 delta** (0.30 to fund the put; 0.20 to keep upside), buy the put at **0.20–0.30 delta** (0.30 for a ~5% floor; 0.20 for a cheaper ~8–10% floor), and build the structure **asymmetrically** — put floor first by risk tolerance, call strike second by premium-matching — expecting a net position delta near **+0.50**. That is simultaneously the retail practitioner consensus, the codified Cboe benchmark convention, and the observed practice of the largest institutional collar programs.

# Industrial IoT Platform Selection for Predictive Maintenance — 50 km² Australian Mining Site

**Scope:** Siemens vs. Honeywell vs. Australian local providers, assessed on (1) durability in extreme heat/dust, (2) edge processing, (3) legacy SCADA integration, and (4) total implementation cost across a 50 km² site.

---

## 1. Direct Answer and Recommendation

**No single vendor should win this procurement outright. The evidence supports a hybrid, two-layer architecture:**

1. **Primary condition-monitoring platform:** **Honeywell Versatilis (HVT) + Experion EHM** for critical and hazardous-area rotating equipment. It has the strongest certified field durability of any candidate (−40 to +80 °C, IP66/67, ATEX/IECEx Zone 0 intrinsic safety as standard), genuine on-sensor edge analytics (FFT at the node), LoRaWAN long-range radio suitable for a 50 km² footprint, and the lowest-friction SCADA path if you run Experion — or a clean MQTT path if you don't. ([Honeywell Versatilis product page](https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter); [HVT Technical Specification](https://prod-edam.honeywell.com/content/dam/honeywell-edam/pmt/hps/products/pmc/field-instruments/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter/pmt-hps-hvt-technical-specification.pdf))

2. **Wide-area / non-critical layer:** an **Australian local LoRaWAN provider** (Meshed, Sentient, iMACHINE, S5 System, Vayeron, Miniotec, or Ampcontrol depending on use case) at roughly **30–40% lower 5-year TCO** than either multinational, with Pilbara/Bowen Basin-proven deployments and local support response. ([Meshed Smart Mining](https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/); [S5 System FAQ](https://s5system.com/faq/))

3. **Unifying integration layer:** a vendor-neutral **OPC UA / Modbus TCP edge gateway** (e.g., OPC Foundation's open-source [UA-EdgeTranslator](https://github.com/OPCFoundation/UA-EdgeTranslator/blob/main/README.md), Softing uaGate MB, or [SAFEgroup's SGAteway](https://safegroup.com.au/sgateway-your-gateway-to-industrial-iot/)) normalising all sensor streams into your existing SCADA/historian, protecting against lock-in and letting you swap analytics layers without re-instrumenting.

**Budget guidance:** plan **A$0.7–1.5M Year-1 installed cost for 500–1,000 monitoring points with 5–8 LoRaWAN gateways**, plus 15–20% contingency. Indicative **5-year TCO: local-led A$0.8–1.3M; Honeywell A$1.1–1.8M; Siemens A$1.0–1.9M** (ranges reconcile four independent cost models; divergence is driven by unpublished software licensing — see §6.4). Before fleet commitment, run a **fixed-price 90-day pilot on 1–3 critical assets** (S5 System offers one at **A$4,900** — [S5 FAQ](https://s5system.com/faq/)) plus a professional RF site survey.

**Where Siemens fits:** Siemens makes excellent sensors (SITRANS MS200 at IP68/IP69) and the strongest *managed* edge-compute platform (Industrial Edge / SCALANCE LPE), but its sensor radios are short-range (Bluetooth LE, Wi-Fi) and cannot economically blanket 50 km², and its analytics default to the cloud. Deploy Siemens selectively — as high-density clusters in the process plant/MCCs, or as a Senseye analytics overlay on your 20–30 most critical assets — not as the sole wide-area platform.

---

## 2. Headline Comparison Matrix

| Criterion | Siemens (MS200/CM-IOT + Insights Hub/Senseye) | Honeywell (Versatilis + Experion EHM/Forge) | Australian local (Meshed, Sentient, iMACHINE, S5, Vayeron, Miniotec, Ampcontrol, MST) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Field sensor durability | IP68/IP69, −30 to +80 °C (MS200); IP66, −40 to +80 °C (CM-IOT) | **IP66/67, −40 to +80 °C, Zone 0 Ex ia standard** | IP67–IP68 typical; IECEx IS options (Vayeron, Miniotec, iMACHINE); **Group I underground coal** (Ampcontrol) |
| Gateway/edge durability | **Weak: CC220 & IOT2050 are IP20, 0–50 °C — need climate-controlled cabinets** | FDAP: −40 to +70 °C, IP66/67, NEMA 4X | IP67 gateways; −40 to +75 °C class (Advantech WISE-6610) |
| Dust hardening evidence | **Strongest documented: SIPLUS tested to IEC 60721-3-3 class 3S4 (sand/dust), 3C4 (corrosive gas)** | IP66/67 + G3 corrosion (ANSI/ISA-S71.04) on FDAP | IP6X dust-tight; purpose-built for Pilbara dust |
| Edge processing | Strongest *managed platform* (Docker, Industrial Edge Management) but cloud-centric analytics by default | **Strongest on-sensor edge** (on-board FFT, event triggers, 20-day logging) + on-prem EHM analytics VM | On-device ML (Miniotec, S5); on-prem data sovereignty (Sentient) |
| Legacy SCADA fit | Best with WinCC/PCS 7; legacy needs OPC UA/MQTT bridge | **Best with Experion; broad protocol menu (OPC, Modbus, HART, DNP3, MQTT)** | Best for heterogeneous Citect/Wonderware/Rockwell brownfield via integrators (Deftec, Sentient, S5) |
| 5-yr TCO (500–1,000 pts) | ~A$1.0–1.9M | ~A$1.1–1.8M | **~A$0.8–1.3M** |
| Lock-in risk | High (per-asset cloud subscriptions) | Moderate (low if Experion incumbent) | Low–moderate |
| Local support | National, corporate channel | Via AU distributors (Territory Instruments, Motherwell) | **WA/QLD on-the-ground, 2–4 wk stock (S5 Perth)** |

---

## 3. Criterion 1 — Durability in Extreme Heat and Dust

### 3.1 Environmental design baseline

Pilbara-class conditions mean sustained >40 °C ambient with a regional record of **50.7 °C at Onslow in January 2022** ([Rio Tinto](https://www.riotinto.com/en/news/stories/adapting-for-extreme-heat)); black-exposed equipment surfaces reach 60–80 °C. Practical procurement rules that follow:

- **Field devices must be rated ≥+70 °C ambient and ≥IP66** (IP6X = dust-tight), or they require cabinet-level mitigation (sunshades, ventilation, derated battery schedules) that adds real cost. Australian mine-spec enclosures are typically IP66/IK10 rated to +60 °C *with* sunshades.
- **Hazardous areas:** IECEx/ATEX certification is required where explosive gas or dust atmospheres exist; **underground coal additionally requires Group I (Ex ia I Ma/M1) certification** — a critical gap flagged in §7.
- **Battery chemistry derates sharply above 40 °C**; vendor battery-life claims are quoted at 25 °C and should be contractually re-based to Pilbara duty cycles.

### 3.2 Siemens

**SITRANS MS200 multisensor** (vibration + temperature, clamp-on) — [Siemens FI 01 catalog](https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1159413/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq_fi01_en.pdf):
- Enclosure **IP68** (later datasheets add **IP69**, 2 m/24 h); operating **−30 to +80 °C**; 3-axis MEMS 15 Hz–3.3 kHz, ±4 g/±16 g, 6.6 kHz sampling; battery 2–5 years.
- Hazardous-area variant (**Ex ia IIC T5**) is special-order, with hazardous-zone operating range restricted to −30 to +50 °C.
- **Weak link:** the companion **SITRANS CC220 gateway is IP20, 0–50 °C, cabinet-mounted**, polling up to 8 sensors over BLE 5.0. Every sensor must be within practical BLE range (~10–30 m industrial) of a cabinet-housed gateway.

**Connection Module IOT** (motor/drivetrain) — [CM-IOT datasheet](https://assets.new.siemens.com/siemens/assets/api/uuid:268a3e4e-97dc-474b-b58c-dd63abb3187b/SIEMENS-Connection-Module-IOT-Technical-datasheet_original.pdf): IP66, −40 to +80 °C safe area (−40 to +60 °C hazardous, ATEX Zone 2/22 with Ex kit), 4×AA lithium up to 4 years, **but Wi-Fi radio with ~100 m range** — again unsuitable as a wide-area technology.

**SIMATIC IOT2050 edge gateway:** **0 to +50 °C, IP20** ([IOT2050 datasheet](https://support.industry.siemens.com/teddatasheet/?caller=SIOS&format=pdf&language=en&mlfbs=6ES7647-0BA00-1YA2)) — must live in an air-conditioned cabinet; this is Siemens' weakest point for Australian summer field deployment.

**Where Siemens is genuinely best-in-class on durability evidence:** the **SIPLUS extreme** I/O line is explicitly tested to **IEC 60721-3-3 class 3S4 (sand and dust) and 3C4 (salt spray/SO₂/H₂S corrosive gas)**, −25 to +70 °C with conformal coating ([SIPLUS datasheet](https://mall.industry.siemens.com/teddatasheet/?caller=Mall&format=PDF&language=en&mlfbs=6AG1151-3BA23-7AB0)), and the **SCALANCE LPE9413** edge processor is fanless −40 to +60 °C ([SCALANCE LPE](https://www.siemens.com/global/en/products/automation/industrial-communication/industrial-ethernet/local-processing.html)). No other candidate publishes equivalent *tested* sand/dust class data.

### 3.3 Honeywell

**Versatilis Transmitter (HVT)** — [product page](https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter), [technical spec](https://prod-edam.honeywell.com/content/dam/honeywell-edam/pmt/hps/products/pmc/field-instruments/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter/pmt-hps-hvt-technical-specification.pdf), AU availability via [Territory Instruments](https://www.territoryinstruments.com/instrumentation/honeywell/honeywell-versatilis/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter) and [Motherwell](https://www.motherwell.net.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Honeywell-Versatilis%E2%84%A2-Transmitter-Technical-Specification.pdf):
- **IP66/IP67, −40 to +80 °C**, 0–100% RH non-condensing.
- **Hazardous-area certifications as standard:** ATEX/IECEx Ex ia (Zone 0 intrinsic safety), UKCA, FM/CSA Class I Div 1, NAMUR NE 95, plus ABS/DNV marine — the broadest standard certification set of any candidate.
- 6-in-1 measurement: triaxial vibration (±16 g, ~5–2500 Hz, ISO 10816-3 velocity 0–100 mm/s), acoustics (20 Hz–20 kHz, 120 dB SPL), surface and ambient temperature, humidity, barometric pressure.
- Battery **3 years** at 5-min sense/30-min transmit, **5 years** at 10-min/60-min; AES-256 on LoRa and BLE; M6 screw/magnetic/epoxy/adhesive mounting.
- Companion **FDAP wireless infrastructure: −40 to +70 °C, IP66/67, NEMA 4X, G3 corrosion class per ANSI/ISA-S71.04** ([Field Device Access Point](https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/wireless/onewireless-network/field-device-access-point)).
- **Caution:** the older XYR 6000 wireless line was discontinued December 2022 (support ends 2027) — specify current Versatilis/SmartLine lines only.

### 3.4 Australian local providers

| Provider | Hardware / certification highlights |
|---|---|
| **S5 System (Perth)** | RotaMon sensor: **IP68 hermetically sealed M12×30 mm bolt form factor**, on-device failure prediction, LoRaWAN/NB-IoT, 5+ yr battery; 2–4 week Perth stock ([RotaMon](https://s5system.com/rotamon/)). Temperature range not publicly published — **obtain in writing before award**. |
| **Miniotec (AU)** | 6-in-1 vibration sensor **IP68, intrinsically safe**, on-device ML ([Miniotec](https://www.miniotec.com/wireless-vibration-sensor)) |
| **Vayeron (QLD)** | Smart-Idler conveyor roller sensor **IP67, IECEx IS certified (2020)**, up to 5,000 rollers per gateway ([datasheet](https://vayeron.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/Smart-Idler%C2%AE-Data-Sheet.pdf)) |
| **Ampcontrol** | iMAC2: **IECEx Group I Ex ia — underground coal certified**, Modbus TCP/IP, proven on conveyors >50 km ([iMAC2 datasheet](https://ampcontrolgroup.com/resource/technical-data-sheet-imac2-controller); [conveyor solutions](https://ampcontrolgroup.com/solutions/conveyor-monitoring-and-control)) |
| **iMACHINE (NSW)** | ACORN SmartNode: Australian designed/manufactured, **IECEx options**, satellite/4G/Wi-Fi/Ethernet backhaul, wireless mesh ([iMACHINE](https://www.imachine.com.au/wireless-remote-operations)) |
| **Meshed** | IP67 gateways, AU915 LoRaWAN up to 20 km, 99.9% uptime SLA; Pilbara lithium site ran on **2 gateways at 99.7% uptime** ([case study](https://www.meshed.network/resources/smart-water-monitoring-lithium-mining/)); iron-ore deployments ([case study](https://www.meshed.network/resources/iron-ore-mining-case-study/)) |
| **MST Global (Komatsu)** | AXON gateway IP65, 0–50 °C — suited to underground/controlled environments rather than exposed surface plant ([AXON datasheet](https://mstglobal.com/wp-content/uploads/AXON-Gateway-Datasheet-Revision-1-20211216-1.pdf)) |
| **Novecom** | Blast vibration monitor certified to **AS 2187.2-2006** ([Novecom](https://novecom.com.au/)) |

### 3.5 Durability verdict

**Honeywell wins for exposed surface plant**: it is the only candidate combining +80 °C field rating, IP66/67, and Zone 0 intrinsic safety *as standard*, with genuine Pilbara thermal headroom. **Siemens' sensors are individually rugged (IP68/69) but its gateway chain (IP20, 50 °C) is the architectural weak point** outdoors. **Local providers are the only route to Group I underground coal certification** (Ampcontrol) and to purpose-built Australian form factors (S5's hermetic bolt, Vayeron's in-roller sensor).

## 4. Criterion 2 — Edge Processing Capabilities

**Honeywell — strongest sensor-level edge.** The HVT computes **on-board FFT (4096-line spectra), RMS, kurtosis/crest factor, sub-band energy, and threshold event triggers at the node**, transmitting only RMS/FFT peaks over LoRaWAN, with **20 days of offline data logging** ([HVT spec](https://prod-edam.honeywell.com/content/dam/honeywell-edam/pmt/hps/products/pmc/field-instruments/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter/pmt-hps-hvt-technical-specification.pdf)). Honeywell APM's mining pedigree includes a primary-crushing deployment with **324 rules-based alerts and 4 MMPCA models with edge buffering through connectivity outages** ([case study](https://process.honeywell.com/content/dam/process/en/documents/gated/hon-ia-hps-enhancing-crushing-availability-case-study.pdf)).

# Q3 2024 Performance Attribution & LP Call Narrative
**Fund:** $5B Tech-Focused Equity Strategy | **Fund:** −8.7% | **Benchmark:** −2.1% | **Active Return:** −650 bps

---

## Executive Summary

Q3 2024 was a violent growth-to-value rotation — arguably a 1-in-10-year regime quarter for style factors. The S&P 500 Equal Weight Index (RSP) returned roughly **+9.6% total return**, its best Q3 since 2010, while the cap-weighted S&P 500 returned +5.89%, the Nasdaq-100 +2.12%, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index **−5.3% to −6.3%**. Over 67% of S&P 500 constituents beat the cap-weighted index versus a historical average of 31% ([Live Oak Q3 letter](https://liveoakprivatewealth.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/LOPW-Q3-Letter-2024.pdf); [Morningstar Q3 review](https://www.morningstar.com/markets/13-charts-stocks-bonds-q3-roller-coaster-rallies)). Utilities (+19.4%), Real Estate (+17.2%), and Industrials (+11.6%) led; IT was the second-worst sector. The fund's two largest holdings were caught directly in the de-rating: **NVDA finished −1.7% (with a ~−26% close-to-close / ~−35% intraday peak-to-trough drawdown mid-quarter)** and **MSFT finished −3.7% to −5.8%** depending on measurement convention. Critically, the top-2 positions explain only ~50–62 bps of the fund's loss — roughly **10% of the active shortfall**; the remaining ~590 bps came from the rest of the AI-leveraged book. Measured against the fund's tech-like benchmark, **security selection drove ~80–85% of active underperformance**; measured against RSP, sector/style allocation explains roughly half. Both lenses are quantified below.

---

## Deliverable 1: NVDA & MSFT vs. RSP — 90-Day Price/Volume Data (64 trading sessions, Jul 1–Sep 30, 2024)

### 1.1 Summary Statistics

| Ticker | 6/28/24 Close | 9/30/24 Close | Q3 Price Return | In-Qtr High | In-Qtr Low | Peak-to-Trough |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NVDA** (split-adj.) | $123.54 | $121.44 | **−1.7%** (−2.3% from 7/1 close of $124.30) | ~$134.91 (7/10 close); $140.76 intraday 6/20 | $98.91 close 8/7; ~$90.7 intraday 8/5; $100.45 9/6 | **≈−26% close / ≈−35% intraday** |
| **MSFT** | $446.95 | $430.30 | **−3.7%** (−5.8% from 7/1 close of $456.73) | $467.56 (7/5) | $395.15 (8/5) | **≈−15.5%** |
| **RSP** | ~$163.10 | $179.16 | **+9.6% total return** (price quotes +8.0% to +9.9% by vendor) | $179.16 (9/30) | $162.83 (8/5) | ≈−4% |

Sources: [exa.ai NVDA series](https://exa.ai/library/markets/stock/NVDA?date=2024-09-30&view=series&from=2024-07-01), [exa.ai RSP series](https://exa.ai/library/markets/stock/RSP?date=2024-09-30&view=series&from=2024-07-01), [TGM RSP](https://tgmcharts.com/stocks/RSP/total-return-cagr), [Citi Wealth Q3](https://marketinsights.citi.com/Market-Commentary/Quarterly-Market-Update/CWB-Market-Performance-Q3-2024-Q4-2024.html). Vendor discrepancies (±50–90 bps) arise from 6/28 vs. 7/1 start convention and dividend adjustment; `auto_adjust=True` in the code below normalizes this.

### 1.2 News Catalysts Mapped to Volume/Price Spikes

|---|---|---|---|
| Jul 11–16 | NVDA/MSFT | Rotation begins | SOX begins 25% peak-to-trough slide off July CPI; capital rotates to small caps ([Liontrust Q3](https://www.liontrust.com/insights/monthly-comms/2024/10/liontrust-us-opportunities-fund-q3-2024-review)) |
| Jul 19 | MSFT | Heavy volume | CrowdStrike faulty update crashes ~8.5M Windows devices globally |
| Jul 30 (AH) | MSFT | **−7% AH; ~33M shs** | FY24 Q4: rev $64.7B beat, but **Azure +29% vs. +31% consensus — first Azure miss since 2022** ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/07/30/microsoft-msft-q4-earnings-report-2024.html)) |

### 1.3 Reproducible Python — Data Pull + All Three Annotated Charts

import yfinance as yf, pandas as pd, numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, matplotlib.dates as mdates

START, END = "2024-06-28", "2024-10-01"   # Q3 2024 window
TKS = ["NVDA","MSFT","RSP","ARKK","FSPTX","SOXX","SOXQ","XSW","IGV","SKYY","CLOU"]
raw  = yf.download(TKS, start=START, end=END, auto_adjust=True, progress=False)
px, vol = raw["Close"].dropna(how="all"), raw["Volume"]
px.to_csv("q3_2024_prices.csv"); vol.to_csv("q3_2024_volumes.csv")   # full 90-day data
# BGIAX is a non-listed mutual fund; if yfinance errors use "0P00000VC9.L" (B-Acc GBP) or FCNTX proxy

EVENTS = [("2024-07-19","CrowdStrike outage"),("2024-07-30","MSFT FQ4: Azure +29% vs 31% est"),
          ("2024-08-05","Yen carry unwind / VIX 65"),("2024-08-28","NVDA FQ2: beat, GM guide 75%"),
          ("2024-09-03","NVDA -9.5% / DOJ subpoena report"),("2024-09-18","Fed -50bps"),
          ("2024-09-23","D.A. Davidson downgrades MSFT")]

# CHART 1 — Absolute price performance, rebased to 100
norm = px.div(px.iloc[0])*100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13,6))
for t,c in [("NVDA","green"),("MSFT","orange"),("RSP","navy")]:
    ax.plot(norm.index, norm[t], lw=2, label=t, color=c)
for d,lbl in EVENTS:
    ax.axvline(pd.Timestamp(d), color="red", ls="--", alpha=0.35)
    ax.annotate(lbl, xy=(pd.Timestamp(d), norm["RSP"].max()*1.01), fontsize=7, rotation=25)
ax.set_title("Chart 1 — Q3 2024 Absolute Price Performance (6/28/24 = 100): NVDA, MSFT vs. RSP")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d"))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart1_absolute.png", dpi=150); plt.close()

# CHART 2 — Rolling 30-day (21 trading-day) relative return vs RSP
rel = px.pct_change().sub(px["RSP"].pct_change(), axis=0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,1, figsize=(13,8), sharex=True)
for ax,t in zip(axes, ["NVDA","MSFT"]):
    r = rel[t].rolling(21).sum()*100
    ax.plot(r.index, r, lw=2, color="darkgreen" if t=="NVDA" else "darkorange")
    ax.fill_between(r.index, r, 0, where=(r>=0), color="green", alpha=0.25)
    ax.fill_between(r.index, r, 0, where=(r<0), color="red", alpha=0.25)
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{t} − RSP, 30d (%)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
axes[0].set_title("Chart 2 — Rolling 30-Day Relative Return vs. RSP")
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d"))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart2_rolling30d.png", dpi=150); plt.close()

# CHART 3 — Volume spikes with news catalysts
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2,1, figsize=(13,8), sharex=True)
for ax,t in zip(axes, ["NVDA","MSFT"]):
    v = vol[t].dropna()/1e6; ma = v.rolling(20).mean()
    ax.bar(v.index, v, color="steelblue", alpha=0.6, width=1.2)
    ax.plot(ma.index, ma, color="red", lw=1.5, label="20d avg")
    for d,lbl in EVENTS:
        td = pd.Timestamp(d); near = min(v.index, key=lambda x: abs(x-td))
        ax.annotate(lbl, xy=(near, v.max()*0.92), fontsize=6.5, rotation=40,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="darkred", lw=0.7), color="darkred")
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{t} volume (M shs)"); ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
axes[0].set_title("Chart 3 — Daily Volume & Catalysts (split-adjusted shares)")
axes[1].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b-%d"))
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig("chart3_volume.png", dpi=150); plt.close()

# BONUS — Peer relative performance (Deliverable 3) and Brinson scaffold (Deliverable 2)
def qtr_ret(t): s = px[t].dropna(); return (s.iloc[-1]/s.iloc[0]-1)*100
peers = ["ARKK","FSPTX","NVDA","MSFT","RSP","SOXX","XSW","CLOU","SKYY"]
print(pd.Series({t: round(qtr_ret(t),2) for t in peers if t in px}).sort_values())

# Brinson-Fachler scaffold — REPLACE illustrative weights with actual holdings
w_fund  = {"Semis":.35,"Software":.25,"Cloud":.20,"ConsTech":.10,"Other":.07,"Cash":.03}
w_bench = {"Semis":.08,"Software":.12,"Cloud":.10,"ConsTech":.25,"Other":.20,"Cash":.25}  # ~RSP-style
r_fund  = {"Semis":-3.5,"Software":-2.0,"Cloud":3.0,"ConsTech":10.0,"Other":5.0,"Cash":1.4}
r_bench = {"Semis":-5.3,"Software":1.0,"Cloud":4.5,"ConsTech":10.5,"Other":8.0,"Cash":9.6}
Rb = sum(w_bench[s]*r_bench[s] for s in w_bench)
alloc  = sum((w_fund[s]-w_bench[s])*(r_bench[s]-Rb) for s in w_bench)
select = sum(w_bench[s]*(r_fund[s]-r_bench[s]) for s in w_bench)
inter  = sum((w_fund[s]-w_bench[s])*(r_fund[s]-r_bench[s]) for s in w_bench)
print(f"Allocation {alloc:.2f}% | Selection {select:.2f}% | Interaction {inter:.2f}% | Total {alloc+select+inter:.2f}%")
```

### 1.4 Top-2 Position Contribution (the load-bearing math)

```
NVDA:  12.0% wt × −1.7%  ≈  −20 bps of fund return
MSFT:   8.0% wt × −3.7%  ≈  −30 bps of fund return
Top-2 combined:            ≈  −50 bps  → only ~10% of the −650 bps active shortfall
Residual (rest of book):   ≈ −600 bps  → the real story
```
