# DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Autism Criteria: A Structured Comparison with Focus on Sensory Processing

## Bottom Line Up Front

Both manuals nest sensory processing differences inside the restricted/repetitive behavior (RRB) domain rather than treating them as a standalone criterion, but they weight them very differently. **DSM-5 (APA, 2013)** makes "hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment" a named, polythetic sub-criterion (B4) — one of four RRB features of which at least **two must be present**. Sensory differences alone therefore cannot satisfy DSM-5's Criterion B. **ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; effective 1 January 2022)** embeds "lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli" within a non-numerical, prototype-based list of ~16 illustrative RRB manifestations, with **no minimum symptom count** in either diagnostic domain. The result is a systematic trade-off that the published evidence supports: DSM-5's stricter algorithm (all 3 social-communication sub-criteria + ≥2 of 4 RRBs) produces documented **under-diagnosis** — a pooled ~31–37% reduction in ASD diagnoses relative to DSM-IV/ICD-10 populations, concentrated among cognitively able adults, women/girls, PDD-NOS/Asperger presentations, and plausibly sensory-predominant profiles — while ICD-11's flexibility carries a hypothesized, still-unquantified **false-positive risk** (Kamp-Becker 2024 calculates ~304 permissible symptom combinations). No large head-to-head DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 diagnostic-accuracy study has been published; WHO, NICE, AAP and APA positions, advocacy stances, safety evidence, and coding implications are detailed below.

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Table

| Row | **DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (APA, 2013; text rev. 2022)** | **ICD-11 (WHO, adopted May 2019; effective 2022; CDDR March 2024)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | **Monothetic:** "Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts," operationalized through **three sub-criteria, all required** (currently or by history): (A1) social-emotional reciprocity; (A2) nonverbal communicative behaviors; (A3) developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships ([IACC reproduction of criteria](https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml)). | **Prototype-based Essential Feature:** "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." Seven illustrative manifestation areas are listed (understanding/interest in verbal and nonverbal communication, integrating language with nonverbal cues, social awareness, imagining/responding to others' feelings, mutual sharing of interests, making and sustaining peer relationships) with **no minimum number required**; ~19 manifestations total described ([WHO ICD-11 6A02](https://www.findacode.com/icd-11/code-437815624.html); [Greaves-Lord, Skuse & Mandy 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/)). |
| **Sensory processing mention/weighting** | **Explicit, equally weighted, polythetic sub-criterion B4:** "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)." Requires **≥2 of 4** B-criteria (B1 stereotyped movement/objects/speech; B2 insistence on sameness; B3 fixated interests; B4 sensory). New in DSM-5 — DSM-IV treated sensory features only as associated features. | **Listed, non-weighted manifestation:** "Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (especially clothing and food), odours and tastes, heat, cold or pain." Sensory features are one of ~16 illustrative RRB manifestations; the requirement is only "a range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns... clearly atypical or excessive for the individual's age and sociocultural context" — **no minimum count**. Deliberate change from ICD-10, where sensory processing was not a core diagnostic feature ([Greaves-Lord et al. 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/)). |
| **Severity specifiers** | **Mandatory three-level system, rated separately for each core domain:** Level 1 "Requiring support"; Level 2 "Requiring substantial support"; Level 3 "Requiring very substantial support," with behavioral anchors per level. | **No severity levels.** Differentiation via subcategories 6A02.0–6A02.5 (plus 6A02.Y/.Z) crossing two dimensions: disorder of intellectual development (present/absent) × functional language (mild/no impairment, impaired, absent). |
| **Age/onset requirements** | Criterion C: "Symptoms must be present in the **early developmental period** (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be **masked by learned strategies** in later life)." DSM-IV's strict <3-years onset was removed. | "Onset occurs during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." Explicitly acknowledges **compensation**: "Some individuals with autism spectrum disorder are able to function adequately in many contexts through exceptional effort, such that their deficits may not be apparent to others." |
| **Functional impairment thresholds** | Criterion D: "Symptoms cause **clinically significant impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." Criterion E: not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay (though co-diagnosis is permitted). | "Deficits are sufficiently severe to cause impairment in **personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning** and are usually a pervasive feature... observable in all settings." Broader enumerated domains; diagnosis "is still appropriate" when exceptional effort masks deficits. |
| **Codes & co-occurring conditions** | 299.00 (F84.0 crosswalk); specifiers for intellectual impairment, language impairment, known genetic/medical condition, associated neurodevelopmental/mental disorder, catatonia (F06.1). Separate diagnosis of **Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder** available for those failing Criterion B. | Stem code **6A02** with intellectual/language subtypes 6A02.0–6A02.5; catatonia coded separately; **no SCD analogue**. Postcoordination architecture allows extension codes, though this is not yet operationalized in most health systems. |

**Key structural contrast:** DSM-5 is algorithmically strict (3-of-3 social + 2-of-4 RRB); ICD-11 is descriptive/prototype-based. Kamp-Becker (2024, *Molecular Psychiatry*) calculates that ICD-11's construct permits roughly **304 (19 × 16) distinct manifestation combinations** satisfying its essential features, versus DSM-5's much narrower combinatoric space — the quantitative core of the inclusivity-versus-specificity debate ([PMC11153155](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)).

---

## (B) Evidence Synthesis: Peer-Reviewed Sources (2013–present)

*Constraint honored: 5 sources — 2 systematic reviews/meta-analyses or systematic comparisons, 2 primary empirical studies, 1 critical perspective. GRADE ratings reflect study design, risk of bias, consistency, directness, and precision.*

### 1. Kulage, Smaldone & Cohn (2014) — Systematic review & meta-analysis
*"How will DSM-5 affect autism diagnosis? A systematic literature review and meta-analysis." J Autism Dev Disord 44(8):1918–1932.*
- **Design:** Systematic review/meta-analysis of 14 studies (from 418 records) applying DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV-TR criteria to the same populations.
- **Sample:** Pooled across 14 studies using ADOS, ADI-R, and checklist-based reference standards.
- **Key statistics:** Pooled decrease in ASD diagnosis under DSM-5 = **31%** (95% CI 20–44%, p = 0.006); Autistic disorder **22%** (95% CI 16–29%, p < .001); **PDD-NOS 70%** (95% CI 55–82%, p = 0.01); Asperger's **70%** but non-significant (95% CI 26–94%, p = 0.38). A 5-year follow-up meta-analysis (Kulage et al. 2019, [DOI: 10.1007/s10803-019-03967-5](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-019-03967-5)) and an independent meta-analysis (Bitsika & Sharpley 2016, *Rev J Autism Dev Disord* 3:119–124) both confirmed a **35–37% reduction** relative to DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR.
- **GRADE:** **Low–Moderate** (consistent direction of effect across studies, but heterogeneous reference standards and observational designs).
- [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/)

### 2. First, Gaebel, Maj et al. (2021) — Systematic category-level comparison
*"An organization- and category-level comparison of diagnostic requirements for mental disorders in ICD-11 and DSM-5." World Psychiatry 20(1):34–51.*
- **Design:** Expert-panel systematic cross-walk of ICD-11 Essential Features vs. DSM-5 criteria for 103 diagnostic entities (the official WHO–APA harmonization-group output).
- **Sample:** 103 diagnostic categories.
- **Key statistics:** 20 disorders (19.4%) rated "**major differences**"; 42 (40.8%) minor definitional; 10 (9.7%) minor due to greater DSM-5 specification; 31 (30.1%) essentially identical. For ASD specifically: DSM-5 requires all three social sub-criteria while ICD-11 lists seven illustrative manifestations with no minimum; the authors note ICD-11's RRB examples are less dominated by intellectual-disability-typical exemplars and foreground sensory manifestations and special interests more characteristic of cognitively able individuals.
- **GRADE:** **Moderate** for descriptive harmonization (comprehensive, authoritative); **Low** for diagnostic-accuracy inference (no patient-level data).
- [DOI: 10.1002/wps.20825](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825)

### 3. Wilson et al. (2013) — Primary empirical study #1
*"Comparison of ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR and DSM-5 in an adult autism spectrum disorder diagnostic clinic." J Autism Dev Disord 43:2515–2525 (King's College London).*
- **Design:** Cross-sectional diagnostic concordance study in a specialist adult clinic using gold-standard instruments.
- **Sample:** **N = 150** intellectually able adults.
- **Key statistics:** Of adults diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, **only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**; a further **19%** met DSM-5 Social Communication Disorder criteria (a category with fewer service entitlements). Of those with DSM-IV-TR Autistic Disorder/Asperger Syndrome, **78%** met DSM-5 criteria. Relaxing the algorithm (fewer required items, or scoring "uncertain" as "present") raised sensitivity **without sacrificing specificity**. Authors warn reduced diagnostic rates "may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services."
- **GRADE:** **Moderate** (single-site, intellectually able adults only, but direct criteria comparison with validated instruments).
- [KCL repository](https://kclpure.kcl.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/)

### 4. Kalra et al. (2021) — Primary empirical study #2
*"Comparison of the diagnostic criteria for ASD using DSM and ICD: A study from North India." J Indian Assoc Child Adolesc Ment Health 17(1):25–47.*
- **Design:** Cross-sectional diagnostic concordance study.
- **Sample:** **N = 100** children aged 2.5–16 years assessed against DSM-5, DSM-IV-TR, and ICD-10 (DCR-10).
- **Key statistics:** DSM-5 ASD showed Cohen's **κ = 0.846** vs. DSM-IV-TR and **κ = 0.874** vs. ICD-10 for childhood autism/autistic disorder; agreement fell to **κ = 0.699 / 0.703** when broader ASD categories were compared. DSM-5 **specificity 1.0 and 0.961** vs. DSM-IV-TR ASD and ICD-10 ASD respectively. Children with atypical autism/PDD-NOS were most likely to lose diagnosis.
- **GRADE:** **Low–Moderate** (single-site, modest sample, non-Western setting limits generalizability).
- [DOI: 10.1177/0973134220210103](https://doi.org/10.1177/0973134220210103)

### 5. Kamp-Becker (2024) — Critical perspective
*"Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11 — a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research." Molecular Psychiatry.*
- **Design:** Textual-critical analysis of ICD-11 CDDR vs. DSM-5.
- **Key statistics/claims:** ICD-11 permits ~**304 (19 × 16) symptom combinations**; drops several exemplars typical of ASD with intellectual disability (object flipping, smelling/touching objects, echolalia, visual fascination) while retaining sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity; "bears a large danger of **false positive diagnoses**, of further increased prevalence rates, limitations of access to ASD-specific services and of increasing the non-specificity of treatments"; unoperationalized "compensation" language undermines behavioral-observation validity.
- **GRADE:** **Low/Very low** for empirical effect estimates (opinion); **High** fidelity as descriptive mapping of the ICD-11 text.
- [PMC11153155](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)

**Supporting quantitative context (2012 field-trial re-analyses, cited as background):** McPartland, Reichow & Volkmar (2012, *JAACAP*, [PMC3424065](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/)) found proposed DSM-5 criteria yielded sensitivity **60.6%** and specificity **94.9%** against clinical diagnosis — with sensitivity collapsing to **0.25 (Asperger's), 0.28 (PDD-NOS), and 0.46 for IQ ≥ 70** vs. 0.70 for IQ < 70 (χ²(1)=34.9, p<.001). Frazier et al. (2012; N=14,744 siblings) found DSM-5 specificity 0.97 vs. DSM-IV 0.86 but sensitivity 0.81 vs. 0.95, recovering to **0.93 sensitivity / 0.95 specificity** when one fewer criterion was required; Huerta et al. (2012; N=4,453) reported 0.91–0.97 sensitivity with final criteria.

**Critical evidence gap:** No large, prospective, blinded head-to-head study applying DSM-5 and ICD-11 criteria to the same population with ASD-specific sensitivity/specificity has been published. The nearest ICD-11 field data are transdiagnostic: 1,806 adults with reliability kappas 0.45–0.88 across disorders (ASD not separately reported; [PMC5980511](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5980511/)) and a Mexico City child/adolescent study (n=52, kappas 0.46–0.53 excluding disruptive disorders; [Psychiatric Services](https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.202000830)). **Aggregate GRADE confidence: Low–Moderate.**

---

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

**World Health Organization.** WHO is ICD-11's publisher and its strongest proponent. ICD-11 was adopted at the 72nd World Health Assembly (May 2019) and took effect for global reporting **1 January 2022** ([WHO classifications](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/classification-of-diseases)). On **8 March 2024** WHO released the *Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements for ICD-11 Mental, Behavioural and Neurodevelopmental Disorders* (CDDR), the full clinical manual for chapter 6A02 ASD ([WHO publication 9789240077263](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240077263)). WHO explicitly endorses the inclusion of atypical sensory responses as a diagnostic requirement — a deliberate upgrade from ICD-10. As of May 2024, **132 Member States** were in implementation phases: 72 commenced, 50 running/expanding pilots, **14 actively collecting/reporting ICD-11 data**; 10 languages released, 25 in translation ([WHO, 8 Feb 2024](https://www.who.int/news/item/08-02-2024-icd-11-2024-release)).

**American Psychiatric Association.** APA maintains DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022; ASD criteria unchanged) as the US diagnostic standard and has **no announced plan to adopt ICD-11 criteria** clinically. DSM-5's B4 was the first formal inclusion of sensory processing as a core ASD criterion in any major system. APA's DSM steering committee has publicly committed to "harmonizing as much as possible with ICD-11" in future revisions, acknowledging the symptom sets are well aligned ([Am J Psychiatry](https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.20250878)).

**American Academy of Pediatrics.** The AAP's 2020 clinical report (*Pediatrics* 145(1):e20193447) grounds practice in DSM-5, stating "the DSM-5 includes sensory symptoms in the diagnostic criteria for ASD," recommends tools such as the Short Sensory Profile, and notes sensory symptoms "may define subtypes of the disorder" ([AAP](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/145/1/e20193447/36917/)). Critically for sensory-focused presentations, the AAP's **2012 policy statement recommends against a standalone Sensory Processing Disorder diagnosis**, holding that sensory problems are likely symptoms of recognized disorders (autism, ADHD, anxiety), and cites inconclusive evidence for sensory integration therapy. The AAP has issued no position endorsing ICD-11 adoption or ICD-11's sensory weighting.

**NICE (UK).** The most explicitly pluralistic body. CG128 (under-19s), CG142 (adults, updated June 2021), and CG170 state that an autism diagnosis should be based on "**either DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria**" ([CG142 recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg142/chapter/recommendations); [CG128](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/CG128/chapter/recommendations)). NICE updated references from ICD-10 to ICD-11 in **March 2022**. CG142 lists "**altered sensory sensitivity, sensory processing difficulties and emotional regulation difficulties**" among core features clinicians should detect. No guideline body anywhere recommends weighting sensory features above other RRB features; NICE's acceptance of both manuals makes ICD-11's more permissive sensory structure clinically usable in the NHS today.

---

## (D) Advocacy Organization Positions

**Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN, US) — most structurally aligned with ICD-11's architecture.** ASAN grounds its positions in the neurodiversity paradigm: "there is no such thing as a 'normal' brain... we shouldn't try to cure or get rid of autism" ([ASAN: What We Believe](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/)). ASAN lobbied the DSM-5 workgroup from 2009–2012, achieving "significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis, addressing disparities... and blocking harmful proposals. Nonetheless, the lack of formal autistic representation... [led to] criteria that are likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale" ([chapter](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13)). Specifically, ASAN's 2012 policy brief and talking points called the **3-of-3 social-communication requirement "an overly restrictive standard"** and raised sensitivity concerns for adults, women/girls, and racial/ethnic minorities ([ASAN DSM-5 brief](https://autisticadvocacy.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/06/ASAN_DSM-5_2_final.pdf)); ASAN also opposed both the SCD category and the two-domain severity scale. In 2023 ASAN reaffirmed support for the unified spectrum diagnosis while standing by its critique ([The Transmitter](https://www.thetransmitter.org/spectrum/debate-remains-over-changes-in-dsm-5-a-decade-on/)). ASAN has **not** issued a formal document endorsing ICD-11 over DSM-5, but every structural feature it demanded — no minimum item counts, masking recognition, full-spectrum inclusion, rejection of deficit-based severity scaling — corresponds to where ICD-11 differs from DSM-5.

**National Autistic Society (NAS, UK) — neutral/pluralistic, neurodiversity-framed.** NAS states an autism diagnosis "should be based on criteria listed in the... DSM-5 or... ICD-11, according to the... NICE guidelines," and pointedly notes that "many people (including most autistic people) do not consider autism to be a disorder, and autism is not a disease" ([NAS](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment)). NAS reframes restricted/repetitive behaviors as "self-soothing or self-regulating behaviours, and focused and dedicated interests" and treats sensory differences as core characteristics. NAS declares neither manual superior; because the NHS is ICD-anchored, its practice effectively runs on ICD-11 under NICE's dual acceptance.

**Autism Speaks (US) — DSM-5-anchored, no comparative position.** Autism Speaks presents DSM-5 as the primary US reference and highlights "the addition of sensory issues as a symptom under the restricted/repetitive behavior category" as one of DSM-5's six major changes ([Autism Speaks DSM-5 FAQ](https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions); [criteria page](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5)). It has published no position on ICD-11 and does not frame the manual choice as a neurodiversity question. Note: ASAN and other autistic-led groups have long criticized Autism Speaks' medicalized framing, which itself bears on which organization's "neurodiversity-affirming" judgment carries weight with the autistic community.

**Synthesis:** No major advocacy organization has formally declared ICD-11 more neurodiversity-affirming than DSM-5. ASAN's documented positions align structurally with ICD-11's design (flexible thresholds, compensation recognition, no severity-level pathology), making it the strongest implicit vote for ICD-11-style criteria; NAS treats the manuals as interchangeable while applying neurodiversity language to both; Autism Speaks remains DSM-5-centric. This is an inference from stated principles, not a claimed formal endorsement.

---

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

**Under-diagnosis risk — documented, concentrated in DSM-5.** The pooled evidence (Section B) shows DSM-5's algorithm removes diagnosis from **31–37%** of previously diagnosed populations, with the steepest losses in PDD-NOS (~70%), Asperger's (~70% in the 2014 meta-analysis), cognitively able individuals (field-trial sensitivity 0.46 for IQ ≥ 70), and adults (only 56% of ICD-10R-diagnosed adults retained in Wilson 2013). The mechanism is arithmetic, not phenotypic: Frazier et al. showed relaxing the DSM-5 algorithm by a single criterion restored sensitivity to 0.93 at 0.95 specificity.

**Sensory-specific under-diagnosis.** Under DSM-5, a person whose **only** RRB manifestation is sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity fails Criterion B (needs ≥2 of 4). Under ICD-11, sensory reactivity within "a range" of atypical patterns can satisfy the RRB essential feature without a mandated companion symptom. No study has yet quantified this scenario directly, but the structural constraint is unambiguous, and sensory-predominant profiles are reported disproportionately among women and cognitively able adults — the same groups DSM-5 already under-captures. In an Italian adult sample, misdiagnosed autistic **females showed significantly higher hyper/hyporeactivity scores than males**, indicating sensory-focused female presentations are especially misdiagnosis-prone ([Brain Sci 2021, 11(7):912](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3425/11/7/912)).

**Gender-related misdiagnosis cascades.** Systematic review/meta-analysis evidence documents male-biased clinical procedures and significantly greater camouflaging/compensation in females ([Neurosci Biobehav Rev meta-analysis](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11065-023-09630-2)). Autistic women commonly accumulate prior diagnoses — anxiety, eating disorders, borderline personality disorder — before ASD is recognized ([PMC12467426](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12467426/); [CNS Spectrums](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cns-spectrums/article/what-misdiagnoses-do-women-with-autism-spectrum-disorder-receive-in-the-dsm5/37409014E08A16D93FF0DB95675E9EED)), leading to years of mismatched interventions (e.g., DBT for presumed BPD) while the underlying autism goes unaddressed. Both manuals acknowledge masking, but ICD-11's operationalization ("diagnosis is still appropriate" when effort masks deficits) is more permissive; DSM-5's remains subordinate to its item-count thresholds.

**Over-diagnosis / false-positive risk — hypothesized for ICD-11.** Kamp-Becker (2024) warns the ~304-combination structure risks false positives, inflated prevalence, diluted service access, and non-specific treatments; ICD-11 manifestations such as "lack of adaptability to new experiences" or "excessive adherence to rules" are difficult to differentiate from anxiety disorders, behavioral inhibition, or OCD. This risk is currently **theoretical**: no completed field trial reports ASD-specific ICD-11 sensitivity/specificity, so the magnitude is unknown — a material evidentiary asymmetry compared with the quantified DSM-5 exclusion data.

**Sensory-only presentations and inappropriate intervention.** Under *both* manuals, sensory differences alone are insufficient for ASD. The AAP's 2012 stance against standalone Sensory Processing Disorder means sensory-focused children who miss ASD criteria risk either no diagnosis (no services) or misattribution; meanwhile, sensory integration therapy — the default intervention offered to such children — carries inconclusive effectiveness evidence per AAP, creating a pathway to **inappropriate or non-evidence-based intervention regardless of manual**. Conversely, uncritical ICD-11 application could extend ASD diagnoses to purely sensory-atypical adults, with downstream risks of inappropriate treatment and prevalence inflation.

**Service-entitlement risk.** Wilson et al. documented that adults failing DSM-5 ASD may be redirected to Social Communication Disorder, which carries fewer service entitlements; ICD-11 has no SCD analogue, eliminating that specific off-ramp but removing a residual diagnostic home for non-RRB social-communication impairment.

---

## (F) Reimbursement / Coding Summary

**United States.** Billing runs on **ICD-10-CM under HIPAA**; DSM-5/DSM-5-TR is the diagnostic reference but claims are submitted as **F84.0 (Autistic disorder)** — a DSM-IV-era code block (F84.0, F84.5 Asperger's, F84.8, F84.9) that maps all DSM-5 ASD diagnoses, severity levels, and specifiers onto the same billing code. The US has **not adopted ICD-11 for morbidity**: NCVHS recommended preparation in 2019 ([NCVHS letter](https://ncvhs.hhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Recommendation-Letter-Preparing-for-Adoption-of-ICD-11-as-a-Mandated-US-Health-Data-Standard-final.pdf)); CDC issued a 2023 RFI; the American Hospital Association's January 2024 response supported transition but urged evaluation of a US Clinical Modification ([AHA](https://www.aha.org/lettercomment/2024-01-12-aha-responds-cdc-rfi-icd-11-morbidity-coding-use)); a 2023 analysis suggests adoption may be possible **without** a CM variant ([PMC10531107](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10531107/)). Implementation is projected **no earlier than 2027–2029**, and a *JAMA Health Forum* analysis estimates a minimum 4–5 year runway, noting only **23.5% of ICD-10-CM codes map to a single ICD-11 stem code** ([JAMA Health Forum 2023](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama-health-forum/fullarticle/2807690)).

**Europe / UK.** WHO's official crosswalk maps F84.0 → **6A02.Z (ASD, unspecified)** — meaning the most common legacy billing path defaults to the *unspecified* ICD-11 code and does not automatically exploit ICD-11's six intellectual/language subcategories (6A02.0–6A02.5). NHS England adopted ICD-11 in March 2022 (prompting NICE's reference update); **14 countries** were reporting ICD-11 data as of May 2024; France is pursuing phased national adoption ([PMC12208713](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12208713/)); Germany (ICD-10-GM) and Spain (ICD-10-ES) remain on national ICD-10 variants during transition.

**Does adopting ICD-11 criteria change coverage?** **No payer — US or EU — has reported coverage changes attributable to adopting ICD-11 *criteria* versus DSM-5 criteria.** Reimbursement tracks the billing code, not the diagnostic manual: US state autism insurance mandates and Medicaid/Medicare reimburse under F84.0 regardless of whether the clinician used DSM-5 or ICD-11 reasoning, and EU systems map ASD codes roughly 1:1 to existing service packages. The real effects are indirect: (1) if ICD-11 criteria are more inclusive, more diagnosed individuals generate more autism-service claims; (2) ICD-11's granularity could eventually support severity-indexed payment models; (3) the transition window creates administrative risk — dual coding, coder retraining, EHR/postcoordination mapping — rather than benefit-design change. For **sensory-focused presentations specifically**: neither ICD-10-CM nor ICD-11 contains a sensory-specific ASD code, sensory features are not required for diagnosis under either manual, and sensory integration therapy remains inconsistently covered and is generally not a reimbursed ASD-specific service.

---

## Overall Conclusion

DSM-5 and ICD-11 converged on the same two-domain autism construct and on elevating sensory processing from an "associated feature" (DSM-IV/ICD-10) to a core diagnostic element — the single most important change for sensory-focused presentations in both systems. They diverge in operationalization: DSM-5's sensory criterion is explicit and equally weighted but fenced by a 2-of-4 RRB threshold and a monothetic 3-of-3 social requirement; ICD-11's sensory wording is broader ("lifelong excessive and persistent... actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures... heat, cold or pain") and unburdened by minimum counts, at the cost of precision (~304 permissible combinations). The quantified evidence to date indicts DSM-5 for **under-diagnosis** (31–37% loss; 56% adult retention; IQ ≥ 70 sensitivity 0.46) while ICD-11's converse **over-diagnosis risk remains a well-argued but unmeasured hypothesis** — making the absence of a blinded head-to-head validation study the field's most pressing gap. Guideline bodies have split the difference (NICE accepts both; APA holds DSM-5; WHO advances ICD-11; AAP stays DSM-5-anchored and rejects standalone SPD), advocacy organizations lean toward ICD-11-style inclusivity without formal endorsement, and reimbursement everywhere still flows through ICD-10-era codes, so the criteria debate currently affects **who gets diagnosed**, not yet **how anyone gets paid**.

# Rubber Leaf Inc. (RLEA): Gross Margin Analysis of the Direct-to-Indirect Supply Transition, Q1 2023 vs. Q1 2024

## Direct Answer

Rubber Leaf's reported gross margin collapsed from **+2.86% in Q1 2023 to −6.65% in Q1 2024, a year-over-year deterioration of 9.52 percentage points**. However, this headline figure badly overstates the operational damage. Excluding the one-time **$190,703 loss on factory relocation** from total cost of sales, Q1 2024's adjusted gross margin is **−0.20%** — essentially breakeven. The relocation charge alone accounts for **6.45 percentage points (~68%) of the 9.52-point decline**; the residual **−3.06 points (~32%)** is structural, reflecting the complete loss of the ~6%-margin direct supply channel and its replacement by a related-party indirect channel earning ~0–1%. The verdict: **the margin collapse is roughly two-thirds temporary transition cost and one-third genuine mix-driven erosion. The indirect model itself was not broken — it held at approximately breakeven in both periods — but the company's core profitability engine is structurally weaker because it has lost its only meaningful gross-profit contributor and is carrying a new factory's fixed costs while awaiting recertification of the direct channel.**

All figures are as filed in Rubber Leaf's Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2024 (filed May 14, 2024; SEC accession 0001493152-24-019316): [10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224019316/form10-q.htm) | [Statements of Operations, XBRL R4](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224019316/R4.htm).

---

## Step 1 — Baseline: Reported Gross Margin and Year-over-Year Change

### Underlying data (as filed)

| Line item | Q1 2023 | Q1 2024 | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sales — direct (third-party OEM) | $897,432 | $0 | −$897,432 |
| Sales — related parties (indirect, Xinsen Group) | $1,448,109 | $2,954,607 | +$1,506,498 |
| **Total revenue** | **$2,345,541** | **$2,954,607** | **+$609,066 (+26.0%)** |
| Cost of sales | $2,278,420 | $2,960,529 | +$682,109 |
| Loss on factory relocation | $0 | $190,703 | +$190,703 |
| **Total cost of sales** | **$2,278,420** | **$3,151,232** | **+$872,812** |
| **Gross profit (loss)** | **$67,121** | **$(196,625)** | **−$263,746** |

Internal consistency checks pass: $2,960,529 + $190,703 = $3,151,232; $2,954,607 − $3,151,232 = $(196,625); $2,345,541 − $2,278,420 = $67,121.

### Calculations

- **Q1 2023 gross margin** = $67,121 ÷ $2,345,541 = **+2.86%**
- **Q1 2024 reported gross margin** = $(196,625) ÷ $2,954,607 = **−6.65%**
- **YoY change = −6.65% − 2.86% = −9.52 percentage points**

This is the headline baseline: revenue **grew 26.0%** yet gross profit swung **$263,746** into loss. The revenue mix shifted violently during the transition — direct (non-related-party) sales to OEM eGT went to **zero** (from 38.3% of revenue), while indirect related-party sales through the Xinsen Group **more than doubled (+104.0%)**, moving the indirect model from 61.7% to **100% of revenue**.

| Revenue mix | Q1 2023 | % of total | Q1 2024 | % of total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Direct supply | $897,432 | 38.3% | $0 | 0.0% |
| Indirect supply | $1,448,109 | 61.7% | $2,954,607 | 100.0% |

---

## Step 2 — Adjusted Q1 2024 Gross Margin (Excluding the Relocation Loss)

Management presents the **$190,703 "Loss on factory relocation"** as a discrete line within total cost of sales, tied to the move to the new Fenghua, Ningbo facility (production suspended July 2023; relocation completed December 2023). Removing it isolates the underlying operating cost structure:

- Adjusted cost of sales = $3,151,232 − $190,703 = **$2,960,529**
- Adjusted gross profit = $2,954,607 − $2,960,529 = **$(5,922)**
- **Adjusted gross margin = −$5,922 ÷ $2,954,607 = −0.20%**

### Reported vs. adjusted comparison

| Measure | Q1 2023 reported | Q1 2024 reported | Q1 2024 adjusted (ex-relocation) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Revenue | $2,345,541 | $2,954,607 | $2,954,607 |
| Total cost of sales | $2,278,420 | $3,151,232 | $2,960,529 |
| Gross profit (loss) | $67,121 | $(196,625) | $(5,922) |
| **Gross margin** | **+2.86%** | **−6.65%** | **−0.20%** |
| Change vs. Q1 2023 baseline | — | **−9.52 pp** | **−3.06 pp** |

The gap between reported (−6.65%) and adjusted (−0.20%) margin is **6.45 percentage points** ($190,703 ÷ $2,954,607) — the pure effect of the one-time charge.

---

## Step 3 — Decomposing the 9.52-Point Swing

| Driver | Margin impact | Share of decline |
|---|---:|---:|
| One-time factory relocation loss | **−6.45 pp** | **~68%** |
| Loss of the ~6%-margin direct model's gross profit (~$54K on $897,432) | ~−2.2 pp | ~24% |
| Operational slippage within the indirect model (~1% → ~0%; cost growth outpacing revenue) | ~−0.9 pp | ~8% |
| **Total** | **−9.52 pp** | 100% |

A dollar bridge of the $263,746 gross-profit decline confirms the arithmetic: revenue added +$609,066; core cost of sales consumed −$682,109; the relocation charge took −$190,703. Note that **core cost of sales grew +29.9% against +26.0% revenue growth** — costs modestly outran revenue even after stripping relocation, which is the fingerprint of the residual structural erosion.

### Segment economics explain the structural component

The filing's business-line schedule ([R27](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224019316/R27.htm)) tags Q1 2023 gross margins at approximately **6% for the direct model and 1% for the indirect model**. Those tags reconcile with the dollar figures (implied GP ≈ $53,846 + $14,481 ≈ $68,327 vs. reported $67,121, rounding aside) and establish a critical fact: **in Q1 2023, essentially all of Rubber Leaf's gross profit came from the direct channel.** The indirect channel was already a ~1%-margin, pass-through-style business. In Q1 2024 the indirect model ran at ~0% — a like-for-like deterioration of only about a point. The dominant *operational* damage was therefore the **absence** of the high-margin direct business, not a collapse in the indirect business the company retained. Management's own MD&A framing in the subsequent filing attributes the margin decline to "generating less sales from its direct supply model which has a higher gross profit margin" ([Q2 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224032199/form10-q.htm)).

*(Caveat: the same XBRL exhibit tags Q1 2024 total gross margin at "7%," which is flatly inconsistent with the reported $196,625 gross loss. That percentage tag appears mis-scaled and should be disregarded; the dollar figures are internally consistent and are the reliable basis for all calculations here.)*

---

## Step 4 — Is This Temporary or Fundamental? Cross-Quarter Evidence

Three pieces of evidence from later filings sharpen the diagnosis:

**1. The relocation cost is genuinely transient.** The quarterly trajectory shows it winding down to zero:

| Period | Factory relocation loss |
|---|---:|
| Q1 2024 | $190,703 |
| Q2 2024 | $167,964 |
| Q3 2024 | $882 |
| Nine months ended Sept 30, 2024 | $359,549 |

*(Source: [Q3 2024 10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224045919/form10-q.htm), filed November 14, 2024.)* This validates treating the Q1 charge — 68% of the margin decline — as a one-time transition cost.

**2. But the fixed-cost problem is not transient.** In Q3 2024 a new line appeared: **"Loss on idle capacity" of $161,903**. The new plant is built but underutilized because direct supply production had still not resumed — pending IATF/QS-16949 recertification of the new facility, eGT's client re-inspection, and resolution of EU tariff negotiations affecting eGT's China-built vehicles. Reported gross margins in Q2 and Q3 2024 were **−8.08%** (−$158,157 on $1,957,758) and **−9.04%** (−$181,127 on $2,003,681) respectively — *worse* than Q1 even as relocation costs vanished, because idle-capacity losses replaced them. Depreciation and amortization rose 38% YoY in Q1 ($120,028 → $165,532) as the new facility's fixed costs came on line.

**3. The strain is visible below the gross line.** Q1 2024 net loss widened to **$(725,110)** from $(199,320); G&A doubled to $391,649; interest expense tripled to $122,535; and stockholders' equity turned **negative at $(1,017,091)** as of March 31, 2024. Segment operating results show the **direct segment lost $(72,840) on zero revenue** (idle carrying costs of the halted operation) while the **corporate segment's operating loss exploded from $(39,793) to $(499,437)** — a larger driver of the operating-loss swing than gross-margin dynamics. An opex bridge of the Q1 operating loss (−$174,658 → −$596,984, worse by $422,326) attributes $263,746 to gross profit and $158,580 to higher operating expenses (G&A +$196,737, partly offset by selling expense −$38,157).

---

## Interpretation: Strengthening or Weakening the Core Profitability Engine?

**The pivot has not broken the indirect model, but it has left Rubber Leaf with a structurally thinner, currently non-viable margin profile.** Three conclusions follow from the dual analysis:

1. **The indirect model is unit-economic-neutral, not value-destroying.** It operated at ~1% gross margin in Q1 2023 and ~0% in Q1 2024 — approximately breakeven in both periods. On an adjusted basis, Q1 2024 cost of sales was $1.002 per $1.000 of revenue. The ~3-point residual margin decline is mostly a **mix effect** (losing the 6%-margin direct business), not a failure of the channel the company kept.

2. **The headline −6.65% overstates operational damage by roughly 2:1.** About two-thirds of the swing is a disclosed, one-time relocation charge that was substantially resolved by Q3 2024 ($882 in that quarter). Treating Q1 2024's reported margin as the new run-rate would be a significant analytical error.

3. **However, the adjusted −0.20% is not a sustainable steady state either.** It still embeds idle-capacity drag and elevated depreciation from the new plant, and it confirms that an indirect-only Rubber Leaf earns essentially no gross profit. The Q3 idle-capacity charge demonstrates the relocation's costs have merely *changed form* — from moving expenses to underutilization losses — until direct production resumes.

**The path back to gross profitability depends on three contingencies, not on the relocation charge rolling off:** (a) completion of IATF/QS-16949 recertification and eGT re-approval so the ~6%-margin direct channel restarts; (b) resolution of the EU tariff uncertainty that delayed eGT orders; and/or (c) renegotiated economics or scale in the indirect channel sufficient to lift it above its structural 0–1% ceiling. If the direct model resumes, the adjusted margin trajectory should improve materially; if it does not, Rubber Leaf remains a near-breakeven gross-margin business carrying a new factory's fixed costs — a position that is already eroding the balance sheet (negative equity of ~$1.0 million) and will require additional capital.

---

## Risks, Caveats, and Data-Integrity Notes

- **Related-party concentration.** 100% of Q1 2024 revenue flowed through the Xinsen Group (Shanghai Xinsen and Xinsen Sealing Products Hangzhou), entities historically tied to CEO/Chairperson Xingxiu Hua, who reduced her Shanghai Xinsen stake from 90% to 15% effective October 1, 2022 (per the significant accounting policies note, [R30](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1893657/000149315224019316/R30.htm)). Thin pass-through margins through a related-party intermediary raise quality-of-revenue and transfer-pricing considerations that a pure margin calculation cannot capture.
- **The adjusted margin is a non-GAAP analytical construct.** Management classified the relocation loss within total cost of sales; the −0.20% figure would not appear in the filed statements. That said, the charge is explicitly broken out as its own line, making the adjustment unambiguous.
- **Segment percentage tags for 2024 are unreliable** (the "7%" total gross margin tag contradicts the reported gross loss); all analysis here rests on the internally consistent dollar figures. Segment-level margin splits (~6%/~1%) are based on rounded whole-percent tags and should be treated as approximate.
- **Not a like-for-like comparison.** With zero direct revenue in Q1 2024, the YoY comparison conflates relocation disruption, mix shift, and any underlying cost inflation; the −3.06 pp "structural" residual contains all three, not purely indirect-model economics.
- **Liquidity/going-concern risk is real but outside the gross-margin frame.** Widening net losses, tripled interest expense, and negative equity mean the company must fund continued losses while awaiting recertification — the timing of which remains uncertain.

---

## Bottom Line

**Year-over-year gross margin change: −9.52 percentage points (+2.86% → −6.65%). Q1 2024 gross margin excluding the $190,703 factory relocation loss: −0.20%, versus −6.65% reported — a 6.45-point gap.** Approximately two-thirds of the headline collapse is a genuinely one-time transition cost (confirmed by its wind-down to $882 by Q3 2024), and one-third is a permanent-looking mix effect from losing the ~6%-margin direct channel. The strategic pivot is best characterized as **temporarily obscured by relocation noise but structurally weakening**: Rubber Leaf's retained indirect engine runs at breakeven, and until the direct supply model is recertified and restarted — or indirect economics improve — the company's core profitability engine produces no meaningful gross profit while absorbing a new facility's fixed costs, as the Q3 2024 idle-capacity losses make clear.

# Selecting a Farm Management & Traceability Platform for a 5,000-Farmer Coffee Cooperative (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)

## Bottom line up front

**The question as framed contains a trap: neither AtSource nor "FairTrace" is a farm-management platform your cooperative can purchase.** AtSource is Olam/ofi's buyer-facing sustainability dashboard, available only inside Olam Group supply chains (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html). "FairTrace" is actually two Fairtrade-owned systems — **Fairtrace** (mandatory transaction reporting for all Fairtrade-certified actors, ~6,000 organizations logging ~500,000 transactions/year) and **Plot Insights** (a free geolocation/EUDR tool for certified cocoa and coffee cooperatives, launched 2024) (https://www.flocert.net/behind-the-scenes-of-the-fairtrace-platform-3-questions-to-luis-pastor/, https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/Press-centre/fairtrade-digital-system-plot-insights-gives-fairtrade-cooperatives-an-eudr-readiness-edge.html). Both are *systems you must feed data into*, not operational tools you deploy.

**The recommended architecture is a layered stack:**

1. **Certification layer (free, mandatory):** Plot Insights + Fairtrace if Fairtrade-certified; Rainforest Alliance's MultiTrace/RACP regardless of what else you choose; EU TRACES for European buyers.
2. **GPS capture layer (free):** TerraTrac (TechnoServe) — open-source, offline-first, with authenticated Galileo positioning.
3. **Operational farm-management layer (the real procurement decision):** choose by budget —
   - **Ultra-low budget:** INATrace (open-source) → total ~$0.60–1.60/farmer/year including hosting and support
   - **Low budget, commercial support:** Koltiva KoltiTrace via a field-agent model → ~$2.92/farmer/year (~$14,600/year for 5,000 farmers), with operations in all three of your countries
   - **Full-featured:** Farmforce — the most mature certification workflows and proven in Ethiopian highland forest coffee, but pricing spans $2–31/farmer/year depending on tier ($10,000–155,000/year); requires a negotiated quote
4. **Farmer communication layer (budget separately):** no platform serves basic feature phones directly; plan for SMS receipts/advisories at $0.01–0.05/message and roughly one Android-equipped field agent per 300–700 farmers.

One-time costs dominate software costs: a full 5,000-plot mapping campaign runs roughly **$20,000 (~$4/farmer, ~$0.01/kg of exported coffee)** using trained local enumerators (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr).

## 1. Correcting the shortlist: what AtSource and "FairTrace" actually are

### Olam AtSource — a buyer's dashboard, not a cooperative tool

- AtSource is Olam Group's sustainability intelligence platform (launched 2018, now governed by ofi). Its methodology states it is **"open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains"** — an independent cooperative cannot subscribe (https://www.atsource.io/methodology.html). No public pricing exists; it follows a custom enterprise model bundled into the commercial relationship (https://netzerocompare.com/software/atsource).
- Traceability is to **farmer-group level** (AtSourceV and AtSource+), and first-mile data is collected by **ofi's own thousands of enumerators** using the proprietary OFIS Android app (GPS capture, offline sync, 9 languages, 21 countries, SMS farm-management plans to farmers) — farmers never touch the system (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/one-stop-tech-platform-yield-traceability-financial-access.html, https://dvi-ke.fao.org/digital_solutions_details.php?id=120).
- Its certification credentials are genuinely strong — co-designed projects with Rainforest Alliance (e.g., the 2017 Sui River Forest Reserve), a Living Income metric originally developed by RA, explicit 4C/Fairtrade premium tracking (13,000 farmers in Côte d'Ivoire), and SAI Platform FSA 3.0 Gold equivalence for AtSource+ — but these accrue to *buyers* of ofi coffee, not to your cooperative (https://www.atsource.io/dashboard.html, https://www.ofi.com/en-us/news-and-events/press-release/atsource-receives-equivalence-under-the-sai-platforms-farm-sustainability-assessment-fsa-3).

**Verdict:** Exclude AtSource from procurement. It is relevant only if a material share of your volume sells through ofi/Olam — in which case it costs you nothing directly, but you cede first-mile data control to ofi's enumerators. Fairtrade explicitly warns that trader-held geolocation data "may not be very accurate" and is often not shared back with cooperatives — an argument for owning your data (https://www.fairtrade.net/en/get-involved/news/heres-how-fairtrade-is-supporting-farmers-and-businesses-eudr).

### Fairtrace + Plot Insights — mandatory Fairtrade infrastructure, not farm management

- **Fairtrace** is FLOCERT's web-based "report and verify" transaction platform (one party reports a sale, the counterparty confirms). It is **required of all Fairtrade-certified supply chain actors** and tracks volumes, Fairtrade Price, and Premium payments. It has no farmer-facing component and no GPS capability (https://www.flocert.net/app/uploads/2023/07/SAM-FairtraceUserGuide-TR-19-en.pdf).
- **Plot Insights** is the mapping counterpart: producer organizations upload plot data as points (<4 ha) or polygons (≥4 ha) at six decimal places in .kml, GeoJSON, Shapefile, Excel, or CSV; the system runs 20+ automated quality validations, provides deforestation-risk analysis powered by Satelligence (Sentinel-1/2 + Landsat, 10 m resolution, 81–93% accuracy across South America, Africa, Asia), and exports **EUDR-ready GeoJSON for the EU TRACES due-diligence platform**. The **GeoLink API** connects Plot Insights to Fairtrace sales contracts for consent-based sharing with buyers (Fairtrace-side geolocation exchange from October 2026) (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf, https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf).
- It satisfies Fairtrade's EUDR-aligned standards (Coffee 3.1.6, Cocoa 3.4.5), is **free for all certified cocoa and coffee producer organizations**, and its interface supports **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, and Vietnamese** — the only platform reviewed with a published language list covering all three of your countries (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf). Scale context: 900+ Fairtrade cocoa/coffee cooperatives representing ~1 million farmers; ~70% of Fairtrade coffee is sold into Europe, making the EUDR function central.

**Verdict:** If you are (or become) Fairtrade-certified, adopt Plot Insights + Fairtrace immediately — they are free, mandatory, and cover your EUDR geolocation compliance layer. But they do not manage farmer registries, harvest collection, payments, internal control system (ICS) inspections, or Rainforest Alliance workflows. You still need an operational platform.

## 3. Criterion 1: Usability for farmers with basic phones

**The most important honest finding: no credible platform lets a farmer on a basic feature phone operate a farm-management workflow.** The universal industry model is:

- **Cooperative field staff carry Android phones** running the offline capture app (plan for roughly **1 agent per 300–700 farmers**, per Farmforce's design assumptions — https://www.klimaantropologen.no/farmforceconnect).
- **Farmers receive SMS** delivery confirmations, payment notifications, price alerts, and agronomic advisories, plus **printed QR-coded receipts** at collection points (Farmforce supports Bluetooth receipt printers; two-way SMS is documented in its CGIAR profile — https://bigdata.cgiar.org/digital-intervention/farmforce/).
- **Farmforce Connect** (farmer app, pilot stage) was purpose-built for low-spec phones, low literacy, minimal storage, unstable connectivity, and once-a-day sync to limit data costs (https://farmforce.com/products/farmer-app/).
- **Koltiva's FarmCloud** (~$1/farmer/year) gives farmers data access and a chatbot; field teams ("KoltiSkills") train farmers in local languages — valuable for low-literacy members (https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/2024-12/Koltiva%20-%20ILO%20AI%20%26%20Agriculture%20Forum.pdf).
- **Fairfood Trace** is the strongest explicit low-tech design: farmers carry NFC cards; collectors run the app (https://fairfood.mintlify.app/introduction).
- **AgUnity** goes furthest on literacy (large colorful icons tested with illiterate farmers, offline QR transactions) but requires buying each farmer a ~$54–75 Android phone — replacing the feature phone rather than supporting it.

**Practical implication:** budget for (a) agent devices, (b) a bulk-SMS/USSD layer ($0.01–0.05/message; USSD via local telecoms is an add-on no shortlisted platform bundles natively), and (c) paper/QR receipts at buying stations. Do not select a platform based on a promised farmer app unless it explicitly supports feature phones.

## 4. Criterion 2: GPS plot mapping in mountainous terrain

**The physics, not the platform, is the constraint.** Consumer smartphone GNSS delivers **3–10 m accuracy** in open sky, degrading under shade canopy and in steep valleys (signal obstruction, multipath, poor satellite geometry). A 2026 academic benchmark of mobile GNSS apps found the best performer at ~3.0 m RMSE against a ≤5 m fit-for-purpose threshold for rural land administration; unassisted devices under tree canopy show ~11–12% area-measurement error — acceptable for compliance, but material if you use area for yield or premium calculations (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12518-026-00785-0, https://www.50x2030.org/sites/default/files/resources/documents/2026-05/IDU-cd6fedd9-8358-44d8-a677-06eb2dba3cb6.pdf).

**Regulatory thresholds your platform must encode from day one:**
- **EUDR:** a single geolocation point suffices for plots **≤4 ha**; **polygons are mandatory for plots >4 ha**; both at **six decimal places** (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/fairthrive/Geolocation%20data%20requirements%20EUDR.pdf).
- **Rainforest Alliance:** group-certified small farms must have **35% of farms mapped as polygons at the first certification audit and 100% by the second audit cycle** (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/it/management-annex-v12).
- Since **16 June 2025**, EUDR-aligned requirements (polygons ≥4 ha, six-decimal geolocation, legality evidence) are integrated assessments for all RA coffee/cocoa farm certificate holders, with an EUDR Data Sharing Policy governing buyer access (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/eudr-data-sharing-policy).

**Platform performance in steep terrain (evidence-ranked):**
1. **OriginTrace** — best documented result: 99.9% valid GPS across 11,348 plots in Rwanda's mountainous Lake Kivu coffee belt, with GPS audit dashboards.
2. **Farmforce** — proven at the hard extreme: 4,550 ha of *forest* coffee in Ethiopia's Bale/Illubabor highlands; its offline-first architecture was "the only reason the pilot produced a coherent dataset" (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/). Built-in polygon drawing, shapefile import, Global Forest Watch deforestation overlay.
3. **TerraTrac** — uniquely partners with **EUSPA for authenticated Galileo signals** (spoof-proof geolocation, meaningful for EU buyers); piloted in Kenya's highlands; point (<4 ha) / polygon (≥4 ha) logic mirrors EUDR; CSV/GeoJSON export (https://www.technoserve.org/tns-labs/terratrac-eudr-compliance/).
4. **Koltiva** — demonstrated highland coffee mapping (Gayo, Toraja; 143.5 ha surveyed in the Goodel trial) and EUDR-aligned capture "even in remote areas."
5. **Plot Insights** — doesn't improve field GPS but provides the best *post-hoc* validation: Satelligence satellite checks (10 m, 81–93% accuracy) catch implausible or deforestation-overlapping plots.

**Field protocol (applies to every platform):** average waypoints 20–30 seconds per vertex, map mid-morning for better satellite geometry, wait for the accuracy readout to stabilize, walk boundaries slowly, capture at plot edges under open sky where possible; budget **~$50–100 per external GNSS antenna** for the steepest/shadiest zones; export GeoJSON for post-processing in free QGIS; use UTM-projected area calculations on slopes (https://www.indonesia-coffee.com/en/articles/indonesian-coffee-eudr-compliance-2025-complete-guide-G5j8W_, https://plotvera.com/guides/eudr-smallholder-geolocation).

## 5. Criterion 3: Certification integration (Rainforest Alliance, Fairtrade, EUDR)

**Critical structural fact:** Rainforest Alliance requires all certified-volume transactions to be reported in **its own platform — MultiTrace within the RA Certification Platform (RACP), now migrating to a new traceability platform via "MyRA"** — at the latest two weeks after quarter-end, with the Sustainability Differential (SD) and Sustainability Investments (SI) recorded separately; traceability models are Identity Preserved, Segregation, and Mass Balance (https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Full-Mutual-Recognition-and-Traceability-for-Coffee-February-2022.pdf, https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/traceability-annex). **No third-party farm platform has a documented native MultiTrace integration** — budget staff time for dual reporting regardless of your choice. The same is true for Fairtrade: Fairtrace reporting is mandatory for certified trade.

| Platform | Fairtrade | Rainforest Alliance | Organic | EUDR/geolocation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AtSource | Premiums tracked (via ofi only) | Co-designed projects; FSA 3.0 equivalence | Yes | Yes (within ofi chains) |
| Fairtrace + Plot Insights | **Native — it *is* the Fairtrade system** | No | No | **Native — GeoJSON to EU TRACES** |
| Farmforce | Explicit module | **Explicit module; RA mapping-status registry; GFW deforestation checks** | Yes | Yes |
| Koltiva KoltiTrace | Complementary | Complementary (explicitly positioned alongside RA/Fairtrade) | Configurable | Yes — core strength |
| Sirio (Nuup) | ICS digital forms | ICS digital forms | ICS digital forms | EUDR-ready polygons |
| SourceTrace | Built-in module | Configurable | Built-in module | Yes |
| TerraTrac | Feeds data | Feeds data | Feeds data | **Primary purpose** |
| INATrace | Customizable (open-source) | Customizable | Customizable | Yes — FAO WHISP check |
| OriginTrace | No native link | No native link | GI-aligned | EUDR-ready |

**Interpretation:** Farmforce is the strongest *single-vendor* answer for running both Fairtrade and RA internal control systems; the open-source options (INATrace) can replicate any audit checklist but require configuration capacity; every option still requires separate data entry into Fairtrace and MultiTrace.

## 6. Criterion 4: Multi-language support

Documented language evidence is thin across the industry — demand written confirmation during procurement.

- **Plot Insights:** the only published list covering all three origins — **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese**.
- **TerraTrac:** **French, Spanish, Amharic, Oromo** (Swahili in development) — the best documented Ethiopia fit; Bahasa Indonesia absent but the open-source codebase allows community localization (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/paul-stewart-1165826_terratrac-activity-7214208074289475584-iPA8).
- **Farmforce:** staff app in English, Spanish, French, Portuguese; deployments across 30+ countries including Indonesia and East Africa; farmer app designed for low literacy (reduces language dependence). Amharic/Oromo/Bahasa interface support not publicly itemized (https://solevant.com/software/farmforce).
- **Koltiva:** operates with localized teams in Indonesia, Colombia, and Ethiopia (15 customer-success offices), implying Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish, and English capability, but no published language list (https://www.koltiva.com/).
- **Sirio:** Spanish-first (Mexico/Guatemala/Honduras) — strong for Colombia, unusable elsewhere.
- **INATrace:** English only out of the box; localization possible given AGPL-3.0 source access.
- **AgUnity:** deployed with local-language/icon-based interfaces in Ethiopia (Amharic context) and PNG.

**Action:** make Spanish + Bahasa Indonesia + Amharic/Oromo interface *and support* availability a contractual requirement, with screenshots, before signature.

## 7. Criterion 5: Offline functionality

All field-capture platforms reviewed offer genuine offline operation; the Fairtrade tools are the exception:

| Platform | Offline capability |
|---|---|
| TerraTrac | **Full offline**; CSV/GeoJSON export; sync on connectivity (https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile) |
| Farmforce | **Offline-first**, proven in patchy 2G/3G Ethiopian forest zones |
| Koltiva (FarmGate/FarmXtension) | Online/offline capture "even in remote areas" |
| Sirio | "Does not even require an internet connection to work" (https://www.ensambles.coffee/post/sirio-empowering-mexican-coffee-farmers) |
| INATrace | **Full offline** (local Realm database, sync later) |
| OriginTrace | **Offline-first** on affordable Android hardware |
| AgUnity | Fully offline QR peer-to-peer transactions |
| Fairfood Trace | Explicit offline onboarding + transactions |
| **Fairtrace / Plot Insights** | **Web-based — no offline field capture.** Prepare files offline (SW Maps, QField, KoboCollect, or TerraTrac) and upload when connected |

This is a further argument for the layered architecture: capture offline in the field with TerraTrac or your operational platform, then upload validated files to Plot Insights from the cooperative office.

- **Training and ICS staffing:** consistently the largest hidden line item; none of the vendors price this transparently.
- Market context: cooperative-scale traceability SaaS generally runs €5,000–20,000/year (https://kolonell.com/en/blog/agri-cooperative-traceability-software-cost-amsterdam-2026).

## 9. Final recommendations

**Tier 1 — Ultra-low budget (~$0.60–1.60/farmer/year software; ~$25,000–30,000 Year 1 all-in):**
- Adopt **Plot Insights + Fairtrace** if Fairtrade-certified (mandatory anyway; covers EUDR geolocation and deforestation screening).
- Deploy **TerraTrac** on agent Androids for offline polygon capture (Galileo-authenticated; Amharic/Oromo/Spanish interfaces; add Bahasa via the open codebase).
- Run **INATrace** (or **Beyco** at €250–500/yr for a lighter option) as the cooperative-owned operational system for farmer registry, transactions, and QR traceability. Requires an IT-capable partner (NGO, GIZ-type program, or local developer) for hosting and customization — assess whether you have this; the long-term risk of free tools is upstream funding and maintenance capacity.

**Tier 2 — Low budget with commercial support (~$2.92/farmer/year):**
- **Koltiva KoltiTrace** via the field-agent model (50 agents), keeping FarmCloud notifications for all 5,000 members. The only candidate with published per-farmer economics *and* operating presence in Indonesia, Colombia, and Ethiopia. Verify in writing: current pricing (the handbook figures are 2020-era), offline sync behavior, and Spanish/Bahasa/Amharic interfaces.
- In Colombia only, evaluate **Sirio (Nuup)** as a near-free alternative if you can join its IDB-backed ecosystem.

**Tier 3 — Full-featured, if a buyer or donor co-funds (~$2–31/farmer/year):**
- **Farmforce** is the most defensible single platform across all six criteria: explicit Fairtrade + RA + Organic + GlobalGAP certification workflows, Global Forest Watch deforestation overlay, offline-first architecture proven in Ethiopian forest coffee, low-spec-phone design principles, SMS receipts, and Bluetooth receipt printing. Obtain a firm negotiated quote before committing — the spread between list and enterprise pricing is an order of magnitude.

**Regardless of tier:**
1. **Plan for dual/triple certification reporting** — MultiTrace (RA), Fairtrace (Fairtrade), TRACES (EU buyers) are obligations your farm platform feeds but cannot replace. Assign staff time accordingly.
2. **Contractually require GeoJSON export** of all your data from any vendor, so you can post-process in QGIS, upload to Plot Insights/RACP, and switch platforms without losing your plot registry. Data ownership should rest with the cooperative — the explicit principle behind Fairtrade's Plot Insights design.
3. **Pilot before scaling:** map 200–300 plots in your steepest, shadiest terrain (e.g., Ethiopian forest coffee zones, Colombian Andes slopes, Gayo/Toraja highlands) with the shortlisted tool, measure polygon validity rates against satellite checks, and only then commit. OriginTrace's 99.9% GPS-validity benchmark in Rwandan highlands is the standard to hold vendors to.
4. **Budget for people, not software:** mapping campaign (~$4/farmer), agent devices and antennas, SMS credits, and ICS training will exceed software license costs on any Tier 1–2 configuration.

**Key open uncertainties to close before contracting:** current Koltiva and Farmforce pricing; written confirmation of Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish, and Amharic/Oromo interface and support; GPS accuracy performance validated in *your* terrain (no vendor publishes metre-level error figures); and Fairtrade certification fees applicable to your members, which sit outside this software comparison.
